KineticLangevin/Geometry.lean.title: A transformed Euclidean norm for position and velocity differences
KineticLangevin/Geometry.lean.summary:
Throughout this section \(\mathcal H\) is a real inner product space with norm \(\|\cdot\|\); completeness is not needed. In the applications \(\mathcal H=\mathbb R^p\), or \(\mathcal H\) is the space \(L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^p)\) of square-integrable random vectors with norm \(\|X\|=(\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2)^{1/2}\). A phase point is a pair \(s=(v,x)\in \mathcal H\times \mathcal H\), velocity first and position second. For real numbers \(\gamma\) (the friction) and \(a\) (a shift) define the linear map

\[T_{\gamma,a}(v,x)=\bigl(v+(\gamma-a)x,\;-v-ax\bigr),\]

the transformed energy \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)=\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2\), where \((y,z)=T_{\gamma,a}s\), and the transformed norm \(\|s\|_{\gamma,a}=\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)^{1/2}\), the norm of \(T_{\gamma,a}s\) in the Euclidean product \(\mathcal H\oplus \mathcal H\), whose norm is \(\|(y,z)\|=(\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2)^{1/2}\). In the notation of Dalalyan and Riou-Durand, \(a=\lambda_-\) and \(\gamma-a=\lambda_+\) (the shift is called \(v\) in their Theorem 1); applied to the difference of two coupled trajectories, \(T_{\gamma,a}\) produces the pair \((\psi_t,z_t)\) of the proof of their Proposition 1.

We prove that \(T_{\gamma,a}\) is invertible when \(\gamma\neq2a\), with explicit inverse; that \((\gamma-2a)^2\|x\|^2\le2\,\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v,x)\); that a phase point with zero velocity has energy \(((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)\|x\|^2\); that \(\|\cdot\|_{\gamma,a}\) satisfies the triangle inequality; and, for the shift \(a=0\), the projection bounds \(\|v\|\le\|s\|_{\gamma,0}\) and \(\|x\|\le(\sqrt2/\gamma)\|s\|_{\gamma,0}\) together with the identity \(\|(0,x)\|_{\gamma,0}=\gamma\|x\|\). These facts are used throughout the contraction arguments for the kinetic diffusion and its discretizations: the discrepancy between two coupled phase points is measured in \(\|\cdot\|_{\gamma,a}\), the initial discrepancy of a coupling with equal velocities is expressed through the position distance, and the final estimate is projected back onto the position coordinate.

steps.title: The transformation and the nonnegativity of its energy
steps.body:
Definitions. For \(\gamma,a\in\mathbb R\) and \(s=(v,x)\in \mathcal H\times \mathcal H\) put

\[T_{\gamma,a}(v,x)=\bigl(v+(\gamma-a)x,\;-v-ax\bigr),\qquad \mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v,x)=\|v+(\gamma-a)x\|^2+\|-v-ax\|^2 .\]

Thus \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)=\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2\) with \((y,z)=T_{\gamma,a}s\). The map \(T_{\gamma,a}\) is linear, because each coordinate of its value is a linear combination of \(v\) and \(x\) with real coefficients.

Claim. For all \(\gamma,a\in\mathbb R\) and all \(s\in \mathcal H\times \mathcal H\), \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)\ge0\).

Proof. The norms \(\|y\|\) and \(\|z\|\) are real numbers, so \(\|y\|^2\ge0\) and \(\|z\|^2\ge0\). A sum of two nonnegative numbers is nonnegative. \(\square\)

No condition on \(\gamma\) or \(a\) is needed here. The energy vanishes exactly on the kernel of \(T_{\gamma,a}\), which by the next step is \(\{0\}\) when \(\gamma\neq2a\). In the contraction arguments \(s\) is the difference of two phase points driven by the same noise. For \(a=\lambda_-\) the two coordinates \(v+\lambda_+x\) and \(-v-\lambda_-x\) of \(T_{\gamma,a}s\) are the quantities \(\psi_t\) and \(z_t\) of the paper's proof of Proposition 1, and \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)\) is the squared Euclidean norm of the vector \((\psi_t,z_t)\) used there.

steps.title: Inverse formulas for position and velocity
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma,a\in\mathbb R\), \(s=(v,x)\in \mathcal H\times \mathcal H\) and \((y,z)=T_{\gamma,a}s\). Then

\[y+z=(\gamma-2a)\,x.\qquad(1)\]

If moreover \(\gamma-2a\neq0\), then

\[x=(\gamma-2a)^{-1}(y+z),\qquad v=-(\gamma-2a)^{-1}\bigl(a\,y+(\gamma-a)\,z\bigr).\qquad(2)\]

Proof. By the definition of \(T_{\gamma,a}\) and distributivity of scalar multiplication, \((\gamma-a)x=\gamma x-ax\), so

\[y+z=v+\gamma x-ax-v-ax=(\gamma-2a)\,x,\]

which is (1). If \(\gamma-2a\neq0\), multiply (1) by \((\gamma-2a)^{-1}\). Since \(c\,(d\,x)=(cd)\,x\) for real \(c,d\) and \((\gamma-2a)^{-1}(\gamma-2a)=1\), we get \((\gamma-2a)^{-1}(y+z)=1\cdot x=x\), the first formula of (2). For the second, expand both terms:

\[\begin{aligned} a\,y+(\gamma-a)\,z&=a v+a(\gamma-a)x-(\gamma-a)v-(\gamma-a)a\,x\\ &=\bigl(a-(\gamma-a)\bigr)v=-(\gamma-2a)\,v , \end{aligned}\]

because the two position terms cancel. Multiplying by \(-(\gamma-2a)^{-1}\) and using \(\bigl(-(\gamma-2a)^{-1}\bigr)\bigl(-(\gamma-2a)\bigr)=(\gamma-2a)^{-1}(\gamma-2a)=1\) gives \(-(\gamma-2a)^{-1}(a\,y+(\gamma-a)z)=v\). \(\square\)

On each pair \((v,x)\) the map \(T_{\gamma,a}\) acts through the \(2\times2\) real matrix with rows \((1,\ \gamma-a)\) and \((-1,\ -a)\), whose determinant is \(-a+(\gamma-a)=\gamma-2a\). Formula (2) is the product with the inverse matrix \((\gamma-2a)^{-1}\) times the matrix with rows \((-a,\ -(\gamma-a))\) and \((1,\ 1)\). The hypothesis \(\gamma\neq2a\) excludes the singular shift \(a=\gamma/2\), at which \(z=-y\) and position and velocity can no longer be recovered; the paper restricts the shift to \([0,\gamma/2)\), where \(\gamma-2a>0\).

steps.title: A bound for the position projection
steps.body:
Claim. For all \(\gamma,a\in\mathbb R\) and all \(s=(v,x)\in \mathcal H\times \mathcal H\),

\[(\gamma-2a)^2\,\|x\|^2\le2\,\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s).\]

Proof. Write \((y,z)=T_{\gamma,a}s\). By the triangle inequality in \(\mathcal H\),

\[\|y+z\|\le\|y\|+\|z\|.\qquad(1)\]

Both sides of (1) are nonnegative, and for real numbers \(0\le u\le w\) we have \(u^2\le w^2\). Squaring (1) therefore gives

\[\|y+z\|^2\le\|y\|^2+2\|y\|\,\|z\|+\|z\|^2\le2\bigl(\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2\bigr)=2\,\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s),\qquad(2)\]

where the second inequality is \(2\|y\|\,\|z\|\le\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2\), equivalent to \((\|y\|-\|z\|)^2\ge0\). By identity (1) of the previous step, \(y+z=(\gamma-2a)x\). Homogeneity of the norm gives \(\|(\gamma-2a)x\|=|\gamma-2a|\,\|x\|\), hence \(\|y+z\|^2=|\gamma-2a|^2\|x\|^2=(\gamma-2a)^2\|x\|^2\). Substituting this into the left-hand side of (2) proves the claim. \(\square\)

No sign condition is used: for \(\gamma=2a\) the claim is the nonnegativity of the energy. When \(\gamma\neq2a\), dividing by \((\gamma-2a)^2\) and taking square roots gives \(\|x\|\le\sqrt2\,\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)^{1/2}/|\gamma-2a|\), the factor \(\sqrt2/(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)\) at the end of the paper's proof of Proposition 1. The constant \(2\) in (2) cannot be improved, since equality holds when \(y=z\).

Squaring (1) and adding this square is precisely the computation in the proof; nlinarith finds it by multiplying the supplied inequalities in pairs.

steps.title: The energy of a phase point with zero velocity
steps.body:
Claim. For all \(\gamma,a\in\mathbb R\) and \(x\in \mathcal H\),

\[\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(0,x)=\bigl((\gamma-a)^2+a^2\bigr)\|x\|^2.\]

Proof. With \(v=0\) the definition gives \(T_{\gamma,a}(0,x)=\bigl((\gamma-a)x,\,-(ax)\bigr)\). The norm is invariant under negation and homogeneous, so

\[\|(\gamma-a)x\|^2=|\gamma-a|^2\|x\|^2=(\gamma-a)^2\|x\|^2,\qquad\|-(ax)\|^2=|a|^2\|x\|^2=a^2\|x\|^2 .\]

Adding the two identities gives the claim. \(\square\)

In a synchronous coupling the two processes start with the same velocity, so the initial difference is \((0,x_0-x_0')\) and its transformed energy is \(((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)\|x_0-x_0'\|^2\). With \(a=\lambda_-\), \(\gamma-a=\lambda_+\) this is the factor \(\lambda_+^2+\lambda_-^2\) inside the prefactor \(\sqrt{2(\lambda_+^2+\lambda_-^2)}/(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)\) of the paper's Proposition 1: the initial transformed discrepancy is determined by the position coupling alone.

The remaining identity \((\gamma-a)^2\|x\|^2+a^2\|x\|^2=((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)\|x\|^2\) is closed by ring.

steps.title: Velocity control at zero shift and the Euclidean phase energy
steps.body:
Definition. The Euclidean phase energy of \(s=(v,x)\in \mathcal H\times \mathcal H\) is \(\|v\|^2+\|x\|^2\), the squared norm of \(s\) in the Euclidean product \(\mathcal H\oplus \mathcal H\).

Claim. For every \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\) and every \(s=(v,x)\in \mathcal H\times \mathcal H\),

\[\|v\|^2\le\mathcal E_{\gamma,0}(s).\]

Proof. For \(a=0\) we have \(\gamma-a=\gamma\) and \(ax=0\), so \(T_{\gamma,0}(v,x)=(v+\gamma x,\,-v)\). Since \(\|-v\|=\|v\|\),

\[\mathcal E_{\gamma,0}(s)=\|v+\gamma x\|^2+\|v\|^2\ge\|v\|^2,\]

because \(\|v+\gamma x\|^2\ge0\). \(\square\)

The bound holds for every real \(\gamma\). With zero shift the second transformed coordinate is the velocity itself (up to sign), which is why the velocity projection costs no constant; for a general shift one would use the inverse formula (2) of the second step instead. The Euclidean phase energy is recorded for comparison with the transformed energy; like the latter it is an explicit sum of squares.

  2. phaseEnergy s is ‖s.1‖ ^ 2 + ‖s.2‖ ^ 2. As with the transformed energy, it is written as a sum of squares so that it is the Euclidean, and not the maximum, norm of the product type. It is a definition only; no property of it is proved in this section.

steps.title: The transformed norm
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\mathcal H\oplus \mathcal H\) denote the product \(\mathcal H\times \mathcal H\) with the inner product \(\langle(y,z),(y',z')\rangle=\langle y,y'\rangle+\langle z,z'\rangle\), whose norm is \(\|(y,z)\|=(\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2)^{1/2}\). For \(\gamma,a\in\mathbb R\) define

\[\|s\|_{\gamma,a}=\bigl\|T_{\gamma,a}s\bigr\|_{\mathcal H\oplus \mathcal H},\qquad s\in \mathcal H\times \mathcal H.\]

Claim. For all \(\gamma,a\) and \(s\), \(\|s\|_{\gamma,a}\ge0\) and \(\|s\|_{\gamma,a}^2=\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)\).

Proof. The first statement holds because a norm is nonnegative. For the second, write \((y,z)=T_{\gamma,a}s\); by the formula for the norm of \(\mathcal H\oplus \mathcal H\), \(\|s\|_{\gamma,a}^2=\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2=\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)\). \(\square\)

The point of the definition is that \(\|\cdot\|_{\gamma,a}\) is the composition of a linear map with a genuine Hilbert-space norm, so it satisfies the triangle inequality (next step), whereas the energy \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}\), a squared quantity, does not. When \(\mathcal H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^p)\), \(\|s\|_{\gamma,a}\) is the root-mean-square transformed distance \(\bigl(\mathbb E[\|y\|_2^2+\|z\|_2^2]\bigr)^{1/2}\) between two coupled random phase points.

steps.title: Triangle inequalities and the passage from energy to norm
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma,a\in\mathbb R\) and \(s,r,t\in \mathcal H\times \mathcal H\), and write \(s=(v,x)\).

(i) \(T_{\gamma,a}(s+t)=T_{\gamma,a}s+T_{\gamma,a}t\).
(ii) \(\|s+t\|_{\gamma,a}\le\|s\|_{\gamma,a}+\|t\|_{\gamma,a}\).
(iii) \(\|s-t\|_{\gamma,a}\le\|s-r\|_{\gamma,a}+\|r-t\|_{\gamma,a}\).
(iv) If \(B\ge0\) and \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)\le B^2\), then \(\|s\|_{\gamma,a}\le B\).
(v) \(\|v\|\le\|s\|_{\gamma,0}\).

Proof. (i) Write \(t=(v',x')\). Distributing the scalars,

\[\begin{aligned} (v+v')+(\gamma-a)(x+x')&=\bigl(v+(\gamma-a)x\bigr)+\bigl(v'+(\gamma-a)x'\bigr),\\ -(v+v')-a(x+x')&=(-v-ax)+(-v'-ax'), \end{aligned}\]

which are the two coordinates of (i).

(ii) By (i) and the triangle inequality of the norm of \(\mathcal H\oplus \mathcal H\),

\[\|s+t\|_{\gamma,a}=\|T_{\gamma,a}s+T_{\gamma,a}t\|_{\mathcal H\oplus \mathcal H}\le\|T_{\gamma,a}s\|_{\mathcal H\oplus \mathcal H}+\|T_{\gamma,a}t\|_{\mathcal H\oplus \mathcal H}=\|s\|_{\gamma,a}+\|t\|_{\gamma,a}.\]

(iii) Since \(s-t=(s-r)+(r-t)\), (ii) applied to \(s-r\) and \(r-t\) gives (iii).

(iv) For real numbers \(u,w\ge0\) one has \(u^2\le w^2\) if and only if \(u\le w\) (the function \(u\mapsto u^2\) is increasing on \([0,\infty)\)). Apply this with \(u=\|s\|_{\gamma,a}\ge0\) and \(w=B\ge0\): by the previous step \(u^2=\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)\le B^2\), so \(u\le B\).

(v) By the velocity bound of the fifth step and the previous step, \(\|v\|^2\le\mathcal E_{\gamma,0}(s)=\|s\|_{\gamma,0}^2\). Both \(\|v\|\) and \(\|s\|_{\gamma,0}\) are nonnegative, so the same monotonicity gives \(\|v\|\le\|s\|_{\gamma,0}\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(B\ge0\) in (iv) is necessary: for \(B<0\) the bound \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s)\le B^2\) may hold while \(\|s\|_{\gamma,a}\le B\) fails. Inequality (iii) is used in the error analysis of the discretizations with \(s\) the numerical state, \(t\) the reference state and \(r\) an intermediate state, so that the error splits into the propagated old discrepancy and the error created in one step, both measured in the same norm.

steps.title: Position projection and equal-velocity initialization at zero shift
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\) and \(x\in \mathcal H\).

(i) If \(\gamma>0\), then \(\|x\|\le(\sqrt2/\gamma)\,\|s\|_{\gamma,0}\) for every \(s=(v,x)\in \mathcal H\times \mathcal H\).
(ii) If \(\gamma\ge0\), then \(\|(0,x)\|_{\gamma,0}=\gamma\,\|x\|\).

Proof. (i) The position bound of the third step with \(a=0\), together with \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,0}(s)=\|s\|_{\gamma,0}^2\), gives

\[\gamma^2\|x\|^2\le2\,\|s\|_{\gamma,0}^2=\bigl(\sqrt2\,\|s\|_{\gamma,0}\bigr)^2,\]

using \((\sqrt2)^2=2\). Since \(\gamma>0\), the number \(\gamma\|x\|\) is nonnegative, and \(\sqrt2\,\|s\|_{\gamma,0}\ge0\); comparing nonnegative squares yields \(\gamma\|x\|\le\sqrt2\,\|s\|_{\gamma,0}\). Dividing by \(\gamma>0\) preserves the inequality and gives (i).

(ii) The zero-velocity identity of the fourth step with \(a=0\) gives \(\|(0,x)\|_{\gamma,0}^2=(\gamma^2+0)\|x\|^2=(\gamma\|x\|)^2\). Both \(\|(0,x)\|_{\gamma,0}\) and \(\gamma\|x\|\) are nonnegative, the latter because \(\gamma\ge0\). Two nonnegative numbers with equal squares are equal, which proves (ii). \(\square\)

Together, (i) and (ii) produce the prefactor \(\sqrt2\) of the paper's Theorem 1 at shift \(0\): if a bound \(\|s_t\|_{\gamma,0}\le e^{-\beta t}\|s_0\|_{\gamma,0}\) holds for a coupled pair with initial difference \(s_0=(0,x_0)\), then \(\|x_t\|\le(\sqrt2/\gamma)e^{-\beta t}\gamma\|x_0\|=\sqrt2\,e^{-\beta t}\|x_0\|\). The prefactor is \(\sqrt2\), not the value \(\sqrt2/\gamma\) printed in display (exp1) of the paper; this is one of the corrections recorded in the reference audit. In iterated estimates the transformed norm is propagated through all steps and the position is projected only once, at the end, so the factor \(\sqrt2\) appears only once.

KineticLangevin/Contraction.lean.title: Decay of the transformed energy under curvature bounds
KineticLangevin/Contraction.lean.summary:
This section proves a deterministic decay estimate for the linear kinetic difference equation

\[v'(t)=-\gamma\,v(t)-H_t\,x(t),\qquad x'(t)=v(t),\]

where \(v,x\) are paths in a real inner product space \(\mathcal H\) and each \(H_t\) is a continuous linear operator on \(\mathcal H\) that is self-adjoint (\(\langle u,H_tw\rangle=\langle w,H_tu\rangle\)) and satisfies the quadratic-form bounds \(m\|u\|^2\le\langle u,H_tu\rangle\le M\|u\|^2\). This is the equation (ODE2) of Dalalyan and Riou-Durand: if \((V_t,L_t)\) and \((V'_t,L'_t)\) solve the kinetic Langevin equation with the same Brownian motion, then \(v=V-V'\) and \(x=L-L'\) solve it with \(H_t=\int_0^1\nabla^2f(L'_t+\theta(L_t-L'_t))\,d\theta\), and \(mI\preceq\nabla^2f\preceq MI\) gives the bounds on \(H_t\). The noise has cancelled, so the equation is an ordinary differential equation.

With the transformation \(T_{\gamma,a}\), the energy \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}\) and the norm \(\|\cdot\|_{\gamma,a}\) of the previous section, we prove: an exact identity for \((\gamma-2a)\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}\) in which the mixed terms cancel because \(H_t\) is self-adjoint; the differential inequality \(\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}\le K\,\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}\) with \(K=2\max\{a^2-m,\,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}/(\gamma-2a)\) whenever \(\gamma-2a>0\); the energy bound \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(t)\le\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(0)e^{Kt}\) by Grönwall's inequality; and, when \(v(0)=0\), the position bound of the paper's Proposition 1,

\[\|x(t)\|\le\frac{\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}}{\gamma-2a}\exp\Bigl\{\frac{\max\{a^2-m,\,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}}{\gamma-2a}\,t\Bigr\}\|x(0)\|.\]

Each estimate is proved both for two-sided derivatives and for right derivatives; the second version applies to paths defined by integral equations on \([0,T]\). The construction of the coupled stochastic solutions and the passage to Wasserstein distances are carried out in later sections.

steps.title: The energy derivative and the cancellation of mixed terms
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\gamma,a\in\mathbb R\), let \(H:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be a continuous linear operator and let \(s=(v,x)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\) with \((y,z)=T_{\gamma,a}s=(v+(\gamma-a)x,\,-v-ax)\). Put

\[D_{\gamma,a}(H;s)=2\,\langle y,\,-a v-Hx\rangle+2\,\langle z,\,(\gamma-a)v+Hx\rangle .\]

If \((v,x)\) solves \(v'=-\gamma v-Hx\), \(x'=v\), then \(y'=v'+(\gamma-a)x'=-av-Hx\) and \(z'=-v'-ax'=(\gamma-a)v+Hx\), so \(D_{\gamma,a}(H;s)=2\langle y,y'\rangle+2\langle z,z'\rangle\) is the derivative of \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}=\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2\) along the solution; this is proved in the fourth step.

Claim. Assume that \(H\) is self-adjoint: \(\langle u,Hw\rangle=\langle w,Hu\rangle\) for all \(u,w\in\mathcal H\). Then for all \(\gamma,a\in\mathbb R\) and all \(s\),

\[(\gamma-2a)\,D_{\gamma,a}(H;s)=2\Bigl(a^2\|y\|^2-\langle y,Hy\rangle+\langle z,Hz\rangle-(\gamma-a)^2\|z\|^2\Bigr).\]

Proof. Put \(c=\gamma-a\), so that \(a+c=\gamma\) and \(a-c=-(\gamma-2a)\). We express both sides through the numbers \(\|v\|^2\), \(\langle v,x\rangle\), \(\|x\|^2\), \(\langle v,Hv\rangle\), \(\langle v,Hx\rangle\), \(\langle x,Hx\rangle\), using bilinearity and symmetry of the real inner product and linearity of \(H\).

Left-hand side. Expanding,

\[\begin{aligned} \langle v+cx,\,-av-Hx\rangle&=-a\|v\|^2-\langle v,Hx\rangle-ac\langle v,x\rangle-c\langle x,Hx\rangle,\\ \langle -v-ax,\,cv+Hx\rangle&=-c\|v\|^2-\langle v,Hx\rangle-ac\langle v,x\rangle-a\langle x,Hx\rangle . \end{aligned}\]

Adding, multiplying by \(2\) and using \(a+c=\gamma\),

\[D_{\gamma,a}(H;s)=-2\bigl(\gamma\|v\|^2+2ac\langle v,x\rangle+2\langle v,Hx\rangle+\gamma\langle x,Hx\rangle\bigr).\qquad(1)\]

Right-hand side. We have \(\|v+cx\|^2=\|v\|^2+2c\langle v,x\rangle+c^2\|x\|^2\) and, using self-adjointness in the form \(\langle x,Hv\rangle=\langle v,Hx\rangle\),

\[\langle v+cx,\,H(v+cx)\rangle=\langle v,Hv\rangle+2c\langle v,Hx\rangle+c^2\langle x,Hx\rangle .\]

Since \(z=-(v+ax)\), the quantities \(\|z\|^2\) and \(\langle z,Hz\rangle\) have the same expansions with \(c\) replaced by \(a\). Therefore

\[\begin{aligned} &a^2\|y\|^2-\langle y,Hy\rangle+\langle z,Hz\rangle-c^2\|z\|^2\\ &\quad=a^2\bigl(\|v\|^2+2c\langle v,x\rangle+c^2\|x\|^2\bigr)-\bigl(\langle v,Hv\rangle+2c\langle v,Hx\rangle+c^2\langle x,Hx\rangle\bigr)\\ &\qquad+\bigl(\langle v,Hv\rangle+2a\langle v,Hx\rangle+a^2\langle x,Hx\rangle\bigr)-c^2\bigl(\|v\|^2+2a\langle v,x\rangle+a^2\|x\|^2\bigr)\\ &\quad=(a^2-c^2)\|v\|^2+2ac(a-c)\langle v,x\rangle+2(a-c)\langle v,Hx\rangle+(a^2-c^2)\langle x,Hx\rangle , \end{aligned}\]

because the terms \(\pm\langle v,Hv\rangle\) and \(\pm a^2c^2\|x\|^2\) cancel. Since \(a^2-c^2=(a-c)(a+c)=(a-c)\gamma\) and \(a-c=-(\gamma-2a)\), the last line equals

\[-(\gamma-2a)\bigl(\gamma\|v\|^2+2ac\langle v,x\rangle+2\langle v,Hx\rangle+\gamma\langle x,Hx\rangle\bigr).\]

Multiplying by \(2\) and comparing with \((\gamma-2a)\) times (1) proves the claim. \(\square\)

Self-adjointness is used once, to merge \(\langle x,Hv\rangle\) with \(\langle v,Hx\rangle\); without it the right-hand side contains \(\langle v,Hx\rangle+\langle x,Hv\rangle\) and the identity fails. The identity is valid for every \(\gamma\) and \(a\) because the factor \(\gamma-2a\) multiplies the derivative instead of dividing the right-hand side. Dividing by \(\gamma-2a=\lambda_+-\lambda_-\) gives the paper's formula \(\frac{d}{dt}\|(\psi_t,z_t)\|^2=\frac{2}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}\{\psi_t^\top(\lambda_-^2I-H_t)\psi_t+z_t^\top(H_t-\lambda_+^2I)z_t\}\).

steps.title: Dissipativity from the lower and upper curvature bounds
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma,a,m,M\in\mathbb R\) with \(\gamma-2a>0\). Let \(H\) be a self-adjoint continuous linear operator on \(\mathcal H\) such that

\[m\|u\|^2\le\langle u,Hu\rangle\le M\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in\mathcal H.\]

Put \(k=\max\{a^2-m,\;M-(\gamma-a)^2\}\). Then for every \(s\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\),

\[D_{\gamma,a}(H;s)\le\frac{2k}{\gamma-2a}\,\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s).\]

Proof. Let \((y,z)=T_{\gamma,a}s\). The lower bound with \(u=y\) gives \(-\langle y,Hy\rangle\le-m\|y\|^2\), and the upper bound with \(u=z\) gives \(\langle z,Hz\rangle\le M\|z\|^2\). Inserting both into the identity of the previous step,

\[(\gamma-2a)\,D_{\gamma,a}(H;s)\le2\Bigl((a^2-m)\|y\|^2+\bigl(M-(\gamma-a)^2\bigr)\|z\|^2\Bigr).\qquad(1)\]

Since \(a^2-m\le k\) and \(\|y\|^2\ge0\), we have \((a^2-m)\|y\|^2\le k\|y\|^2\); likewise \((M-(\gamma-a)^2)\|z\|^2\le k\|z\|^2\). Hence (1) gives

\[(\gamma-2a)\,D_{\gamma,a}(H;s)\le2k\bigl(\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2\bigr)=2k\,\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(s).\qquad(2)\]

Dividing (2) by the positive number \(\gamma-2a\) preserves the inequality and gives the claim. \(\square\)

The lower curvature bound controls the first transformed coordinate and the upper bound the second; the maximum is a coefficient that dominates both. No relation between \(m\) and \(M\) and no sign of \(m\) is assumed. The hypothesis \(\gamma-2a>0\) is used only in the final division: for \(\gamma-2a<0\) the division would reverse (2). In the paper this is the inequality \(\frac{d}{dt}\|(\psi_t,z_t)\|^2\le\frac{2\{(\lambda_-^2-m)\vee(M-\lambda_+^2)\}}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}\|(\psi_t,z_t)\|^2\).

steps.title: The case of zero shift
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma,m,M\in\mathbb R\) with \(\gamma>0\) and \(m+M\le\gamma^2\), and let \(H\) satisfy the hypotheses of the previous step. Then for every \(s\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\),

\[D_{\gamma,0}(H;s)\le-\frac{2m}{\gamma}\,\mathcal E_{\gamma,0}(s).\]

Proof. Apply the previous step with \(a=0\); its hypothesis \(\gamma-2\cdot0=\gamma>0\) holds. The constant becomes \(k=\max\{-m,\;M-\gamma^2\}\). From \(m+M\le\gamma^2\) we get \(M-\gamma^2\le-m\), so \(k=-m\), and the coefficient \(2k/(\gamma-0)\) equals \(-2m/\gamma\). \(\square\)

When \(m>0\), the fifth step turns this into \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,0}(t)\le\mathcal E_{\gamma,0}(0)e^{-2mt/\gamma}\), so the transformed norm decays at the rate \(m/\gamma\). This is the rate of display (contr:2) of the paper, which holds in the friction regime \(\gamma\ge\sqrt{M+m}\) and is used for the first-order sampler.

The final simpa only evaluates \(0^2=0\), \(0-m=-m\) and \(\gamma-0=\gamma\), replaces the maximum by \(-m\) using max_eq_left hm (\(\max\{u,w\}=u\) when \(w\le u\)), and moves the signs with neg_mul, mul_neg and mul_zero.

steps.title: Derivative of the energy along a kinetic path
steps.body:
A function \(u:\mathbb R\to\mathcal H\) is differentiable at \(t\) with derivative \(u'(t)\in\mathcal H\) if \(\|(u(t+h)-u(t))/h-u'(t)\|\to0\) as \(h\to0\), \(h\neq0\).

Claim. Let \(\gamma,a\in\mathbb R\), let \(H\) be a continuous linear operator on \(\mathcal H\) (no symmetry is needed), let \(v,x:\mathbb R\to\mathcal H\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\). Assume that \(v\) and \(x\) are differentiable at \(t\) with

\[v'(t)=-\gamma v(t)-Hx(t),\qquad x'(t)=v(t).\]

Then \(F(r)=\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v(r),x(r))\) is differentiable at \(t\) and \(F'(t)=D_{\gamma,a}\bigl(H;(v(t),x(t))\bigr)\).

Proof. Put \(y(r)=v(r)+(\gamma-a)x(r)\) and \(z(r)=-v(r)-ax(r)\). Sums and constant multiples of functions differentiable at \(t\) are differentiable at \(t\), with the corresponding linear combination of derivatives, so (all functions evaluated at \(t\))

\[\begin{aligned} y'(t)&=-\gamma v-Hx+(\gamma-a)v=-av-Hx,\\ z'(t)&=-(-\gamma v-Hx)-av=(\gamma-a)v+Hx . \end{aligned}\]

Next, if \(u\) is differentiable at \(t\), then \(r\mapsto\|u(r)\|^2\) is differentiable at \(t\) with derivative \(2\langle u(t),u'(t)\rangle\). Indeed, by bilinearity, with \(\Delta=u(t+h)-u(t)\),

\[\frac{\|u(t+h)\|^2-\|u(t)\|^2}{h}=2\Bigl\langle u(t),\frac{\Delta}{h}\Bigr\rangle+h\,\Bigl\|\frac{\Delta}{h}\Bigr\|^2 .\]

As \(h\to0\), \(\Delta/h\to u'(t)\); by continuity of the inner product the first term tends to \(2\langle u(t),u'(t)\rangle\), and the second tends to \(0\cdot\|u'(t)\|^2=0\). Applying this to \(y\) and \(z\) and adding,

\[F'(t)=2\langle y(t),-av(t)-Hx(t)\rangle+2\langle z(t),(\gamma-a)v(t)+Hx(t)\rangle=D_{\gamma,a}\bigl(H;(v(t),x(t))\bigr).\ \square\]

Only the value of the operator at the time considered enters the computation. In the next step the operator varies with time, \(H=H_t\), and no regularity of \(t\mapsto H_t\) is required; this matters because the averaged Hessian of the coupling depends on both random trajectories.

steps.title: Integration of the energy differential inequality
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma,a,m,M,T\in\mathbb R\) with \(\gamma-2a>0\). Let \(v,x:\mathbb R\to\mathcal H\) be continuous on \([0,T]\), and let \((H_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}\) be continuous linear operators on \(\mathcal H\). Assume that for every \(t\in[0,T)\): \(H_t\) is self-adjoint, \(m\|u\|^2\le\langle u,H_tu\rangle\le M\|u\|^2\) for all \(u\), and \(v,x\) are differentiable at \(t\) with \(v'(t)=-\gamma v(t)-H_tx(t)\) and \(x'(t)=v(t)\). Put \(K=2\max\{a^2-m,\,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}/(\gamma-2a)\). Then for every \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v(t),x(t))\le\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v(0),x(0))\,e^{Kt}.\]

Proof. Let \(F(t)=\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v(t),x(t))\). It is continuous on \([0,T]\), being built from the continuous paths \(v,x\) by linear combinations, norms, squares and a sum. For \(t\in[0,T)\), the previous step with \(H=H_t\) shows that \(F\) is differentiable at \(t\) with \(F'(t)=D_{\gamma,a}(H_t;(v(t),x(t)))\), and the second step with \(H=H_t\) gives \(F'(t)\le KF(t)\). The claim now follows from the following form of Grönwall's inequality.

Lemma. Let \(F\) be continuous on \([0,T]\), have a right derivative \(F'(t)\) at every \(t\in[0,T)\), and satisfy \(F'(t)\le KF(t)\) there. Then \(F(t)\le F(0)e^{Kt}\) for \(t\in[0,T]\).

Proof of the lemma. Put \(G(t)=e^{-Kt}F(t)\). By the product rule, \(G\) has right derivative \(e^{-Kt}(F'(t)-KF(t))\le0\) at every \(t\in[0,T)\). Fix \(\varepsilon>0\) and let \(G_\varepsilon(t)=G(t)-G(0)-\varepsilon t\); it is continuous on \([0,T]\) and has right derivative at most \(-\varepsilon\) on \([0,T)\). Let \(t^*\) be the supremum of the set of \(\tau\in[0,T]\) such that \(G_\varepsilon\le0\) on \([0,\tau]\); this set contains \(0\). By continuity \(G_\varepsilon(t^*)\le0\). If \(t^*<T\), the right derivative of \(G_\varepsilon\) at \(t^*\) is negative, so there is \(\delta>0\) with \(G_\varepsilon(\tau)<G_\varepsilon(t^*)\le0\) for \(\tau\in(t^*,t^*+\delta)\), which contradicts the definition of \(t^*\). Hence \(G(t)\le G(0)+\varepsilon t\) on \([0,T]\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\); letting \(\varepsilon\to0\) gives \(G(t)\le G(0)=F(0)\), that is, \(F(t)\le F(0)e^{Kt}\).

A two-sided derivative is in particular a right derivative, so the lemma applies to \(F\), and the claim follows. \(\square\)

The differential inequality has no additive term because the two coupled trajectories are driven by the same noise, which cancels in their difference. If \(T<0\) the interval \([0,T]\) is empty and the statement is void.

steps.title: Position decay when the initial velocities agree
steps.body:
Claim. Assume the hypotheses of the previous step and, in addition, \(v(0)=0\). Then for every \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[(\gamma-2a)^2\|x(t)\|^2\le2\bigl((\gamma-a)^2+a^2\bigr)\,e^{Kt}\,\|x(0)\|^2,\qquad K=\frac{2\max\{a^2-m,\,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}}{\gamma-2a}.\]

Proof. By the position bound of the previous section, \((\gamma-2a)^2\|x(t)\|^2\le2\,\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v(t),x(t))\). By the previous step, \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v(t),x(t))\le\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v(0),x(0))e^{Kt}\). Since \(v(0)=0\), the zero-velocity identity of the previous section gives \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(0,x(0))=((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)\|x(0)\|^2\). Chaining the three facts (multiplication by \(2>0\) preserves inequalities),

\[(\gamma-2a)^2\|x(t)\|^2\le2\,\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(0,x(0))\,e^{Kt}=2\bigl((\gamma-a)^2+a^2\bigr)\|x(0)\|^2e^{Kt}.\ \square\]

In the application \(v\) and \(x\) are the velocity and position differences of two kinetic diffusions driven by the same Brownian motion and started with the same velocity, so \(v(0)=0\). Taking square roots (last step) gives the prefactor \(\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}/(\gamma-2a)\) of Proposition 1; it measures the conditioning of \(T_{\gamma,a}\), while the exponential describes the decay in time.

steps.title: Right derivatives at the initial time
steps.body:
A function \(u:\mathbb R\to\mathcal H\) has right derivative \(u'(t)\) at \(t\) if \(\|(u(t+h)-u(t))/h-u'(t)\|\to0\) as \(h\to0\) with \(h>0\).

Claim. (i) The fourth step remains true if both derivatives in the hypothesis and the derivative in the conclusion are right derivatives. (ii) The fifth step remains true if, for every \(t\in[0,T)\), the hypotheses \(v'(t)=-\gamma v(t)-H_tx(t)\) and \(x'(t)=v(t)\) are only assumed for right derivatives: under the same remaining hypotheses, \(\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v(t),x(t))\le\mathcal E_{\gamma,a}(v(0),x(0))e^{Kt}\) for all \(t\in[0,T]\).

Proof. (i) The rules used in the fourth step — linearity of the derivative and the formula \(2\langle u(t),u'(t)\rangle\) for the derivative of \(\|u\|^2\) — hold for one-sided limits with the same proofs, restricting \(h\) to \(h>0\). (ii) The Grönwall lemma of the fifth step assumes only right derivatives, and the dissipativity inequality of the second step is pointwise; with (i) in place of the fourth step, the proof of the fifth step applies verbatim. \(\square\)

This variant is needed for paths defined by integral equations on \([0,T]\). The difference of two solutions driven by the same Brownian motion is the integral of a continuous function, so it has a right derivative at every \(t\in[0,T)\), including \(t=0\), although each Brownian-driven velocity is nowhere differentiable and the paths are not given for negative times.

steps.title: Position decay for an arbitrary admissible shift
steps.body:
Claim. Assume the hypotheses of part (ii) of the previous step (right derivatives) and \(v(0)=0\). Put \(\kappa=\max\{a^2-m,\,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}/(\gamma-2a)\). Then for every \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[\|x(t)\|\le\frac{\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}}{\gamma-2a}\,e^{\kappa t}\,\|x(0)\|.\]

Proof. Exactly as in the sixth step, using the energy bound of the previous step, the zero-velocity identity and the position bound of the previous section,

\[(\gamma-2a)^2\|x(t)\|^2\le2\bigl((\gamma-a)^2+a^2\bigr)e^{2\kappa t}\|x(0)\|^2,\qquad(1)\]

because \(K=2\kappa\). By the addition formula of the exponential, \((e^{\kappa t})^2=e^{\kappa t}e^{\kappa t}=e^{2\kappa t}\); and \(\bigl(\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}\bigr)^2=2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)\) because the radicand is nonnegative. So (1) reads

\[\bigl((\gamma-2a)\|x(t)\|\bigr)^2\le\Bigl(\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}\;e^{\kappa t}\|x(0)\|\Bigr)^2 .\]

Both bases are nonnegative (\(\gamma-2a>0\), norms and square roots are nonnegative, the exponential is positive), so \((\gamma-2a)\|x(t)\|\le\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}\,e^{\kappa t}\|x(0)\|\). Dividing by \(\gamma-2a>0\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

KineticLangevin/Dynamics.lean.title: Existence for the kinetic integral equation
KineticLangevin/Dynamics.lean.summary:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a real normed space, \(g:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\) a Lipschitz map (in the application \(g=\nabla f\)), \(\gamma,u\ge0\) the friction and the inverse mass, and \(B:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X\) a continuous path with \(B(0)=0\). This section proves that the kinetic integral equation

\[v_t=v_0-\int_0^t\bigl(\gamma v_s+u\,g(x_s)\bigr)\,ds+B_t,\qquad x_t=x_0+\int_0^tv_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T,\]

has a continuous solution on every finite horizon \([0,T]\) when \(\mathcal X\) is complete. With \(B=\sqrt{2\gamma u}\,W\) for a Brownian path \(W\) this is the integral form of the kinetic Langevin equation (kinetic) of Dalalyan and Riou-Durand, \(dV_t=-(\gamma V_t+u\nabla f(L_t))\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma u}\,dW_t\), \(dL_t=V_t\,dt\); the noise enters the velocity only. The statement is pathwise: \(B\) is an arbitrary continuous path, so it applies to every continuous Brownian trajectory, and also to continuous paths with values in a space of square-integrable random vectors.

The phase space \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) is given here the maximum norm \(\|(v,x)\|_\infty=\max\{\|v\|,\|x\|\}\), which is equivalent to the Euclidean product norm and is used only for existence. The drift is shown to be Lipschitz for this norm, and existence follows from the Picard theorem for integral equations with Lipschitz drift and continuous additive forcing, proved for the overdamped Langevin equation. Uniqueness, probability laws and contraction estimates are not part of this section.

steps.title: The drift and the sign convention of the integral equation
steps.body:
Definition. For \(g:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\) and \(\gamma,u\in\mathbb R\), the negative kinetic drift is the map \(G:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\),

\[G(v,x)=\bigl(\gamma v+u\,g(x),\;-v\bigr).\]

The kinetic integral equation with initial point \(y_0=(v_0,x_0)\) and forcing \(B\) is

\[Y_t-y_0=-\int_0^tG(Y_s)\,ds+(B_t,0).\qquad(1)\]

Claim. A continuous path \(Y_t=(v_t,x_t)\) satisfies (1) at time \(t\ge0\) if and only if

\[v_t=v_0-\int_0^t\bigl(\gamma v_s+u\,g(x_s)\bigr)\,ds+B_t,\qquad x_t=x_0+\int_0^tv_s\,ds .\]

Proof. The integral of a continuous path in \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) is computed coordinatewise: the coordinate projections are continuous linear maps and therefore commute with the integral. The first coordinate of (1) is the velocity equation. The second coordinate is \(x_t-x_0=-\int_0^t(-v_s)\,ds+0=\int_0^tv_s\,ds\). \(\square\)

The drift is written with a minus sign so that (1) has the form \(Y_t-y_0=-\int_0^tG(Y_s)\,ds+\beta_t\) of the general existence theorem, in which \(G\) plays the role of a gradient. The forcing \((B_t,0)\) has zero position component: the position is the integral of a continuous velocity and is therefore continuously differentiable, \(x'_t=v_t\), even when \(B\) is only continuous.

steps.title: A Lipschitz bound for the phase drift in the maximum norm
steps.body:
A map \(F\) between normed spaces is \(K\)-Lipschitz, \(K\ge0\), if \(\|F(s)-F(t)\|\le K\|s-t\|\) for all \(s,t\).

Claim. Equip \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) with the maximum norm \(\|(v,x)\|_\infty=\max\{\|v\|,\|x\|\}\). Let \(L,\gamma,u\ge0\) and let \(g\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. Then \(G\) is \((\gamma+uL+1)\)-Lipschitz.

Proof. Let \(s=(v,x)\), \(t=(w,y)\) and \(R=\|s-t\|_\infty\). By definition of the maximum norm, \(\|v-w\|\le R\) and \(\|x-y\|\le R\); hence \(\|g(x)-g(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\le LR\), using \(L\ge0\). It suffices to bound both coordinates of \(G(s)-G(t)\) by \((\gamma+uL+1)R\).

Velocity coordinate. By linearity, \(\gamma v+ug(x)-(\gamma w+ug(y))=\gamma(v-w)+u(g(x)-g(y))\). By the triangle inequality and homogeneity, with \(|\gamma|=\gamma\) and \(|u|=u\) because both are nonnegative,

\[\bigl\|\gamma(v-w)+u(g(x)-g(y))\bigr\|\le\gamma\|v-w\|+u\|g(x)-g(y)\|\le\gamma R+uLR\le(\gamma+uL+1)R .\]

Position coordinate. \(\|-v-(-w)\|=\|w-v\|=\|v-w\|\le R\le(\gamma+uL+1)R\), because \((\gamma+uL)R\ge0\).

The maximum of the two coordinate norms is therefore at most \((\gamma+uL+1)R\). \(\square\)

The constant is not optimal; its only role is to make the existence theorem applicable. The maximum norm is convenient because both coordinate projections have norm one. The contraction rates of the kinetic diffusion are derived separately from curvature bounds, in the transformed Euclidean norm.

steps.title: Finite-horizon existence for continuous forcing
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mathcal X\) be a real Banach space, let \(L,\gamma,u\ge0\), let \(g:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz, let \(y_0\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\), let \(B:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X\) be continuous with \(B(0)=0\), and let \(T\ge0\). Then there is a continuous path \(Y:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) with \(Y(0)=y_0\) such that for every \(t\in[0,T]\)

\[Y(t)-y_0=-\int_0^tG(Y(s))\,ds+(B(t),0).\]

Proof. We use the Picard existence theorem proved for the overdamped Langevin equation : if \(\mathcal Z\) is a real Banach space, \(F:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z\) is Lipschitz, \(z_0\in\mathcal Z\), \(\beta:\mathbb R\to\mathcal Z\) is continuous with \(\beta(0)=0\) and \(T\ge0\), then there is a continuous \(Z:\mathbb R\to\mathcal Z\) with \(Z(0)=z_0\) and \(Z(t)-z_0=-\int_0^tF(Z(s))\,ds+\beta(t)\) for \(t\in[0,T]\). (Its proof: on an interval of length \(\delta\) with \(K\delta\le1/2\), \(K\) the Lipschitz constant, the map \(Z\mapsto z_0-\int_0^{\cdot}F(Z(s))\,ds+\beta\) is a contraction with constant \(1/2\) on the complete space of continuous paths with the supremum norm, because \(\|\int(F(Z)-F(Z'))\|\le K\delta\sup\|Z-Z'\|\); Banach's fixed point theorem gives a solution there, and finitely many such pieces are joined to cover \([0,T]\).)

Apply it with \(\mathcal Z=\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) under the maximum norm, which is complete because \(\mathcal X\) is; with \(F=G\), which is \((\gamma+uL+1)\)-Lipschitz by the previous step; with \(z_0=y_0\); and with \(\beta(t)=(B(t),0)\). The path \(\beta\) is continuous because both coordinates are continuous, and \(\beta(0)=(B(0),0)=(0,0)\). The resulting \(Z\) is the required \(Y\). \(\square\)

Completeness of \(\mathcal X\) is needed for the fixed point argument and for the integral; it holds for \(\mathbb R^p\) and for \(L^2\) spaces of random vectors. This theorem gives existence only, for a fixed continuous forcing path; uniqueness of the solution, its measurability in the Brownian input and the law of the solution are established in later sections.

KineticLangevin/Coefficients.lean.title: Exponential response coefficients and their Gram covariances
KineticLangevin/Coefficients.lean.summary:
For a real friction \(\gamma\) define functions \(\psi_k,\varphi_k:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(k\in\mathbb N\), by

\[\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t},\qquad\psi_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^t\psi_k(s)\,ds,\qquad\varphi_0=0,\qquad\varphi_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\psi_k(s)\,ds .\]

These are the coefficients of the exponential integrators of Dalalyan and Riou-Durand: the KLMC update (KLMC) uses \(\psi_0(h),\psi_1(h),\psi_2(h)\) and the noise covariance \(\int_0^h(\psi_0,\psi_1)^\top(\psi_0,\psi_1)\,dt\); the second-order update (KLMC2) adds \(\varphi_2(h),\varphi_3(h)\) and the four-kernel covariance \(\int_0^h(\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3)^\top(\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3)\,dt\). Defining \(\psi_k\) by integrals, rather than by closed formulas with powers of \(\gamma\) in the denominator, makes every statement valid for all real \(\gamma\), including \(\gamma=0\).

We prove: continuity and the derivative rules \(\psi_0'=-\gamma\psi_0\), \(\psi_{k+1}'=\psi_k\); the division-free friction identities \(\gamma\psi_1(t)=1-\psi_0(t)\) and \(\gamma\psi_2(t)=t-\psi_1(t)\) with the resulting closed formulas for \(\gamma\neq0\); a time-scaling identity; values at \(t=0\), nonnegativity, positivity and the bounds \(\psi_0\le1\), \(\psi_1(t)\le t\), \(\psi_2(t)\le t^2/2\), \(\psi_k(t)\le t^k/k!\) for \(\gamma,t\ge0\); the corresponding facts for \(\varphi_k\), including \(\varphi_{k+1}\le\psi_{k+1}\), \(\gamma\varphi_2(t)=\psi_1(t)-t\psi_0(t)\) and the exact balance \(\varphi_2+\gamma\varphi_3=\psi_2\), which gives \(\varphi_2\le\psi_2\) (the paper prints the reverse inequality \(\psi_2\le\varphi_2\)); and, for Gram matrices \(C_{ij}=\int_0^hk_i(t)k_j(t)\,dt\) of continuous kernels, the representation of the quadratic form as an integral of a square and hence positive semidefiniteness for \(h\ge0\). For the KLMC covariance we compute the entries \(C_{11}=\int_0^he^{-2\gamma t}dt\) and \(C_{12}=\psi_1(h)^2/2\) and the variance balance \(\psi_0(h)^2+2\gamma C_{11}=1\). Gaussian random variables with these covariances are constructed in later sections.

steps.title: Definition, continuity and derivatives of the response coefficients
steps.body:
Definition. For \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), define \(\psi_k:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) recursively by \(\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\) and \(\psi_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^t\psi_k(s)\,ds\), where for \(t<0\) the integral is oriented, \(\int_0^t=-\int_t^0\). When the dependence on the friction matters we write \(\psi_k^{(\gamma)}\).

Claim. For every \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\): (i) \(\psi_k\) is continuous on \(\mathbb R\); (ii) \(\psi_{k+1}\) is differentiable at every \(t\in\mathbb R\) with \(\psi_{k+1}'(t)=\psi_k(t)\); (iii) \(\psi_0\) is differentiable at every \(t\) with \(\psi_0'(t)=-\gamma\psi_0(t)\).

Proof. (i) By induction on \(k\). The function \(\psi_0\) is the composition of the continuous maps \(t\mapsto-\gamma t\) and \(\exp\). If \(\psi_k\) is continuous, it is integrable on every bounded interval, and a primitive \(t\mapsto\int_0^t\psi_k\) of such a function is continuous (indeed \(|\int_t^{t'}\psi_k|\le|t'-t|\sup|\psi_k|\) on bounded sets); so \(\psi_{k+1}\) is continuous.

(ii) By (i), \(\psi_k\) is continuous, and the fundamental theorem of calculus states that \(t\mapsto\int_0^t\psi_k(s)\,ds\) is differentiable at every point where the integrand is continuous, with derivative \(\psi_k(t)\).

(iii) By the chain rule, the derivative of \(t\mapsto e^{-\gamma t}\) is \(-\gamma e^{-\gamma t}=-\gamma\psi_0(t)\). \(\square\)

Thus \(\psi_0\) is the solution of the friction equation \(y'=-\gamma y\), \(y(0)=1\), and \(\psi_{k}\) is its \(k\)-fold primitive vanishing at \(0\). In the frozen-force integrator, \(\psi_0(h)\) multiplies the old velocity and \(\psi_1(h)\), \(\psi_2(h)\) multiply the frozen force in the velocity and position updates.

steps.title: Friction identities and closed formulas
steps.body:
Claim. For all \(\gamma,t\in\mathbb R\),

\[\gamma\,\psi_1(t)=1-\psi_0(t),\qquad(1)\] \[\gamma\,\psi_2(t)=t-\psi_1(t).\qquad(2)\]

If \(\gamma\neq0\), then

\[\psi_1(t)=\frac{1-e^{-\gamma t}}{\gamma},\qquad\psi_2(t)=\frac{t-(1-e^{-\gamma t})/\gamma}{\gamma}.\qquad(3)\]

Proof. (1) By the previous step, \(s\mapsto1-\psi_0(s)\) is differentiable with derivative \(\gamma\psi_0(s)\), which is continuous. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (the integral of a continuous derivative is the increment of the function),

\[\gamma\,\psi_1(t)=\int_0^t\gamma\,\psi_0(s)\,ds=\bigl(1-\psi_0(t)\bigr)-\bigl(1-\psi_0(0)\bigr)=1-\psi_0(t),\]

since \(\psi_0(0)=1\); the first equality takes the constant \(\gamma\) out of the integral.

(2) Integrate (1), viewed as an identity between continuous functions of \(s\), over \([0,t]\): by linearity of the integral,

\[\gamma\,\psi_2(t)=\int_0^t\gamma\,\psi_1(s)\,ds=\int_0^t\bigl(1-\psi_0(s)\bigr)\,ds=t-\psi_1(t).\]

(3) If \(\gamma\neq0\), divide (1) by \(\gamma\) to obtain the first formula; insert it into (2) and divide by \(\gamma\) again to obtain the second. \(\square\)

Identities (1) and (2) hold for every real \(\gamma\); at \(\gamma=0\) they reduce to \(0=0\) and carry no information, while the closed formulas (3) are meaningless. This is why the integral definition is used throughout. In the frozen-force step, (1) and (2) express that the velocity and position responses to a constant force combine consistently with the friction.

steps.title: Scaling of the response coefficients under a change of time
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(c,\gamma,t,h\in\mathbb R\) with \(c\neq0\), and \(k\in\mathbb N\). Then

\[\psi_k^{(c\gamma)}(t)=c^{-k}\,\psi_k^{(\gamma)}(ct),\qquad\psi_k^{(c\gamma)}(h/c)=\frac{\psi_k^{(\gamma)}(h)}{c^k}.\]

Proof. The first identity is proved by induction on \(k\), for all \(t\) simultaneously. For \(k=0\): \(\psi_0^{(c\gamma)}(t)=e^{-c\gamma t}=e^{-\gamma(ct)}=c^0\psi_0^{(\gamma)}(ct)\). Assume it for \(k\) and all \(t\). Then, by the induction hypothesis and the substitution \(r=cs\) (\(ds=c^{-1}dr\), valid for \(c\neq0\) with either sign, the limits becoming \(0\) and \(ct\)),

\[\psi_{k+1}^{(c\gamma)}(t)=\int_0^tc^{-k}\psi_k^{(\gamma)}(cs)\,ds=c^{-k}\,c^{-1}\int_0^{ct}\psi_k^{(\gamma)}(r)\,dr=c^{-(k+1)}\psi_{k+1}^{(\gamma)}(ct).\]

For the second identity apply the first with \(t=h/c\), use \(c\cdot(h/c)=h\) and \(c^{-k}=1/c^k\). \(\square\)

Multiplying the friction by \(c\) and dividing time by \(c\) changes \(\psi_k\) only by the factor \(c^{-k}\). This is the coefficient form of the time change of Lemma 1 of the paper, which reduces a general inverse mass \(u\) to \(u=1\) by rescaling time and friction by \(\sqrt u\).

steps.title: Initial values, sign and elementary bounds
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma,t\in\mathbb R\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\).
(i) \(\psi_0(0)=1\) and \(\psi_k(0)=0\) for \(k\ge1\).
(ii) If \(t\ge0\), then \(\psi_k(t)\ge0\).
(iii) If \(t>0\), then \(\psi_k(t)>0\).
(iv) If \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), then \(\psi_0(t)\le1\), \(\psi_1(t)\le t\) and \(\psi_2(t)\le t^2/2\).

Statements (i)–(iii) hold for every real \(\gamma\).

Proof. (i) \(\psi_0(0)=e^0=1\), and for \(k\ge1\), \(\psi_k(0)\) is an integral over the degenerate interval \([0,0]\).

(ii) Induction on \(k\), for all \(t\ge0\): \(\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}>0\); if \(\psi_k\ge0\) on \([0,\infty)\), then \(\psi_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^t\psi_k\ge0\) as the integral of a nonnegative function over \([0,t]\) with \(t\ge0\).

(iii) Induction on \(k\), for all \(t>0\). The case \(k=0\) is the positivity of the exponential. If \(\psi_k(\tau)>0\) for all \(\tau>0\), then on \([0,t]\) the function \(\psi_k\) is continuous, nonnegative by (ii), and positive at the point \(t\). A continuous nonnegative function that is positive at one point of \([0,t]\), \(t>0\), is positive on a subinterval of positive length by continuity, so its integral over \([0,t]\) is positive. Hence \(\psi_{k+1}(t)>0\).

(iv) Since \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), \(-\gamma t\le0\) and \(\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\le1\). Applying this at every \(s\in[0,t]\) and integrating (monotonicity of the integral over \([0,t]\), \(t\ge0\)) gives \(\psi_1(t)\le\int_0^t1\,ds=t\). Applying the last bound at every \(s\in[0,t]\) and integrating gives \(\psi_2(t)\le\int_0^ts\,ds=t^2/2\). \(\square\)

The bounds (iv) use \(\gamma\ge0\): for negative friction \(\psi_0\) grows exponentially. They are the estimates \(\psi_1(h)\le h\), \(\psi_2(h)\le h^2/2\) used to control the frozen-force terms of one integrator step.

steps.title: Zero friction and the Taylor bound
steps.body:
Claim. (i) For all \(t\in\mathbb R\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\), \(\psi_k^{(0)}(t)=t^k/k!\); in particular \(\psi_0^{(0)}=1\), \(\psi_1^{(0)}(t)=t\), \(\psi_2^{(0)}(t)=t^2/2\).
(ii) If \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), then \(\psi_k^{(\gamma)}(t)\le t^k/k!\) for every \(k\in\mathbb N\).

Proof. (i) Induction on \(k\) for all \(t\). For \(k=0\), \(\psi_0^{(0)}(t)=e^{0}=1=t^0/0!\). If \(\psi_k^{(0)}(s)=s^k/k!\) for all \(s\), then

\[\psi_{k+1}^{(0)}(t)=\int_0^t\frac{s^k}{k!}\,ds=\frac{t^{k+1}}{(k+1)\,k!}=\frac{t^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}.\]

The three special cases are \(k=0,1,2\).

(ii) We show by induction on \(k\) that \(\psi_k^{(\gamma)}(t)\le\psi_k^{(0)}(t)\) for all \(t\ge0\). For \(k=0\) this is \(e^{-\gamma t}\le1\), proved in the previous step. If it holds for \(k\), then for \(t\ge0\) the inequality holds at every \(s\in[0,t]\), and integrating over \([0,t]\) gives it for \(k+1\). Combining with (i) yields (ii). \(\square\)

Friction can only decrease the positive-time responses; the undamped responses are the Taylor coefficients \(t^k/k!\) of the free motion. Statement (ii) extends the bounds \(\psi_1(t)\le t\), \(\psi_2(t)\le t^2/2\) of the previous step to every order.

steps.title: The Hessian response coefficients
steps.body:
Definition. For \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\) put \(\varphi_0=0\) and \(\varphi_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\psi_k(s)\,ds\), the convolution of \(\psi_0\) with \(\psi_k\) on \([0,t]\).

Claim. For all \(\gamma,t\in\mathbb R\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\):
(i) \(\varphi_{k+1}(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\int_0^te^{\gamma s}\psi_k(s)\,ds\);
(ii) \(\varphi_k\) is continuous;
(iii) \(\varphi_k(0)=0\);
(iv) if \(t\ge0\), then \(\varphi_k(t)\ge0\).

Proof. (i) For each \(s\), \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}=e^{-\gamma t}e^{\gamma s}\) by the addition formula of the exponential; the constant factor \(e^{-\gamma t}\) is taken out of the integral.

(ii) \(\varphi_0=0\) is continuous. For \(k+1\), by (i), \(\varphi_{k+1}\) is the product of the continuous function \(e^{-\gamma t}=\psi_0(t)\) and the primitive \(t\mapsto\int_0^te^{\gamma s}\psi_k(s)\,ds\) of a continuous function, which is continuous.

(iii) \(\varphi_0(0)=0\), and \(\varphi_{k+1}(0)\) is an integral over a degenerate interval.

(iv) For \(k=0\) it is trivial. For \(k+1\) and \(s\in[0,t]\), the integrand \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\psi_k(s)\) is the product of a positive number and a number that is nonnegative by the previous steps (\(s\ge0\)); the integral over \([0,t]\), \(t\ge0\), of a nonnegative function is nonnegative. \(\square\)

In the second-order scheme, \(\varphi_2(h)\) and \(\varphi_3(h)\) multiply the Hessian correction \(\nabla^2f(\vartheta_k)v_k\) in the velocity and position updates. The factorization (i) separates the dependence on the upper limit of integration and is the form used to prove continuity.

steps.title: Comparison of the convolved and plain primitives
steps.body:
Claim. (i) If \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), then \(\varphi_{k+1}(t)\le\psi_{k+1}(t)\) for every \(k\in\mathbb N\).
(ii) At zero friction, \(\varphi_{k+1}^{(0)}(t)=\psi_{k+1}^{(0)}(t)\) for all \(k\) and \(t\).

Proof. (i) Let \(s\in[0,t]\). Then \(t-s\ge0\) and \(\gamma\ge0\), so \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}=\psi_0(t-s)\le1\) by the bound of the fourth step, and \(\psi_k(s)\ge0\) because \(s\ge0\). For \(0\le b\) and \(a\le1\) we have \(ab\le b\); hence \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\psi_k(s)\le\psi_k(s)\). Integrating over \([0,t]\) (monotonicity of the integral, \(t\ge0\)) gives \(\varphi_{k+1}(t)\le\int_0^t\psi_k=\psi_{k+1}(t)\).

(ii) For \(\gamma=0\) the weight \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\) equals \(1\), so the two integrals coincide. \(\square\)

This is the general form of the coefficient comparison \(\varphi_{k+1}\le\psi_{k+1}\) recorded in the reference audit; for \(k=1\) it gives \(\varphi_2\le\psi_2\), the reverse of the intermediate inequality \(\psi_2\le\varphi_2\) printed in Step 2 of the proof of Proposition 3 of the paper.

steps.title: Division-free identities for the first convolved coefficients
steps.body:
Claim. For all \(\gamma,t\in\mathbb R\):

\[\varphi_1(t)=t\,\psi_0(t),\qquad\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\,ds=\psi_1(t),\qquad\gamma\,\varphi_2(t)=\psi_1(t)-t\,\psi_0(t).\]

Proof. First identity: for every \(s\), \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\psi_0(s)=e^{-\gamma(t-s)-\gamma s}=e^{-\gamma t}=\psi_0(t)\), so the integrand is constant and \(\varphi_1(t)=\int_0^t\psi_0(t)\,ds=t\,\psi_0(t)\).

Second identity: the substitution \(r=t-s\) maps \([0,t]\) onto itself with reversed orientation, so \(\int_0^t\psi_0(t-s)\,ds=\int_0^t\psi_0(r)\,dr=\psi_1(t)\).

Third identity: for every \(s\), by the friction identity \(\gamma\psi_1(s)=1-\psi_0(s)\) and the computation in the first identity,

\[\gamma\,e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\psi_1(s)=e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\bigl(1-\psi_0(s)\bigr)=e^{-\gamma(t-s)}-\psi_0(t).\]

Integrating over \([0,t]\) and using the second identity, \(\gamma\varphi_2(t)=\psi_1(t)-t\,\psi_0(t)\). \(\square\)

The weight \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\) is the velocity response to an impulse at time \(s\), so \(\varphi_{k+1}\) is the velocity response to a forcing \(\psi_k\). The identities hold for all real \(\gamma\), without division by the friction.

steps.title: The balance between the second-order coefficients
steps.body:
Claim. For all \(\gamma,t\in\mathbb R\),

\[\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\,s\,ds=\psi_2(t),\qquad(1)\] \[\varphi_2(t)+\gamma\,\varphi_3(t)=\psi_2(t).\qquad(2)\]

Consequently, if \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), then \(\varphi_2(t)\le\psi_2(t)\).

Proof. (1) Let \(G(s)=(t-s)\psi_1(s)+\psi_2(s)\). By the product rule and \(\psi_1'=\psi_0\), \(\psi_2'=\psi_1\),

\[G'(s)=-\psi_1(s)+(t-s)\psi_0(s)+\psi_1(s)=(t-s)\,\psi_0(s).\]

The derivative is continuous, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus and \(\psi_1(0)=\psi_2(0)=0\),

\[\int_0^t(t-s)\psi_0(s)\,ds=G(t)-G(0)=\psi_2(t)-\bigl(t\,\psi_1(0)+\psi_2(0)\bigr)=\psi_2(t).\]

The substitution \(s\mapsto t-s\) turns the left-hand side into \(\int_0^ts\,\psi_0(t-s)\,ds=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}s\,ds\), which proves (1).

(2) By the definitions and linearity of the integral, \(\varphi_2(t)+\gamma\varphi_3(t)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\bigl(\psi_1(s)+\gamma\psi_2(s)\bigr)\,ds\). By the friction identity \(\gamma\psi_2(s)=s-\psi_1(s)\), the bracket equals \(s\), and (1) gives (2).

Finally, if \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), then \(\gamma\varphi_3(t)\ge0\) by nonnegativity of \(\varphi_3\), and (2) gives \(\varphi_2(t)\le\psi_2(t)\). \(\square\)

The paper computes \(\varphi_2+\gamma\varphi_3\) in Step 1 of the proof of Proposition 3 and bounds it by \(t^2/2\); identity (2) shows that it equals \(\psi_2\) exactly. The chain of inequalities in Step 2 of that proof, \(0\le\psi_2\le\varphi_2\le\varphi_2+\gamma\varphi_3\le t^2/2\), has its second inequality reversed; the correct chain is \(0\le\varphi_2\le\varphi_2+\gamma\varphi_3=\psi_2\le t^2/2\), which serves the same purpose in the paper's spectral-norm bound.

steps.title: Gram matrices of continuous kernels
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\iota\) be an index set, \((k_i)_{i\in\iota}\) real functions on \(\mathbb R\) and \(h\in\mathbb R\). The Gram matrix of the kernels on \([0,h]\) is \(C_{ij}=\int_0^hk_i(t)k_j(t)\,dt\). If \(W\) is a standard Brownian motion and the \(k_i\) are continuous, the Wiener integrals \(\int_0^hk_i(t)\,dW_t\) are jointly Gaussian with covariance matrix \(C\) by the Itô isometry; this is the origin of the noise covariances of the paper.

Claim. (i) \(C\) is symmetric. (ii) If \(\iota\) is finite and every \(k_i\) is continuous, then for every \(z\in\mathbb R^\iota\)

\[\sum_{i}\sum_{j}z_iC_{ij}z_j=\int_0^h\Bigl(\sum_iz_ik_i(t)\Bigr)^2dt .\]

(iii) If in addition \(h\ge0\), then \(C\) is positive semidefinite: \(\sum_{i,j}z_iC_{ij}z_j\ge0\) for all \(z\).

Proof. (i) \(k_i(t)k_j(t)=k_j(t)k_i(t)\) for every \(t\), so \(C_{ij}=C_{ji}\).

(ii) Each function \(t\mapsto z_ik_i(t)k_j(t)z_j\) is continuous, hence integrable on \([0,h]\). By linearity of the integral (finitely many terms),

\[\sum_{i,j}z_iC_{ij}z_j=\int_0^h\sum_{i,j}z_ik_i(t)k_j(t)z_j\,dt=\int_0^h\Bigl(\sum_iz_ik_i(t)\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_jz_jk_j(t)\Bigr)dt,\]

and the last integrand is the square in the claim.

(iii) By (ii) the quadratic form is the integral over \([0,h]\), \(h\ge0\), of a nonnegative function, hence nonnegative; together with (i) this is positive semidefiniteness. \(\square\)

The continuity hypothesis is used only to justify the integrability of the products and the exchange of the finite sum with the integral. Positive semidefiniteness guarantees that a centred Gaussian vector with covariance \(C\) exists.

steps.title: The covariance matrices of the two schemes
steps.body:
Definitions. The KLMC kernels are \((\psi_0,\psi_1)\) and the KLMC2 kernels are \((\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3)\). Their Gram matrices on \([0,h]\),

\[C=\int_0^h(\psi_0,\psi_1)^\top(\psi_0,\psi_1)\,dt,\qquad\bar C=\int_0^h(\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3)^\top(\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3)\,dt,\]

are the covariance matrices \(\mathbf C\) and \(\bar{\mathbf C}\) of the paper, which describe the joint law of one coordinate of the (unscaled) noise vector in the KLMC and KLMC2 updates.

Claim. For every \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\) all six kernels are continuous, and for every \(h\ge0\) the matrices \(C\) and \(\bar C\) are positive semidefinite.

Proof. The functions \(\psi_0,\psi_1\) are continuous by the first step and \(\varphi_2,\varphi_3\) by the sixth step. The previous step applies to both finite families. \(\square\)

Positive definiteness for \(h>0\), which requires linear independence of the kernels on \([0,h]\), is proved in a later section; semidefiniteness suffices for the existence of the Gaussian innovations.

steps.title: Entries of the KLMC covariance and the velocity variance balance
steps.body:
Claim. For all \(\gamma,h\in\mathbb R\), the KLMC Gram matrix \(C\) satisfies

\[C_{11}=\int_0^he^{-2\gamma t}\,dt=\psi_1^{(2\gamma)}(h),\qquad C_{12}=\int_0^h\psi_0\psi_1\,dt=\frac{\psi_1(h)^2}{2},\qquad\psi_0(h)^2+2\gamma\,C_{11}=1 .\]

Proof. First, \(\psi_0(t)^2=e^{-2\gamma t}=\psi_0^{(2\gamma)}(t)\) by the addition formula, so \(C_{11}=\int_0^h\psi_0^{(2\gamma)}=\psi_1^{(2\gamma)}(h)\).

Second, \(s\mapsto\psi_1(s)^2/2\) has derivative \(\psi_1(s)\psi_1'(s)=\psi_0(s)\psi_1(s)\), which is continuous; by the fundamental theorem of calculus and \(\psi_1(0)=0\), \(C_{12}=\psi_1(h)^2/2-0\).

Third, the friction identity with friction \(2\gamma\) gives \(2\gamma\,\psi_1^{(2\gamma)}(h)=1-\psi_0^{(2\gamma)}(h)=1-\psi_0(h)^2\). Hence \(\psi_0(h)^2+2\gamma C_{11}=\psi_0(h)^2+1-\psi_0(h)^2=1\). \(\square\)

The last identity is the stationarity of the velocity update: if \(v\) has identity covariance and \(\xi\) is independent with covariance \(C_{11}I\), then \(\psi_0(h)v+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi\) again has covariance \((\psi_0(h)^2+2\gamma C_{11})I=I\). It holds for every real \(\gamma\) and \(h\).

KineticLangevin/Integrator.lean.title: The exponential integrator and its Hessian correction
KineticLangevin/Integrator.lean.summary:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a real normed space, \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\) the friction, \(h\) the step size and \(F:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\) a force field (in the paper \(F=\nabla f\)). Phase points are pairs \((v,x)\), velocity first. The coefficients \(\psi_k,\varphi_k\) are those of the previous section. This section defines the deterministic maps from which the samplers are built, with the innovations supplied as arguments:

\[\Phi_h\bigl((v,x),(\xi,\xi')\bigr)=\bigl(\psi_0(h)v-\psi_1(h)F(x)+\xi,\;x+\psi_1(h)v-\psi_2(h)F(x)+\xi'\bigr),\]

the KLMC step \(\Phi_h((v,x),\sqrt{2\gamma}(\xi,\xi'))\), which is display (KLMC) of Dalalyan and Riou-Durand, and the second-order (KLMC2) step, which subtracts \(\varphi_2(h)H(x)v\), \(\varphi_3(h)H(x)v\) and uses four innovations \(\xi^{(1)},\dots,\xi^{(4)}\) as in display (KLMC2), with a general operator field \(H\) in place of \(\nabla^2f\).

We prove that the deterministic part of \(\Phi_h\) is the exact solution at time \(h\) of the frozen-force equation \(v'=-\gamma v-F(x_0)\), \(x'=v\), started at \((v_0,x_0)\); that the step is the identity for \(h=0\) without noise; that two steps with the same innovation differ by an expression in which the innovation has cancelled; that at zero friction the step is the constant-acceleration update; and that the second-order step with zero Hessian is the first-order step. Finally the numerical chains are defined for a prescribed innovation sequence. The Gaussian law of the innovations is not part of these definitions; it is imposed and constructed in later sections.

steps.title: The exact response to a frozen force
steps.body:
Definition. For \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(v,x,F\in\mathcal X\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\) put

\[V(t)=\psi_0(t)\,v-\psi_1(t)\,F,\qquad X(t)=x+\psi_1(t)\,v-\psi_2(t)\,F .\]

Claim. For every \(t\in\mathbb R\), \(X\) and \(V\) are differentiable at \(t\) and

\[X'(t)=V(t),\qquad V'(t)=-\gamma\,V(t)-F .\]

Proof. A function \(t\mapsto c(t)\,w\), with \(c\) a real differentiable function and \(w\in\mathcal X\) fixed, has derivative \(c'(t)\,w\). Using \(\psi_1'=\psi_0\) and \(\psi_2'=\psi_1\) (first step of the previous section),

\[X'(t)=\psi_0(t)\,v-\psi_1(t)\,F=V(t).\]

Using \(\psi_0'=-\gamma\psi_0\) and \(\psi_1'=\psi_0\), \(V'(t)=-\gamma\psi_0(t)v-\psi_0(t)F\). On the other hand, by the friction identity \(\gamma\psi_1(t)=1-\psi_0(t)\),

\[-\gamma V(t)-F=-\gamma\psi_0(t)v+\gamma\psi_1(t)F-F=-\gamma\psi_0(t)v-\bigl(1-\gamma\psi_1(t)\bigr)F=-\gamma\psi_0(t)v-\psi_0(t)F .\]

The two expressions coincide. \(\square\)

Since \(V(0)=v\) and \(X(0)=x\) (values of \(\psi_k\) at \(0\)), the pair \((V,X)\) is the solution of the kinetic equation without noise in which the force is frozen at the constant vector \(F\). In the numerical scheme \(F=F(x_k)\) is the force at the current position, and the only approximation made by the deterministic part of the step is this freezing. The friction identity is what makes the formula exact for every real \(\gamma\), including \(\gamma=0\).

steps.title: The exponential step and the KLMC step
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(F:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\), \(\gamma,h\in\mathbb R\). The exponential step with innovation \((\xi,\xi')\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) is

\[\Phi_h\bigl((v,x),(\xi,\xi')\bigr)=\bigl(\psi_0(h)v-\psi_1(h)F(x)+\xi,\;x+\psi_1(h)v-\psi_2(h)F(x)+\xi'\bigr),\]

and the KLMC step is \(\Phi_h((v,x),\sqrt{2\gamma}\,(\xi,\xi'))\), where \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) is the real square root.

Claim. In the notation of the previous step with frozen force \(F(x)\),

\[\Phi_h\bigl((v,x),(\xi,\xi')\bigr)=\bigl(V(h)+\xi,\;X(h)+\xi'\bigr),\]

and the velocity and position coordinates of \(\Phi_h\) are the two displayed expressions.

Proof. Both statements hold by the definitions: \(V(h)=\psi_0(h)v-\psi_1(h)F(x)\) and \(X(h)=x+\psi_1(h)v-\psi_2(h)F(x)\). \(\square\)

With \(F=\nabla f\), \((v,x)=(v_k,\vartheta_k)\) and \((\xi,\xi')=(\xi_{k+1},\xi'_{k+1})\), the KLMC step is the recursion (KLMC) of the paper. The paper requires the innovations to be centred Gaussian, independent across steps and coordinates, with covariance matrix \(\mathbf C=\int_0^h(\psi_0,\psi_1)^\top(\psi_0,\psi_1)\,dt\) in each coordinate; these probabilistic requirements are not part of the map. If \(\gamma<0\) the real square root returns \(0\); in the applications \(\gamma>0\).

steps.title: Zero step size and subtraction with a common innovation
steps.body:
Claim. (i) For every \(F\), \(\gamma\) and \((v,x)\), \(\Phi_0((v,x),(0,0))=(v,x)\).
(ii) For all phase points \((v,x)\), \((v',x')\) and every innovation \(\eta\),

\[\begin{aligned} &\Phi_h((v,x),\eta)-\Phi_h((v',x'),\eta)\\ &\quad=\Bigl(\psi_0(h)(v-v')-\psi_1(h)\bigl(F(x)-F(x')\bigr),\\ &\qquad\quad(x-x')+\psi_1(h)(v-v')-\psi_2(h)\bigl(F(x)-F(x')\bigr)\Bigr). \end{aligned}\]

(iii) The same identity holds for two KLMC steps with a common innovation.

Proof. (i) \(\psi_0(0)=1\) and \(\psi_1(0)=\psi_2(0)=0\), so \(\Phi_0((v,x),(0,0))=(v-0+0,\;x+0-0+0)=(v,x)\).

(ii) Subtract the two definitions coordinatewise; the innovation appears with opposite signs and cancels, and the scalar coefficients are distributed over the differences.

(iii) A KLMC step is an exponential step with innovation \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\eta\), which is again common to both; apply (ii). \(\square\)

Identity (ii) is the algebraic core of the synchronous coupling of two chains: when the same Gaussian innovations drive both chains, the difference of the states evolves by a deterministic map, and no moment of the noise enters the comparison of one step.

steps.title: Constant-acceleration motion at zero friction
steps.body:
Claim. For \(\gamma=0\), every \(h\in\mathbb R\), every phase point \((v,x)\) and every innovation,

\[\text{KLMC step}=\Bigl(v-h\,F(x),\;x+h\,v-\frac{h^2}{2}F(x)\Bigr).\]

Proof. At zero friction \(\psi_0=1\), \(\psi_1(h)=h\) and \(\psi_2(h)=h^2/2\) (zero-friction formulas of the previous section), and the innovation is multiplied by \(\sqrt{2\cdot0}=0\). \(\square\)

Without friction there is no fluctuation either: the step reduces to the exact motion under the constant force \(F(x)\) during time \(h\), as in a Taylor expansion of order two of the position.

steps.title: The Hessian-corrected step
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(H:\mathcal X\to\mathcal L(\mathcal X)\) assign to each position a continuous linear operator (in the paper \(H=\nabla^2f\)). For a phase point \((v,x)\) and innovations \(\xi^{(1)},\dots,\xi^{(4)}\in\mathcal X\), the second-order step is

\[\begin{aligned} v^+&=\psi_0(h)v-\psi_1(h)F(x)-\varphi_2(h)H(x)v+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\bigl(\xi^{(1)}-H(x)\xi^{(3)}\bigr),\\ x^+&=x+\psi_1(h)v-\psi_2(h)F(x)-\varphi_3(h)H(x)v+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\bigl(\xi^{(2)}-H(x)\xi^{(4)}\bigr). \end{aligned}\]

Claim. If \(H\equiv0\), the second-order step coincides with the KLMC step driven by the innovation \((\xi^{(1)},\xi^{(2)})\).

Proof. With \(H(x)=0\), the terms \(\varphi_2(h)H(x)v\), \(\varphi_3(h)H(x)v\), \(H(x)\xi^{(3)}\) and \(H(x)\xi^{(4)}\) vanish, and what remains is the definition of the KLMC step with innovation \((\xi^{(1)},\xi^{(2)})\). \(\square\)

This is display (KLMC2) of the paper. The corrections linearize the force along the free motion: over the step the force \(\nabla f(x_t)\) is approximated by \(\nabla f(x)+\nabla^2f(x)(x_t-x)\), and the displacement \(x_t-x\) contains the deterministic part \(\psi_1(t)v\) and a stochastic part, which produce the \(\varphi\) terms and the innovations \(\xi^{(3)},\xi^{(4)}\). The four innovations are required to be jointly Gaussian with covariance \(\bar{\mathbf C}\) of the previous section; this is not part of the map.

steps.title: The numerical chains for prescribed innovations
steps.body:
Definition. Given an initial phase point \(y_0\) and innovations \((\eta_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) in \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\), the KLMC chain is defined recursively by

\[y_0=\text{the initial point},\qquad y_{k+1}=\text{KLMC step}(y_k,\eta_k),\qquad k\in\mathbb N .\]

The second-order chain is defined in the same way from the second-order step and innovations \((\xi_k^{(1)},\dots,\xi_k^{(4)})_{k\in\mathbb N}\).

Claim. The KLMC chain satisfies \(y_0=\) the initial point and \(y_{k+1}=\text{KLMC step}(y_k,\eta_k)\) for every \(k\).

Proof. These are the defining equations of the recursion. \(\square\)

For a fixed innovation sequence the chain is a deterministic sequence. It becomes the KLMC (respectively KLMC2) Markov chain of the paper when the initial point is random and the innovations are independent Gaussian vectors with the prescribed covariance, independent of the initial point.

KineticLangevin/OBABO.lean.title: The OBABO composition and its difference identities
KineticLangevin/OBABO.lean.summary:
Let \(\mathcal V\) be a real vector space (no norm is needed), \(F:\mathcal V\to\mathcal V\) a force field and phase points \(z=(v,x)\in\mathcal V\times\mathcal V\), velocity first. The OBABO integrator is the composition of five substeps: an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck velocity update \(O\) with damping \(\delta\), noise coefficient \(\sigma\) and a supplied noise vector \(\xi\); a half kick \(B_{h/2}\), which changes the velocity by \(-(h/2)F(x)\); a drift \(A_h\), which moves the position by \(hv\); a second half kick; and a second Ornstein–Uhlenbeck update with a new noise vector \(\xi'\). The three middle substeps form the velocity Verlet step.

This section proves pathwise identities for these maps, for arbitrary supplied vectors: the expanded formula of one OBABO step; the inverse of each kick and drift; the conjugation of kicks and drifts by velocity reversal; the identity \(V_{-h}\circ V_h=\mathrm{id}\) for the Verlet step \(V_h\); the triviality of OBABO for \(h=0\), \(\delta=1\), \(\sigma=0\); the difference of two OBABO steps driven by the same noises, in which both noises cancel; and, for the standard damping \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\), the identity \(\delta^2u+\bigl(\sqrt{u(1-\delta^2)}\bigr)^2=u\), which expresses that each Ornstein–Uhlenbeck half step preserves the velocity variance \(u\). Probability laws of the noises and convergence of the scheme are treated in later sections.

steps.title: The substeps and the expanded OBABO step
steps.body:
Definitions. For \(\delta,\sigma,h\in\mathbb R\), \(\xi\in\mathcal V\) and \(z=(v,x)\) put

\[O_{\delta,\sigma,\xi}(v,x)=(\delta v+\sigma\xi,\;x),\qquad B_h(v,x)=(v-hF(x),\;x),\qquad A_h(v,x)=(v,\;x+hv),\] \[\Psi(z;\xi,\xi')=O_{\delta,\sigma,\xi'}\circ B_{h/2}\circ A_h\circ B_{h/2}\circ O_{\delta,\sigma,\xi}\,(z).\]

Claim. With \(v_{1/2}=\delta v+\sigma\xi-\tfrac h2F(x)\) and \(x^+=x+h\,v_{1/2}\),

\[\Psi\bigl((v,x);\xi,\xi'\bigr)=\Bigl(\delta\bigl(v_{1/2}-\tfrac h2F(x^+)\bigr)+\sigma\xi',\;x^+\Bigr).\]

Proof. Apply the five maps in turn:

\[\begin{aligned} (v,x)&\overset{O}{\mapsto}(\delta v+\sigma\xi,x) \overset{B_{h/2}}{\mapsto}(v_{1/2},x)\\ &\overset{A_h}{\mapsto}(v_{1/2},x^+) \overset{B_{h/2}}{\mapsto}\bigl(v_{1/2}-\tfrac h2F(x^+),x^+\bigr)\\ &\overset{O}{\mapsto}\Bigl(\delta\bigl(v_{1/2}-\tfrac h2F(x^+)\bigr)+\sigma\xi',x^+\Bigr). \qquad\square \end{aligned}\]

The second kick uses the force at the new position \(x^+\). The two Ornstein–Uhlenbeck substeps use different noise vectors \(\xi\) and \(\xi'\), which in the stochastic scheme are independent standard Gaussian vectors.

In obaboStep_expanded the intermediate quantities are introduced by let vhalf := … and let xnext := …, the \(v_{1/2}\) and \(x^+\) of the claim; the statement is a definitional equality, proved by rfl.

steps.title: Inverses of the kick and drift and velocity reversal
steps.body:
Definition. The velocity reversal is \(R(v,x)=(-v,x)\).

Claim. For all \(h\in\mathbb R\) and \(z\in\mathcal V\times\mathcal V\):
(i) \(B_{-h}(B_hz)=z\) and \(A_{-h}(A_hz)=z\);
(ii) \(R(Rz)=z\);
(iii) \(R(B_h(Rz))=B_{-h}z\) and \(R(A_h(Rz))=A_{-h}z\).

Proof. Let \(z=(v,x)\). (i) \(B_{-h}(v-hF(x),x)=(v-hF(x)+hF(x),x)=(v,x)\), because the kick does not change the position at which the force is evaluated. \(A_{-h}(v,x+hv)=(v,x+hv-hv)=(v,x)\), because the drift does not change the velocity. (ii) \(-(-v)=v\). (iii) \(R(B_h(-v,x))=R(-v-hF(x),x)=(v+hF(x),x)=B_{-h}(v,x)\) and \(R(A_h(-v,x))=R(-v,x-hv)=(v,x-hv)=A_{-h}(v,x)\). \(\square\)

Statement (iii) says that reversing the velocity turns a kick or drift forward in time into the same substep backward in time; this is the algebraic form of the time reversibility of Hamiltonian dynamics.

steps.title: The Verlet step has an exact inverse
steps.body:
Definition. The velocity Verlet step is \(V_h=B_{h/2}\circ A_h\circ B_{h/2}\).

Claim. (i) For all \(h\) and \(z\), \(V_{-h}(V_hz)=z\).
(ii) For every \(F\), \(z\), \(\xi\), \(\xi'\), the OBABO step with \(h=0\), \(\delta=1\), \(\sigma=0\) is the identity: \(\Psi(z;\xi,\xi')=z\).

Proof. (i) Since \((-h)/2=-(h/2)\),

\[V_{-h}\circ V_h=B_{-h/2}\circ A_{-h}\circ B_{-h/2}\circ B_{h/2}\circ A_h\circ B_{h/2}.\]

By (i) of the previous step the innermost pair \(B_{-h/2}\circ B_{h/2}\) is the identity, then \(A_{-h}\circ A_h\), then \(B_{-h/2}\circ B_{h/2}\). (ii) With \(h=0\) the kicks and the drift are the identity, and with \(\delta=1\), \(\sigma=0\) so are both Ornstein–Uhlenbeck substeps. \(\square\)

The Verlet step is palindromic, which is why running it with the negated step undoes it exactly. Combined with (iii) of the previous step it gives \(R\circ V_h\circ R=V_{-h}=V_h^{-1}\), the reversibility used for Metropolis corrections of Hamiltonian proposals.

steps.title: Synchronous noises cancel in the difference of two steps
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(z=(v,x)\), \(w=(v',x')\), \(h,\delta,\sigma\in\mathbb R\) and \(\xi,\xi'\in\mathcal V\). Put

\[a=\delta(v-v')-\tfrac h2\bigl(F(x)-F(x')\bigr),\quad x^+=x+h\bigl(\delta v+\sigma\xi-\tfrac h2F(x)\bigr),\quad y^+=x'+h\bigl(\delta v'+\sigma\xi-\tfrac h2F(x')\bigr).\]

Then the two OBABO steps \(\Psi(z;\xi,\xi')=(v^+,x^+)\) and \(\Psi(w;\xi,\xi')=(v'^+,y^+)\), driven by the same noises, satisfy

\[v^+-v'^+=\delta\Bigl(a-\tfrac h2\bigl(F(x^+)-F(y^+)\bigr)\Bigr),\qquad x^+-y^+=x-x'+h\,a .\]

Proof. By the expanded formula of the first step, the half-step velocities are \(v_{1/2}=\delta v+\sigma\xi-\frac h2F(x)\) and \(v'_{1/2}=\delta v'+\sigma\xi-\frac h2F(x')\); their difference is \(a\), the noise \(\sigma\xi\) cancelling. The new positions are \(x^+=x+hv_{1/2}\) and \(y^+=x'+hv'_{1/2}\), whose difference is \(x-x'+ha\). The new velocities are \(\delta(v_{1/2}-\frac h2F(x^+))+\sigma\xi'\) and \(\delta(v'_{1/2}-\frac h2F(y^+))+\sigma\xi'\); subtracting, \(\sigma\xi'\) cancels and the difference is \(\delta(a-\frac h2(F(x^+)-F(y^+)))\). \(\square\)

Under a synchronous coupling both thermostat noises disappear from the difference, which therefore evolves deterministically; but the second kick still involves the forces at the new positions \(x^+\), \(y^+\), which depend on the noise \(\xi\). The contraction analysis of OBABO starts from this identity.

steps.title: The standard damping and the preservation of the velocity variance
steps.body:
Definitions. For \(\gamma,h\in\mathbb R\) put \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) and \(\varsigma^2=1-\delta^2\).

Claim. (i) \(\delta>0\) and \(\delta^2=e^{-\gamma h}\).
(ii) If \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(h\ge0\), then \(1-\delta^2\ge0\).
(iii) If \(\gamma\ge0\), \(h\ge0\) and \(u\ge0\), then

\[\delta^2u+\Bigl(\sqrt{u\,(1-\delta^2)}\Bigr)^2=u .\]

Proof. (i) The exponential is positive, and \(\delta^2=e^{-\gamma h/2}e^{-\gamma h/2}=e^{-\gamma h}\) by the addition formula. (ii) \(-\gamma h\le0\), so \(\delta^2=e^{-\gamma h}\le1\). (iii) By (ii) and \(u\ge0\), the radicand \(u(1-\delta^2)\) is nonnegative, so the square of its square root equals it; then \(\delta^2u+u(1-\delta^2)=u\). \(\square\)

Interpretation: if a velocity coordinate has variance \(u\) and \(\xi\) is an independent standard Gaussian, then \(\delta v+\sqrt{u(1-\delta^2)}\,\xi\) again has variance \(\delta^2u+u(1-\delta^2)=u\). With \(u\) the inverse mass, this is the choice \(\sigma=\sqrt{u(1-e^{-\gamma h})}\) of the noise coefficient for which each half thermostat preserves the Gaussian velocity marginal; the identity itself is a statement about real numbers.

KineticLangevin/Gaussian.lean.title: Gaussian response laws and independent innovation sequences
KineticLangevin/Gaussian.lean.summary:
To define the random update, specify a probability measure with the required covariance. This section constructs centered finite-dimensional Gaussian probability measures with the Gram covariance and an infinite product giving one independent block per time and spatial coordinate. Correlation is retained within each block. The exact covariance theorem requires a nonnegative step and continuous kernels; the Gaussian measure has total mass one even outside that parameter regime.

The noise construction distinguishes independence of different blocks from correlation of responses inside a block. Both features are needed to identify the sampler law and its common-source coupling.

steps.title: Construction and moments of a centered Gaussian measure
steps.body:
For a finite kernel index set, the centered Gaussian response law is the multivariate Gaussian with mean zero and the defined Gram matrix. The named instances establish Gaussianity and total probability mass using the distribution constructor. The mean theorem computes its vector expectation as zero, and finite Gaussian response moments invokes the finite Gaussian second-moment theorem. These are derived properties of a specified probability measure, rather than moment fields of an abstract noise source. They hold even if the covariance argument is degenerate; identifying its entries with the requested matrix uses the positive-semidefinite theorem below.

A covariance Gram matrix determines a centered Gaussian law by applying a square-root linear map to a standard Gaussian. The resulting law is a probability measure even when the covariance is singular. Finite-dimensional Gaussian moments then provide the integrability needed for every coordinate calculation.

steps.title: Coordinate means, second moments, and covariances
steps.body:
Each coordinate projection is a continuous linear functional. Commuting it with the vector integral proves zero coordinate mean, and composing the finite-second-moment identity with that functional proves coordinate \(L^{2}\) integrability. For continuous kernels and \(h\ge0\), Gram positivity permits the multivariate-Gaussian covariance formula:

\[\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=\int_0^hk_i(t)k_j(t)dt,\quad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\int_0^hk_i(t)^2dt.\]

The covariance formulas apply because the Gram matrix has been proved positive semidefinite. The variance proof only rewrites a product as a square. This identifies the exact correlated coordinate law required by the integrators, while its representation as Brownian stochastic integrals is a separate identity.

For centered variables, covariance is simply the expectation of their product. Thus each entry of the constructed matrix has an immediate probabilistic meaning. Diagonal entries give variances; off-diagonal entries describe the dependence between distinct response coordinates generated from the same noise.

steps.title: Gaussian measures for the two response families
steps.body:
The two-response Gaussian law uses the kernel vector \((\psi_0,\psi_1)\); the four-response Gaussian law uses \((\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3)\). They are therefore probability measures on two- and four-dimensional Euclidean space. Each is the linear pushforward of a normalized Gaussian measure and therefore has total mass one. The first law correlates a coordinate's velocity and position increments; the second also couples the Hessian-correction integrals. Separate spatial coordinates will use separate copies of these entire blocks, rather than separate copies of their individual components.

The two-block and four-block laws are different-dimensional Gaussian vectors with the response covariances specified earlier. They should not be confused with a collection of independent scalar draws. Independence can instead be used before applying the linear covariance factor.

steps.title: Independent response blocks indexed by time and coordinate
steps.body:
The path space is \(\Omega=(\mathbb R^{\iota})^{\mathbb N\times\mathrm{Fin}(d)}\). Define its law as the infinite product of the kernel Gaussian. Evaluation at \((n,i)\) is measurable and has exactly the original Gaussian law, by the infinite-product marginal theorem. The coordinate-evaluation family is jointly independent by independence of the product coordinates. Thus a time step retains all within-block covariance while distinct iteration–coordinate pairs are independent. Each factor has total mass one, and therefore so does the product. Measurability of the coordinate maps gives the stated pushforward law.

Use a product probability space indexed by time and spatial coordinate, with one Gaussian response block at each index. Product structure gives independence of different indices. Within each block the full response covariance is retained, so the correct velocity–position correlation survives spatial assembly.
