steps.title: Spatial assembly of innovations and their moments
steps.body:
Evaluation on the infinite product is measure preserving, so composing the finite-block \(L^{2}\) identity with evaluation gives a finite second moment for each block. Its expectation is zero by the established the distributional identity integral transformation. The first-order Gaussian innovation collects component zero across spatial coordinates into velocity and component one into position. The second-order Gaussian innovation similarly collects each of the four components into a Euclidean vector. The Euclidean identification equips the coordinate functions with the Euclidean norm. Each coordinate map is measurable; finite coordinate assembly is therefore measurable as well. These maps define the innovation sequences used in the integrator recursions.

The Euclidean squared norm is the sum of the coordinate squares. Integrating this finite sum turns scalar moment identities into vector moment identities, with the spatial dimension appearing explicitly. This is the origin of the square-root-dimension factor in first-order error bounds.

steps.title: Second and mixed moments from covariance
steps.body:
The Gaussian coordinates have zero mean. Thus their variance equals \(\int X_i^2\), and their covariance equals \(\int X_iX_j\). The variance is the integral of the centered square, and covariance is the integral of the product of the centered coordinates. Substitution of the zero means gives the second and mixed moments. Each conclusion is an equality for the constructed Gaussian measure: \(\mathbb E X_i^2=\int_0^hk_i^2\) and \(\mathbb E X_iX_j=\int_0^hk_ik_j\). These formulas can be used in numerical-error calculations without assuming moments of an unspecified noise source.

Polarization supplies cross moments from covariance once the means are known to vanish. Integrability of each product follows from Cauchy–Schwarz and the finite second moments. Consequently the covariance calculation is a legitimate expectation identity, rather than a purely matrix comparison.

steps.title: The scalar KLMC Gaussian transition
steps.body:
The scalar exponential transition measure maps the constructed correlated two-dimensional Gaussian through the scalar KLMC step at a fixed phase state. The map is continuous in its innovation, so the pushforward remains a probability measure. Both output coordinates are a constant frozen-force response plus \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\) times a Gaussian coordinate. Their finite second moments follow by adding a constant \(L^{2}\) function to a scalar multiple of the proved Gaussian \(L^{2}\) coordinate. steps.title: Conclude the law-to-law kinetic theorem
steps.body:
The kinetic position law is the explicit independent-product pushforward for this endpoint map. Its probability theorem follows from endpoint measurability. Substituting the derived coefficient \(q=\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}\) in the general random-map transport theorem gives

\[W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0).\]

The source law may be any fixed probability law of initial velocity and continuous forcing, independent of initial position. The statement therefore applies to any such stochastic realization; a stationary Gibbs law is unnecessary for comparing two evolving laws. The extended-valued theorem retains infinite initial costs, and the real-valued theorem explicitly requires finite initial Wasserstein distance. The full all-friction spectral prefactor and a specified Brownian-source identification are separate refinements beyond this simple-friction law theorem.

The conclusion concerns the independently defined output laws for each initial distribution. Dependence on the auxiliary initial coupling has disappeared through the marginal identities. The coupling argument therefore proves a property of the kinetic transition family.

The exponential schemes use correlated Brownian integrals, for example \(\xi_v=\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\,dB_s\) and \(\xi_x=\int_0^t\psi_1(t-s)\,dB_s\). An isonormal Gaussian map assigns a centered Gaussian random variable to every deterministic square-integrable time function. Its covariance is the time-function inner product. This single source realizes all response integrals together and makes their cross covariances available automatically.

steps.title: Square-integrability of a continuous response kernel
steps.body:
For a continuous scalar response \(k\), define \(K_{k,t}(s)=1_{(0,t]}(s)k(t-s)\). The time reversal is essential: a Brownian fluctuation arriving at time \(s\) has \(t-s\) units of damping before the endpoint. Continuity of \(k\) gives a finite bound on the compact interval \([0,t]\). Since \((0,t]\) has finite Lebesgue measure, this bound proves square integrability.

The integral of the squared kernel is bounded by the interval length times the square of the compact bound. Thus the zero extension defines an \(L^{2}\) equivalence class. Its representative agrees almost everywhere with the indicator expression, so pointwise kernel identities give equalities of these equivalence classes.

The response kernel is supported on the finite interval preceding the endpoint. Its boundedness and continuity give a finite square integral there. Extending it by zero creates an element of the time Hilbert space to which the Gaussian map can be applied.

steps.title: Continuity in mean square with a varying endpoint
steps.body:
A moving indicator has a discontinuity at its endpoint, so pointwise continuity at every time coordinate is unavailable. Fix an endpoint \(t\). For every \(r\ne t\), the membership of \(r\) in \((0,s]\) is constant for all \(s\) sufficiently close to \(t\). If \(r<t\), ordinary continuity of \(k(s-r)\) applies; if \(r>t\), the kernel stays zero. The single exceptional time coordinate has Lebesgue measure zero.

The exact norm formula is

\[\|K_{k,s}-K_{k,t}\|_H^2=\int_{\mathbb R}|K_{k,s}(r)-K_{k,t}(r)|^2\,dr.\]

For \(s\) near \(t\), both kernels are supported in the fixed finite interval \((0,t+1]\). Compactness gives a common bound \(C\) for their values. The squared difference is therefore bounded by the integrable function \(4C^2 1_{(0,t+1]}\). Dominated convergence makes the squared \(L^{2}\) distance tend to zero; continuity of the square root gives convergence of the distance itself.

The pointwise limit follows by distinguishing \(r<t\), \(r>t\), and \(r\le0\), For each strict inequality, the same inequality holds for nearby endpoints. The \(L^{2}\) inner-product formula applied to the difference gives the norm formula. The compact bound and the null exceptional singleton justify dominated convergence, followed by continuity of the square root. This proves continuity as an \(L^{2}\)-valued map; it does not assert that the selected representatives have continuous sample paths.

Changing the endpoint changes both the kernel values and their support. On a common bounded interval the responses admit an integrable dominating bound. Pointwise convergence away from the moving endpoint and dominated convergence then yield convergence in the time Hilbert norm.

steps.title: Fubini for the deterministic time kernels
steps.body:
The essential primitive identity is

\[K_{\psi_1,t}=\int_0^t K_{\psi_0,s}\,ds\quad\text{in }L^2(\mathbb R,dr).\]

Point evaluation on \(L^{2}\) is not continuous, so one cannot simply evaluate a Bochner integral at a time coordinate and interchange the two integrals. The inner product with a kernel is the ordinary integral \(\int_0^s f(r)e^{-\gamma(s-r)}\,dr\), a fact obtained from the almost-everywhere kernel representatives.

The restriction of an \(L^{2}\) function to a finite-measure interval is integrable, so the product is integrable on the square. This establishes the hypothesis of Fubini's theorem; the interchange is proved rather than assumed. After swapping, the inner integral is

\[\int_r^t e^{-\gamma(s-r)}\,ds=\psi_1(t-r).\]

Thus the two inner products agree for every \(f\), and equality of all inner products gives the vector identity.

The two triangular integrals have the restricted domains determined by \((0,t]\cap(-\infty,s]=(0,s]\) and \((0,t]\cap[r,\infty)=[r,t]\). Changing inclusion of an endpoint does not change a Lebesgue integral. The finite-interval \(L^{1}\) bound and the bounded exponential weight give product integrability. Fubini therefore applies, and the continuous inner-product functional commutes with the Bochner integral. Equality against every test vector gives the claimed Hilbert-space identity.

The triangular integration region has finite measure and the response kernels satisfy the required norm bound there. Fubini may therefore interchange the time primitive and the isonormal response. This is the rigorous origin of the positional innovation as an integrated velocity innovation.

These identities express dissipation in terms of the residual force relative to a scalar curvature.

The same scalar argument applies to KIPLMC1 with its thermal radius and a separately bounded concentration term.

The persistent bias and the decaying transient are bounded by separate fractions of the requested error tolerance. The specific numerical allocation leaves enough a strict allowance for the \(\sqrt2\) positional prefactor and the rounded count. Adding the two verified contributions gives the final \(\varepsilon\) guarantee.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianMoments.lean.title: Finiteness and quadratic moments of the Hamiltonian Gibbs measure
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianMoments.lean.summary:
The weak Hamiltonian limit needs finite mass and an integrable quadratic expression in velocity and force. This section derives both for the exponential Hamiltonian density in finite dimensions. It factors that density into a radial Gaussian velocity weight and the potential Gibbs weight, uses existing direct Gaussian-domination estimates, and transfers position moments to force moments by Lipschitz growth.

Strong convexity makes the Gibbs phase measure finite and gives the moments required by the rejection bound. Smoothness converts position control into force control, establishing the integrability assumptions of the weak limit.

steps.title: Factor the Hamiltonian density
steps.body:
Because \(H(v,x)=f(x)+\|v\|^2/2\), the positive exponential weight factors as \(e^{-H(v,x)}=e^{-\|v\|^2/2}e^{-f(x)}\). Therefore its product-Haar weighted measure is the product of the separately weighted velocity and position measures. The identity for products of density-weighted measures applies because the nonnegative density is the product of the two coordinate densities, as follows from the exponential addition identity. Normalization has not been assumed or imposed at this step.

The kinetic and potential parts of the Hamiltonian depend on different coordinates, so their exponential weights factor. Product integration separates velocity Gaussian integrals from position Gibbs integrals. This factorization is valid for the reference measure before normalization.

steps.title: Derive finite mass of both factors and their product
steps.body:
The velocity weight is the radial Gaussian with precision \(1/2\), whose ordinary integral is finite. The position weight has finite mass by the previously proved strong-convexity Gaussian domination: a supporting quadratic lower bound for \(f\) makes \(e^{-f}\) integrable. The proof converts these finite ordinary integrals to finite extended density integrals, instantiates finite weighted measures, and uses the exact factorization to prove finiteness of the full phase measure.

Strong convexity gives a quadratic lower bound for the potential. Its exponential is dominated by a shifted Gaussian density, yielding finite positive partition mass. The velocity factor is an ordinary Gaussian integral, so the phase measure also has finite positive mass.

steps.title: Derive velocity and position second moments before normalization
steps.body:
A quadratic factor is absorbed by radial Gaussian decay, so \(\int\|v\|^2e^{-\|v\|^2/2}\,dv<\infty\). The same strong-convexity tail estimate gives \(\int\|x\|^2e^{-f(x)}\,dx<\infty\). The argument uses the ordinary-integral characterization of integration under a density, checks that each exponential density is finite and measurable, and invokes the existing Gaussian-tail estimates. These are moments of the unnormalized factors, obtained without assuming stationarity of a process.

Polynomial factors remain integrable under the Gaussian density upper bound. Thus both velocity and position second moments exist before taking ratios by the partition function. Establishing this first ensures that later normalized moment expressions represent finite expectations.

steps.title: Transfer position moments to force moments
steps.body:
Gradient Lipschitz continuity implies \(\| abla f(x)\|\le M\|x\|+\| abla f(0)\|\). Squaring and using \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) gives \(\| abla f(x)\|^2\le2M^2\|x\|^2+2\| abla f(0)\|^2\). The right-hand side is integrable under the finite position Gibbs weight by its second moment. The argument derives the force growth inequality from the Lipschitz difference bound and triangle inequality, then applies domination by this explicit integrable upper bound.

Force Lipschitzness gives \(\| abla f(x)\|\le\| abla f(x_0)\|+M\|x-x_0\|\). Squaring and using \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) reduces force moments to the finite position second moment. Choosing a minimizer removes the constant force term when available.

steps.title: Assemble the precise phase bound needed by the weak limit
steps.body:
On the factored finite phase measure, \(\|v\|^2\) is integrable by pulling the velocity moment through the first coordinate, and \(\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\) is integrable by pulling the force moment through the second coordinate. Their sum is exactly the quadratic expression in the rejection bound. The argument rewrites the phase measure by its proved factorization, supplies finiteness of both factors, and adds these two coordinate integrability results. Thus every tail premise in the later Hamiltonian stationarity limit follows from positive strong convexity and a Lipschitz gradient.

The rejection upper bound is a fixed quadratic combination of velocity and force norms. The preceding moment bounds therefore make its target integral finite. This is the exact integrability required to make the accumulated rejection error vanish in the Hamiltonian-flow limit.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianStationarity..title: Gibbs invariance of the Hamiltonian integral flow
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianStationarity..summary:
Let \(E\) be a separable real Hilbert space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with an \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient, and write phase points velocity first, \(z=(v,x)\in E\times E\). The Hamiltonian is \(H(v,x)=f(x)+\tfrac12\|v\|^2\). For a reference measure \(\mu\) on \(E\) that is s-finite and invariant under all translations \(x\mapsto a+x\) and under \(x\mapsto-x\), the (unnormalised) Gibbs measure is the measure \(\pi\) on \(E\times E\) with density \(e^{-H}\) relative to the product measure \(\mu\otimes\mu\):

\[\pi(A)=\int_A e^{-f(x)-\|v\|^2/2}\,(\mu\otimes\mu)(dv\,dx)\qquad\text{for Borel }A\subseteq E\times E.\]

The Hamiltonian flow \(\Phi_T\) maps an initial state \(z=(v,x)\) to the value at time \(T\) of the continuous solution of the integral equations \(V_t=v-\int_0^t\nabla f(X_s)\,ds\), \(X_t=x+\int_0^tV_s\,ds\), \(0\le t\le T\); this is the kinetic integral equation with zero friction, unit inverse mass and zero forcing, whose solution exists by the Picard argument and is unique by the Gronwall stability estimate. The module proves that \(\Phi_T\) is continuous and that it preserves the Gibbs measure, \(\pi\circ\Phi_T^{-1}=\pi\).

The invariance is not obtained by differentiating the density. Instead \(\Phi_T\) is approximated by \(N\) velocity Verlet steps of size \(T/N\). A Verlet step followed by a Metropolis accept/reject decision with velocity reversal preserves \(\pi\) exactly; the rejection probability is of order \(h^2\); hence the law of \(N\) uncorrected Verlet steps differs from \(\pi\), on bounded test functions, by at most a multiple of \(T^2/N\), and this error vanishes in the limit \(N\to\infty\), in which the Verlet iterates converge to \(\Phi_T\). In finite dimension with Lebesgue reference measure, strong convexity of \(f\) supplies the finiteness of \(\pi\) and the moment needed for the rejection bound. The invariance is used for the normalised Gibbs target and in the analysis of the exact OBABO scheme and its phase laws.

steps.title: Continuity of the time-\(T\) Hamiltonian map
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) have a gradient \(\nabla f\) that is \(M\)-Lipschitz for some \(M\ge0\), and let \(T\ge0\). Then the map \(z\mapsto\Phi_T(z)\) from \(E\times E\) to \(E\times E\) is continuous. In particular it is Borel measurable.

Proof. Recall the general kinetic integral equation with Lipschitz force \(g\), friction \(\gamma\ge0\), inverse mass \(u\ge0\) and continuous velocity forcing \(B\) on \([0,T]\) with \(B(0)=0\):

\[Y_t-z=-\int_0^t\bigl(\gamma V_s+u\,g(X_s),\,-V_s\bigr)\,ds+\bigl(B(t),0\bigr),\qquad Y_t=(V_t,X_t),\quad 0\le t\le T.\]

It was shown earlier that the endpoint \(Y_t\) of its solution depends Lipschitz continuously on the pair \((z,B)\), where \(z\) ranges over \(E\times E\) with the norm \(\|(v,x)\|=\max(\|v\|,\|x\|)\) and \(B\) over the space of continuous paths \([0,T]\to E\) with the supremum norm: if \(L\) is the Lipschitz constant of \(g\) and \(t\in[0,T]\), then

\[\|Y_t(z,B)-Y_t(z',B')\|\le3e^{(\gamma+uL+1)t+t}\,\max\bigl(\|z-z'\|,\ \sup_{s\le T}\|B(s)-B'(s)\|\bigr).\]

Take \(g=\nabla f\), \(L=M\), \(\gamma=0\), \(u=1\) and \(t=T\). The map \(\iota:z\mapsto(z,0)\), which pairs an initial state with the zero path, is continuous (each component is continuous), and by definition \(\Phi_T(z)=Y_T(z,0)=Y_T\circ\iota(z)\). A composition of continuous maps is continuous, so \(\Phi_T\) is continuous; explicitly, \(\|\Phi_T(z)-\Phi_T(z')\|\le3e^{(M+2)T}\|z-z'\|\). A continuous map between topological spaces equipped with their Borel \(\sigma\)-algebras is measurable, because preimages of open sets are open. \(\square\)

Measurability of \(\Phi_T\) is what makes the image measure \(\pi\circ\Phi_T^{-1}\) in the next step meaningful.

steps.title: Invariance of the Gibbs measure under a finite second moment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a separable real Hilbert space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra and let \(\mu\) be an s-finite measure on \(E\) that is invariant under every translation \(x\mapsto a+x\) and under the reflection \(x\mapsto-x\). Let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient (\(M\ge0\)), let \(T\ge0\), and let \(\pi\) be the Gibbs measure with density \(e^{-H}\) relative to \(\mu\otimes\mu\). Assume that \(\pi\) is a finite measure and that

\[\int_{E\times E}\bigl(\|v\|^2+\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\bigr)\,\pi(dv\,dx)<\infty .\]

Then the image of \(\pi\) under the time-\(T\) Hamiltonian map is \(\pi\): \(\pi\bigl(\Phi_T^{-1}(A)\bigr)=\pi(A)\) for every Borel set \(A\subseteq E\times E\).

Proof. We use four results proved earlier. For a step \(h\in\mathbb R\) write \(K_s(v,x)=(v-s\nabla f(x),x)\) (kick), \(D_h(v,x)=(v,x+hv)\) (drift), \(V_h=K_{h/2}\circ D_h\circ K_{h/2}\) (velocity Verlet step), \(R(v,x)=(-v,x)\) (velocity reversal), and

\[a_h(z)=\min\Bigl\{1,\ \exp\bigl(-(H(V_hz)-H(z))\bigr)\Bigr\}\in[0,1]\]

(the Metropolis acceptance probability of the Verlet proposal).

  1. Exact invariance of corrected Verlet. For every \(h\), with \(a=a_h\), \[(a\,\pi)\circ V_h^{-1}+\bigl((1-a)\,\pi\bigr)\circ R^{-1}=\pi,\] where \(a\,\pi\) denotes the measure with density \(a\) relative to \(\pi\). This uses that \(K_s\), \(D_h\) and \(R\) preserve \(\mu\otimes\mu\) (by the translation and reflection invariance of \(\mu\) and Tonelli's theorem), that \(H\circ R=H\), and that \(f\) and \(\nabla f\) are measurable.
  2. Weak error of \(N\) uncorrected steps. If \(\pi\) is finite and the identity of item 1 holds, then for every measurable \(F:E\times E\to\mathbb C\) with \(|F|\le C\) and every \(N\in\mathbb N\), \[\Bigl|\int F(V_h^Nz)\,\pi(dz)-\int F\,d\pi\Bigr|\le N\cdot2C\int(1-a_h)\,d\pi .\] (One step changes \(\int G\,d\pi\) by at most \(2C\int(1-a_h)\,d\pi\) for every \(|G|\le C\), because item 1 rewrites \(\int G\,d\pi\) as \(\int(a_hG\circ V_h+(1-a_h)G\circ R)\,d\pi\); applying this to \(G=F\circ V_h^{n}\) and telescoping over \(n=0,\dots,N-1\) with the triangle inequality gives the bound.)
  3. Rejection estimate. For \(0\le h\le1\), with \(\kappa=M(2M+11)/8\), \[\int(1-a_h)\,d\pi\le h^2\kappa\int\bigl(\|v\|^2+\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\bigr)\,\pi(dv\,dx).\] This is the integrated form of the pointwise bound \(1-a_h(z)\le h^2\kappa(\|v\|^2+\|\nabla f(x)\|^2)\); it requires the integrability assumed in the claim.
  4. Convergence of Verlet. For every \(z\), \(V_{T/(n+1)}^{\,n+1}(z)\to\Phi_T(z)\) as \(n\to\infty\).
  5. Limit principle. Let \(\pi\) be a finite measure on a separable Banach space \(\mathcal H\), let \(Y\) and \(Y_n\) (\(n\in\mathbb N\)) be measurable maps of \(\mathcal H\) with \(Y_n(z)\to Y(z)\) for every \(z\), and let \(\delta_n\to0\). Suppose that for every measurable \(F:\mathcal H\to\mathbb C\) with \(|F|\le1\) there is \(n_0\) such that \(|\int F\circ Y_n\,d\pi-\int F\,d\pi|\le\delta_n\) for \(n\ge n_0\). Then \(\pi\circ Y^{-1}=\pi\). (For \(F(z)=e^{i\ell(z)}\) with \(\ell\) a continuous linear functional, dominated convergence with the constant dominating function \(1\), integrable because \(\pi\) is finite, gives \(\int F\circ Y_n\,d\pi\to\int F\circ Y\,d\pi\); the hypothesis gives \(\int F\circ Y_n\,d\pi\to\int F\,d\pi\); hence \(\pi\circ Y^{-1}\) and \(\pi\) have the same characteristic functional and are equal.)

Put \(\kappa=M(2M+11)/8\), \(B=\int(\|v\|^2+\|\nabla f(x)\|^2)\,d\pi\), which is finite by assumption, and for \(n\in\mathbb N\)

\[h_n=\frac{T}{n+1},\qquad \delta_n=\frac{2T^2\kappa B}{n+1}.\]

Both sequences have the form \(c/(n+1)\) with a constant \(c\), so \(h_n\to0\) and \(\delta_n\to0\). We apply the limit principle with \(\mathcal H=E\times E\) (a separable Banach space), \(Y=\Phi_T\), which is measurable by the previous step, and \(Y_n=V_{h_n}^{\,n+1}\). Each \(V_h\) is measurable, being a composition of maps built from addition, scalar multiplication and the continuous map \(\nabla f\); hence so is each iterate. The pointwise convergence \(Y_n(z)\to\Phi_T(z)\) is item 4.

It remains to verify the weak-error hypothesis. Fix a measurable \(F\) with \(|F|\le1\). Since \(h_n\to0\), there is \(n_0\) with \(h_n<1\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). Fix \(n\ge n_0\), put \(h=h_n\) and \(N=n+1\). Then \(0\le h\le1\), because \(T\ge0\). By item 1 the hypothesis of item 2 holds, and item 2 with \(C=1\) gives

\[\Bigl|\int F(V_h^Nz)\,\pi(dz)-\int F\,d\pi\Bigr|\le 2N\int(1-a_h)\,d\pi .\qquad(1)\]

Item 3 applies because \(0\le h\le1\), and multiplying it by \(2N\ge0\) gives \(2N\int(1-a_h)\,d\pi\le2Nh^2\kappa B\). Finally

\[2Nh^2\kappa B=2N\frac{T^2}{N^2}\kappa B=\frac{2T^2\kappa B}{N}=\delta_n .\qquad(2)\]

Combining (1) and (2), \(|\int F\circ Y_n\,d\pi-\int F\,d\pi|\le\delta_n\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). The limit principle yields \(\pi\circ\Phi_T^{-1}=\pi\). \(\square\)

The hypotheses enter as follows. Finiteness of \(\pi\) is needed in items 2 and 5 (bounded functions must be integrable and dominated convergence must apply). The second moment makes \(B\) finite, so that \(\delta_n\to0\). Differentiability of \(f\) makes \(f\) continuous, hence measurable, which is needed for the density \(e^{-H}\) and the acceptance probability \(a_h\). The Lipschitz constant \(M\) enters the rejection constant \(\kappa\) and the convergence of the Verlet scheme. The invariance properties of \(\mu\) are used only in item 1.

steps.title: Invariance under strong convexity in finite dimension
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space with its Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\) (the Haar measure giving volume one to the cube spanned by an orthonormal basis). Let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex for some \(m>0\), that is,

\[f(ax+by)\le af(x)+bf(y)-ab\,\frac m2\,\|x-y\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in E,\ a,b\ge0,\ a+b=1,\]

and let \(\nabla f\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz. Then for every \(T\ge0\) the Gibbs measure \(\pi\) with density \(e^{-f(x)-\|v\|^2/2}\) relative to \(\lambda\otimes\lambda\) satisfies \(\pi\circ\Phi_T^{-1}=\pi\).

Proof. Lebesgue measure on \(E\) is \(\sigma\)-finite (hence s-finite), invariant under translations and invariant under \(x\mapsto-x\), and \(E\), being finite-dimensional, is complete and separable. It therefore suffices to check the two additional assumptions of the previous step.

Finiteness of \(\pi\). The density factorises, \(e^{-H(v,x)}=e^{-\|v\|^2/2}e^{-f(x)}\), so by Tonelli's theorem \(\pi\) is the product of the measures \(e^{-\|v\|^2/2}\lambda(dv)\) and \(e^{-f(x)}\lambda(dx)\). The first is finite (a Gaussian integral). For the second, strong convexity and differentiability give the quadratic lower bound \(f(x)\ge f(x_0)+\langle\nabla f(x_0),x-x_0\rangle+\frac m2\|x-x_0\|^2\), so \(e^{-f}\) is dominated by a constant multiple of a Gaussian density and is integrable. Both factors being finite, \(\pi\) is finite. These facts were proved in the module on Hamiltonian moments.

Second moment. In the same module it is shown that \(\int\|v\|^2e^{-\|v\|^2/2}\lambda(dv)<\infty\) (a Gaussian second moment) and that \(\int\|\nabla f(x)\|^2e^{-f(x)}\lambda(dx)<\infty\). For the latter, the Lipschitz bound and the triangle inequality give \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le M\|x\|+\|\nabla f(0)\|\), hence, by \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\), \[\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\le2M^2\|x\|^2+2\|\nabla f(0)\|^2 ;\] the right-hand side is integrable against \(e^{-f(x)}\lambda(dx)\) because this measure is finite and has a finite second moment \(\int\|x\|^2e^{-f(x)}\lambda(dx)\), again by the Gaussian domination of \(e^{-f}\). Since each of the two summands \(\|v\|^2\) and \(\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\) depends on one coordinate only and the other factor of the product measure is finite, both summands are \(\pi\)-integrable, and so is their sum.

The previous step now gives \(\pi\circ\Phi_T^{-1}=\pi\). \(\square\)

The hypotheses of this claim concern the potential \(f\) only; finiteness of \(\pi\) and the second moment are derived, not assumed.

KineticLangevin/BrownianSegmentEquations.title: Brownian integral identities on translated time intervals
KineticLangevin/BrownianSegmentEquations.summary:
This module works with one scalar Brownian motion constructed on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) from an isonormal Gaussian map. Let \(L^2(\mathbb R)\) be the real Hilbert space of (classes of) functions on \(\mathbb R\) that are square integrable for Lebesgue measure, and let \(I:L^2(\mathbb R)\to L^2(\mathbb P)\) be a linear isometry whose values are centred Gaussian random variables; such a map is built from a Hilbert basis of \(L^2(\mathbb R)\) and an independent family of standard Gaussian variables. The Brownian motion is \(B_t=I(\mathbf 1_{(0,t]})\), \(t\ge0\), so that \(\mathbb E[B_sB_t]=\langle\mathbf 1_{(0,s]},\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}\rangle=\min(s,t)\). For a continuous \(k:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) and \(t\ge0\) the time kernel \(\kappa^k_t\in L^2(\mathbb R)\) is the class of \(r\mapsto\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}(r)\,k(t-r)\), and \(I(\kappa^k_t)\) is the Wiener integral \(\int_0^tk(t-r)\,dB_r\).

For \(a\ge0\) let \(\tau_a\) be the translation \((\tau_ag)(r)=g(r-a)\) of \(L^2(\mathbb R)\); it is a linear isometry because Lebesgue measure is translation invariant. The segment response

\[J^a_t(k)=I(\tau_a\kappa^k_t)=\int_a^{a+t}k(a+t-r)\,dB_r,\qquad a,t\ge0,\]

is the Wiener integral of \(k\) against the Brownian fluctuations on the interval \((a,a+t]\). With \(\psi_0(u)=e^{-\gamma u}\) and \(\psi_1(u)=\int_0^u\psi_0(s)\,ds\) put \(V^a_t=J^a_t(\psi_0)\) and \(P^a_t=J^a_t(\psi_1)\) (velocity and position responses), and \(W^a_t=B_{a+t}-B_a\) (Brownian increment). The module proves, as identities in \(L^2(\mathbb P)\), that \(J^a_t(1)=W^a_t\), that \(t\mapsto J^a_t(k)\) is continuous, that \(P^a_t=\int_0^tV^a_s\,ds\), that \(V^a_t+\gamma P^a_t=W^a_t\), and the integration-by-parts formulas \(P^a_t=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}W^a_s\,ds\) and \(V^a_t=W^a_t-\gamma\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}W^a_s\,ds\). The case \(a=0\) was treated in the module on Brownian convolutions; the translated versions show that the Gaussian innovations used on the numerical interval \((a,a+t]\) are built from the same Brownian path as the continuous kinetic diffusion on that interval, and they are used to construct exact kinetic segments driven by the same increments.

steps.title: The Brownian increment on a translated interval
steps.body:
Definition. For \(a,t\ge0\) the Brownian increment on \((a,a+t]\) is \(W^a_t=B_{a+t}-B_a\in L^2(\mathbb P)\).

Claim. For all \(a,t\ge0\), the segment kernel of the constant function \(1\) satisfies

\[\tau_a\kappa^1_t=\mathbf 1_{(0,a+t]}-\mathbf 1_{(0,a]}\quad\text{in }L^2(\mathbb R),\qquad\text{hence}\qquad J^a_t(1)=W^a_t .\]

Proof. By definition of the translation, \((\tau_a\kappa^1_t)(r)=\kappa^1_t(r-a)=\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}(r-a)=\mathbf 1_{(a,a+t]}(r)\) for almost every \(r\) (the elements of \(L^2(\mathbb R)\) are classes, so the identity of representatives is an almost-everywhere identity). Next we show \(\mathbf 1_{(0,a+t]}(r)-\mathbf 1_{(0,a]}(r)=\mathbf 1_{(a,a+t]}(r)\) for every real \(r\), distinguishing three cases.

  • If \(r\le0\) or \(r>a+t\), all three indicators vanish.
  • If \(0<r\le a\), then also \(r\le a+t\) because \(t\ge0\); the left-hand side is \(1-1=0\), and \(r\notin(a,a+t]\).
  • If \(a<r\le a+t\), then \(r>0\) because \(a\ge0\); the left-hand side is \(1-0=1\), and \(r\in(a,a+t]\).

Two elements of \(L^2(\mathbb R)\) with almost everywhere equal representatives are equal, which proves the first identity. Applying the linear map \(I\) gives

\[J^a_t(1)=I(\tau_a\kappa^1_t)=I(\mathbf 1_{(0,a+t]})-I(\mathbf 1_{(0,a]})=B_{a+t}-B_a=W^a_t .\qquad\square\]

The nonnegativity of \(a\) and \(t\) is used in the case distinction; it ensures \((0,a]\subseteq(0,a+t]\).

steps.title: Continuity and the time primitive of the velocity response
steps.body:
Claim. (a) For every continuous \(k\) and every \(a\ge0\), the map \(t\mapsto J^a_t(k)\) from \([0,\infty)\) to \(L^2(\mathbb P)\) is continuous. (b) If \(\gamma\ge0\), then for all \(a,t\ge0\)

\[P^a_t=\int_0^tV^a_s\,ds ,\]

where the right-hand side is the Bochner integral in the Hilbert space \(L^2(\mathbb P)\) of the continuous map \(s\mapsto V^a_s\).

Recall that for a continuous map \(F:[0,t]\to\mathcal X\) into a Banach space \(\mathcal X\), the Bochner integral \(\int_0^tF(s)\,ds\) exists and equals the limit of Riemann sums, and that every bounded linear map \(\Lambda:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) between Banach spaces satisfies \(\Lambda\bigl(\int_0^tF(s)\,ds\bigr)=\int_0^t\Lambda(F(s))\,ds\).

Proof. (a) In the module on Brownian convolutions it was proved that \(t\mapsto\kappa^k_t\) is continuous from \([0,\infty)\) into \(L^2(\mathbb R)\) (by dominated convergence: on a bounded time range the kernels are bounded by \(\sup|k|\) and supported in a bounded interval). The maps \(\tau_a\) and \(I\) are linear isometries, hence continuous, and \(J^a_t(k)=I(\tau_a(\kappa^k_t))\) is a composition of continuous maps.

(b) Put \(\Lambda=I\circ\tau_a\), a bounded linear map from \(L^2(\mathbb R)\) to \(L^2(\mathbb P)\). For \(\gamma\ge0\) the deterministic primitive identity

\[\kappa^{\psi_1}_t=\int_0^t\kappa^{\psi_0}_s\,ds\qquad\text{in }L^2(\mathbb R)\qquad(1)\]

was proved earlier: both sides have inner product \(\int_0^tg(r)\psi_1(t-r)\,dr\) with every \(g\in L^2(\mathbb R)\), by Fubini's theorem applied to \((s,r)\mapsto\mathbf 1_{\{r\le s\}}e^{-\gamma(s-r)}g(r)\) on \((0,t]^2\) and the computation \(\int_r^te^{-\gamma(s-r)}\,ds=\psi_1(t-r)\). The function is integrable on \((0,t]^2\) because \(g\) is integrable on the bounded interval \((0,t]\) (Cauchy–Schwarz) and \(0\le e^{-\gamma(s-r)}\le1\) when \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(r\le s\); this is where \(\gamma\ge0\) is used. The map \(s\mapsto\kappa^{\psi_0}_s\) is continuous by (a), hence integrable on \([0,t]\). Applying \(\Lambda\) to (1) and moving \(\Lambda\) inside the integral,

\[P^a_t=\Lambda(\kappa^{\psi_1}_t)=\Lambda\Bigl(\int_0^t\kappa^{\psi_0}_s\,ds\Bigr)=\int_0^t\Lambda(\kappa^{\psi_0}_s)\,ds=\int_0^tV^a_s\,ds .\qquad\square\]

The identity holds in \(L^2(\mathbb P)\); no pointwise evaluation of the random variables is involved.

steps.title: The damped Brownian integral equation
steps.body:
Claim. (a) For every real \(\gamma\) and all \(a,t\ge0\),

\[V^a_t+\gamma P^a_t=W^a_t .\]

(b) If \(\gamma\ge0\), then for all \(a,t\ge0\)

\[V^a_t=W^a_t-\gamma\int_0^tV^a_s\,ds .\]

Proof. (a) The response functions satisfy \(\gamma\psi_1(u)=1-\psi_0(u)\) for every real \(u\): both sides vanish at \(u=0\) and have derivative \(\gamma e^{-\gamma u}\), so they agree by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Multiplying by the indicator, \(\kappa^{\psi_0}_t+\gamma\kappa^{\psi_1}_t=\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}=\kappa^1_t\) in \(L^2(\mathbb R)\). The case \(a=0\) of the claim, \(I(\kappa^{\psi_0}_t)+\gamma I(\kappa^{\psi_1}_t)=B_t\), is the image of this identity under \(I\). Applying instead the linear map \(\Lambda=I\circ\tau_a\) and the previous step's identity \(\Lambda(\kappa^1_t)=J^a_t(1)=W^a_t\),

\[V^a_t+\gamma P^a_t=\Lambda(\kappa^{\psi_0}_t)+\gamma\Lambda(\kappa^{\psi_1}_t)=\Lambda\bigl(\kappa^{\psi_0}_t+\gamma\kappa^{\psi_1}_t\bigr)=\Lambda(\kappa^1_t)=W^a_t .\]

(b) For \(\gamma\ge0\) the previous step gives \(P^a_t=\int_0^tV^a_s\,ds\). Substituting this into (a) and moving \(\gamma\int_0^tV^a_s\,ds\) to the right-hand side gives the claim. \(\square\)

Identity (b) says that \(s\mapsto V^a_s\) solves the linear equation \(dV=-\gamma V\,ds+dW^a\) in integral form, with the Brownian increment of the interval \((a,a+t]\) as forcing; this is the velocity equation of the kinetic diffusion without the force term.

steps.title: The ordinary Brownian convolution formula
steps.body:
Claim. If \(\gamma\ge0\), then for all \(a,t\ge0\)

\[P^a_t=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\,W^a_s\,ds\qquad\text{and}\qquad V^a_t=W^a_t-\gamma\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\,W^a_s\,ds,\]

with Bochner integrals in \(L^2(\mathbb P)\) of continuous integrands.

Proof. The case \(a=0\) of the first formula, \(P_t=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}B_s\,ds\) with \(P_t=I(\kappa^{\psi_1}_t)\), was proved in the module on Brownian convolutions: the map \(s\mapsto e^{\gamma s}P_s\) has derivative \(e^{\gamma s}(V_s+\gamma P_s)=e^{\gamma s}B_s\) for \(s>0\), by the product rule, \(P_s=\int_0^sV_r\,dr\) and part (a) of the previous step with \(a=0\); integrating from \(0\) to \(t\) and using \(P_0=0\) gives \(e^{\gamma t}P_t=\int_0^te^{\gamma s}B_s\,ds\).

We transfer this formula to the interval \((a,a+t]\). The map \(s\mapsto\mathbf 1_{(0,s]}=\kappa^1_s\) is continuous into \(L^2(\mathbb R)\) by part (a) of the second step, hence so is \(s\mapsto e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\mathbf 1_{(0,s]}\), and its integral over \([0,t]\) exists. Since \(I\) commutes with this integral and \(I(\mathbf 1_{(0,s]})=B_s\),

\[I(\kappa^{\psi_1}_t)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}B_s\,ds=I\Bigl(\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\mathbf 1_{(0,s]}\,ds\Bigr).\]

The map \(I\) is injective, being an isometry, so

\[\kappa^{\psi_1}_t=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\mathbf 1_{(0,s]}\,ds\qquad\text{in }L^2(\mathbb R).\qquad(1)\]

Apply \(\Lambda=I\circ\tau_a\) to (1), move it inside the integral, use linearity to pull out the scalar \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\), and use \(\Lambda(\mathbf 1_{(0,s]})=\Lambda(\kappa^1_s)=W^a_s\) from the first step:

\[P^a_t=\Lambda(\kappa^{\psi_1}_t)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\Lambda(\mathbf 1_{(0,s]})\,ds=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}W^a_s\,ds .\]

For the velocity, substitute this expression for \(P^a_t\) into the identity \(V^a_t+\gamma P^a_t=W^a_t\) of the previous step and solve for \(V^a_t\). \(\square\)

The right-hand sides involve only the continuous path \(s\mapsto W^a_s\) and ordinary integrals, so they can be inserted into the pathwise kinetic integral equation with continuous forcing.

KineticLangevin/MildEquation.lean.title: The exponential integral formula for velocity
KineticLangevin/MildEquation.lean.summary:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a real Banach space, let \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\) and \(T\ge0\). The velocity of the kinetic diffusion satisfies an integral equation of the form \(V_t-V_0=-\int_0^t(\gamma V_s+F_s)\,ds+W_t\), where \(F\) is the force term along the path and \(W\) is the noise. The first-order KLMC update instead uses the variation-of-constants (mild) form

\[V_T=e^{-\gamma T}V_0-\int_0^Te^{-\gamma(T-s)}F_s\,ds+B_T,\]

in which the noise enters through the filtered process \(B\) solving \(B_t=W_t-\gamma\int_0^tB_s\,ds\) (in the stochastic application \(B_T=\int_0^Te^{-\gamma(T-s)}\,dW_s\)). This module proves that every continuous solution of the integral equation satisfies the mild form. The noise \(W\) is not differentiated: only \(V\), \(F\) and \(B\) are assumed continuous, and the identity is derived from the two integral equations.

The result is used with \(\mathcal X=L^2\) of random vectors, to identify the velocity of an exact kinetic segment with the expression whose force term is frozen by the KLMC step, when both are driven by the same Brownian increments.

steps.title: Subtract the filtered noise and apply an integrating factor
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mathcal X\) be a real Banach space, \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(T\ge0\), and let \(V,F,W,B:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X\) with \(V\), \(F\), \(B\) continuous (no regularity of \(W\) is assumed). Suppose that for every \(t\in[0,T]\)

\[V_t-V_0=-\int_0^t(\gamma V_s+F_s)\,ds+W_t\qquad(1)\] \[B_t=W_t-\gamma\int_0^tB_s\,ds.\qquad(2)\]

Then

\[V_T=e^{-\gamma T}V_0-\int_0^Te^{-\gamma(T-s)}F_s\,ds+B_T .\]

The integrals are Bochner integrals of continuous \(\mathcal X\)-valued functions on bounded intervals; they are linear in the integrand, commute with multiplication by real scalars, and satisfy the fundamental theorem of calculus.

Proof. Step 1: \(B_0=0\). At \(t=0\) both integrals vanish, so (1) gives \(0=W_0\), and then (2) gives \(B_0=W_0=0\).

Step 2: the equation for \(D=V-B\). The function \(D\) is continuous. For \(t\in[0,T]\), linearity of the integral (all integrands are continuous, hence integrable on \([0,t]\)) gives

\[\int_0^t(\gamma D_s+F_s)\,ds=\int_0^t(\gamma V_s+F_s)\,ds-\gamma\int_0^tB_s\,ds .\]

Subtracting (2) from (1) rearranged as \(V_t=V_0-\int_0^t(\gamma V_s+F_s)\,ds+W_t\), the noise \(W_t\) cancels:

\[D_t=V_t-B_t=V_0-\int_0^t(\gamma V_s+F_s)\,ds+\gamma\int_0^tB_s\,ds=V_0-\int_0^t(\gamma D_s+F_s)\,ds .\qquad(3)\]

Step 3: derivative of \(D\). Fix \(s\in(0,T)\). The integrand \(u\mapsto\gamma D_u+F_u\) is continuous, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus the function \(t\mapsto V_0-\int_0^t(\gamma D_u+F_u)\,du\) is differentiable at \(s\) with derivative \(-(\gamma D_s+F_s)\). By (3) this function coincides with \(D\) on the open interval \((0,T)\), which is a neighbourhood of \(s\); derivatives depend only on the values near the point, so \(D'(s)=-(\gamma D_s+F_s)\).

Step 4: integrating factor. For \(s\in(0,T)\), the product rule for a real function times a vector function gives

\[\frac{d}{ds}\bigl(e^{\gamma s}D_s\bigr)=\gamma e^{\gamma s}D_s+e^{\gamma s}D'(s)=\gamma e^{\gamma s}D_s-e^{\gamma s}(\gamma D_s+F_s)=-e^{\gamma s}F_s .\]

The function \(s\mapsto e^{\gamma s}D_s\) is continuous on \([0,T]\), differentiable on \((0,T)\), and its derivative \(s\mapsto-e^{\gamma s}F_s\) is continuous, hence integrable on \([0,T]\). The fundamental theorem of calculus therefore gives, using \(D_0=V_0-B_0=V_0\) from Step 1,

\[e^{\gamma T}D_T-V_0=-\int_0^Te^{\gamma s}F_s\,ds .\qquad(4)\]

Step 5: conclusion. Multiply (4) by \(e^{-\gamma T}\). Since \(e^{-\gamma T}e^{\gamma T}=1\) and scalar multiplication commutes with the integral, \(e^{-\gamma T}e^{\gamma s}=e^{-\gamma(T-s)}\) gives

\[D_T=e^{-\gamma T}V_0-\int_0^Te^{-\gamma(T-s)}F_s\,ds .\]

Adding \(B_T\) to both sides, \(V_T=D_T+B_T\) is the claimed formula. \(\square\)

No sign condition on \(\gamma\) is needed, and \(T=0\) is allowed (then the claim reads \(V_0=V_0+B_0\), consistent with Step 1). Continuity of \(B\) is used in Step 2 to integrate \(B\) and in Step 4 to integrate the derivative; without it the difference \(D\) need not be differentiable.

KineticLangevin/OBABORemainder.lean.title: Discrete remainder bounds in the OBABO energy
KineticLangevin/OBABORemainder.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a real inner product space and write phase points velocity first, \(s=(v,x)\in H\times H\). For real parameters \(a,b\) the weighted phase energy and its polarisation are

\[\mathcal E_{a,b}(v,x)=\|x\|^2+2b\langle x,v\rangle+a\|v\|^2,\qquad \mathcal B_{a,b}(s,s')=\langle x,x'\rangle+b\bigl(\langle x,v'\rangle+\langle v,x'\rangle\bigr)+a\langle v,v'\rangle\]

for \(s=(v,x)\), \(s'=(v',x')\). The OBABO analysis uses \(a=1/L\), \(b=1/\gamma\) with friction \(\gamma>0\) and a constant \(L>0\) (the Lipschitz constant of the gradient in the application) satisfying \(4L\le\gamma^2\); we then write \(\mathcal E=\mathcal E_{1/L,1/\gamma}\) and \(\mathcal B=\mathcal B_{1/L,1/\gamma}\). Recall from the module on the OBABO energy that if \(b\ge0\) and \(4b^2\le a\), then

\[\tfrac12\bigl(\|x\|^2+a\|v\|^2\bigr)\le\mathcal E_{a,b}(v,x)\le\tfrac32\bigl(\|x\|^2+a\|v\|^2\bigr),\]

and that for \(a=1/L,b=1/\gamma\) the condition \(4b^2\le a\) is \(4L\le\gamma^2\). Multiplying by \(2L\), respectively \(L\), this gives the two forms used repeatedly below:

\[L\|x\|^2+\|v\|^2\le2L\,\mathcal E(v,x),\qquad L\,\mathcal E(r)\le\tfrac32\bigl(L\|r_2\|^2+\|r_1\|^2\bigr)\quad\text{for }r=(r_1,r_2).\qquad(\ast)\]

This module proves the purely algebraic part of the one-step contraction of the OBABO scheme. It realises \(\mathcal E_{a,b}\) as the square of a Hilbert norm, expands the energy of a state of the form \(s+hA+r\) (Euler increment along the kinetic drift \(A=(-\gamma v-F,v)\) plus a remainder \(r\)), bounds each term, and concludes that the difference of two synchronously coupled OBABO steps contracts the energy by the factor \(1-mh/(3\gamma)\) whenever the step satisfies \(33\gamma^3h\le m\), \(\gamma h\le1\) and \(12\gamma^2h^2\le1\). The force, the damping factor \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) and the dissipativity inequality are inputs here; they are supplied from the potential in the module on OBABO contraction.

steps.title: The weighted energy as the square of a Hilbert norm
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(H\oplus_2H\) denote \(H\times H\) with the inner product \(\langle(p,q),(p',q')\rangle=\langle p,p'\rangle+\langle q,q'\rangle\) and the Euclidean norm \(\|(p,q)\|_2=(\|p\|^2+\|q\|^2)^{1/2}\). For \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) define

\[T_{a,b}(v,x)=\bigl(x+bv,\ \sqrt{a-b^2}\,v\bigr)\in H\oplus_2H,\qquad N_{a,b}(s)=\|T_{a,b}s\|_2,\]

where \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) is the nonnegative square root (and \(\sqrt y=0\) for \(y<0\)), and let \(\mathcal B_{a,b}\) be the pairing defined above.

Claim. Assume \(b^2\le a\). Then for all \(s,s'\in H\times H\):

  1. \(N_{a,b}(s)^2=\mathcal E_{a,b}(s)\);
  2. \(\mathcal B_{a,b}(s,s')=\langle T_{a,b}s,T_{a,b}s'\rangle\);
  3. \(\mathcal B_{a,b}(s,s')\le N_{a,b}(s)\,N_{a,b}(s')\).

Proof. Put \(c=\sqrt{a-b^2}\); since \(a-b^2\ge0\), \(c^2=a-b^2\). (1) By the definition of the Euclidean norm, the expansion \(\|x+bv\|^2=\|x\|^2+2b\langle x,v\rangle+b^2\|v\|^2\) and \(\|cv\|^2=c^2\|v\|^2\),

\[N_{a,b}(v,x)^2=\|x\|^2+2b\langle x,v\rangle+b^2\|v\|^2+(a-b^2)\|v\|^2=\mathcal E_{a,b}(v,x).\]

(2) By bilinearity of the inner product,

\[\langle T_{a,b}s,T_{a,b}s'\rangle=\langle x+bv,x'+bv'\rangle+c^2\langle v,v'\rangle=\langle x,x'\rangle+b\langle x,v'\rangle+b\langle v,x'\rangle+(b^2+a-b^2)\langle v,v'\rangle,\]

which is \(\mathcal B_{a,b}(s,s')\). (3) follows from (2) and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in \(H\oplus_2H\). \(\square\)

Thus, when \(b^2\le a\), \(N_{a,b}\) is a seminorm on \(H\times H\) whose square is the energy, and \(\mathcal B_{a,b}\) is the associated symmetric bilinear form. The Euclidean product norm is needed here: with the maximum norm on \(H\times H\) the square of the norm of \(T_{a,b}s\) would not be \(\mathcal E_{a,b}(s)\).

steps.title: Expansion of the energy of an Euler step plus a remainder
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(a,b,h,c\in\mathbb R\) and \(s,t,A,r\in H\times H\).

  1. \(\mathcal E_{a,b}(s+t)=\mathcal E_{a,b}(s)+2\mathcal B_{a,b}(s,t)+\mathcal E_{a,b}(t)\) and \(\mathcal E_{a,b}(cs)=c^2\mathcal E_{a,b}(s)\).
  2. If \(b^2\le a\), then \(\mathcal E_{a,b}(s+t)\le2\mathcal E_{a,b}(s)+2\mathcal E_{a,b}(t)\).
  3. If \(b^2\le a\), then \[\mathcal E_{a,b}(s+hA+r)\le\mathcal E_{a,b}(s)+2h\,\mathcal B_{a,b}(s,A)+2N_{a,b}(s)N_{a,b}(r)+2h^2\mathcal E_{a,b}(A)+2\mathcal E_{a,b}(r).\]
  4. If \(\gamma\ne0\) and \(L\ne0\), then for all \(v,x,F\in H\) \[2\,\mathcal B_{1/L,1/\gamma}\bigl((v,x),(-\gamma v-F,v)\bigr)=\mathcal D(v,x,F):=\frac{-2L\langle x,F\rangle+(2L-2\gamma^2)\|v\|^2-2\gamma\langle v,F\rangle}{\gamma L}.\]

Proof. (1) Write \(s=(v,x)\), \(t=(v',x')\). Expanding each square and the mixed term by bilinearity,

\[\begin{aligned}\mathcal E_{a,b}(s+t)&=\|x\|^2+2\langle x,x'\rangle+\|x'\|^2+2b\bigl(\langle x,v\rangle+\langle x,v'\rangle+\langle x',v\rangle+\langle x',v'\rangle\bigr)\\&\quad+a\bigl(\|v\|^2+2\langle v,v'\rangle+\|v'\|^2\bigr),\end{aligned}\]

and collecting the terms that involve both \(s\) and \(t\) gives \(2\langle x,x'\rangle+2b(\langle x,v'\rangle+\langle v,x'\rangle)+2a\langle v,v'\rangle=2\mathcal B_{a,b}(s,t)\), using symmetry \(\langle x',v\rangle=\langle v,x'\rangle\). The scaling identity holds because every term of \(\mathcal E_{a,b}\) is quadratic in \(s\).

(2) By (1) and part 3 of the previous step, \(\mathcal E_{a,b}(s+t)\le\mathcal E_{a,b}(s)+2N(s)N(t)+\mathcal E_{a,b}(t)\), with \(N=N_{a,b}\). From \((N(s)-N(t))^2\ge0\) we get \(2N(s)N(t)\le N(s)^2+N(t)^2=\mathcal E_{a,b}(s)+\mathcal E_{a,b}(t)\), by part 1 of the previous step. Adding gives the claim.

(3) Group \(s+hA+r=s+(hA+r)\) and apply (1): \(\mathcal E(s+hA+r)=\mathcal E(s)+2\mathcal B(s,hA+r)+\mathcal E(hA+r)\). By bilinearity \(\mathcal B(s,hA+r)=h\mathcal B(s,A)+\mathcal B(s,r)\), and \(\mathcal B(s,r)\le N(s)N(r)\) by the previous step. By (2) and the scaling identity, \(\mathcal E(hA+r)\le2\mathcal E(hA)+2\mathcal E(r)=2h^2\mathcal E(A)+2\mathcal E(r)\). Adding these three bounds gives (3).

(4) With \(s=(v,x)\) and \(s'=(-\gamma v-F,v)\), so that \(v'=-\gamma v-F\) and \(x'=v\),

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal B_{1/L,1/\gamma}(s,s')&=\langle x,v\rangle +\frac1\gamma\bigl(\langle x,-\gamma v-F\rangle+\|v\|^2\bigr)\\ &\quad+\frac1L\langle v,-\gamma v-F\rangle\\ &=-\frac{\langle x,F\rangle}{\gamma}+\frac{\|v\|^2}{\gamma} -\frac{\gamma\|v\|^2}{L}-\frac{\langle v,F\rangle}{L}. \end{aligned}\]

since the terms \(\langle x,v\rangle\) cancel. Multiplying by \(2\) and writing everything over the common denominator \(\gamma L\) gives \(\mathcal D(v,x,F)\). \(\square\)

Along the kinetic drift \(\dot v=-\gamma v-F\), \(\dot x=v\), the derivative of \(\mathcal E(v,x)\) equals \(2\mathcal B(s,\dot s)=\mathcal D(v,x,F)\); inequality (3) is the discrete counterpart of this derivative for one Euler step \(s+hA\) perturbed by \(r\).

steps.title: Bounds for the drift and for the remainder
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma>0\), \(L>0\) with \(4L\le\gamma^2\), \(h\in\mathbb R\), and \(v,x,F\in H\).

  1. If \(\|F\|\le\frac{17}{16}L\|x\|+\frac\gamma8\|v\|\), then \(\mathcal E(-\gamma v-F,v)\le\frac{13}{4}\gamma^2\,\mathcal E(v,x)\).
  2. If \(r=(r_1,r_2)\in H\times H\) satisfies \[\|r_2\|\le h^2\Bigl(\frac\gamma2\|v\|+\frac L2\|x\|\Bigr),\qquad \|r_1\|\le h^2\Bigl(\frac9{16}\gamma L\|x\|+\frac58\gamma^2\|v\|\Bigr),\] then \(\mathcal E(r)\le3h^4\gamma^4\,\mathcal E(v,x)\).

Proof. (1) Write \(A=(-\gamma v-F,v)\): its velocity component is \(-\gamma v-F\) and its position component is \(v\). By definition and expansion of \(\|\gamma v+F\|^2\),

\[\begin{aligned} L\,\mathcal E(A)&=L\|v\|^2-2L\|v\|^2-\frac{2L}{\gamma}\langle v,F\rangle\\ &\quad+\gamma^2\|v\|^2+2\gamma\langle v,F\rangle+\|F\|^2\\ &=(\gamma^2-L)\|v\|^2+\|F\|^2 +2\Bigl(\gamma-\frac L\gamma\Bigr)\langle v,F\rangle. \end{aligned}\]

Since \(L\le\gamma^2/4\), we have \(0\le\gamma-L/\gamma\le\gamma\), so by Cauchy–Schwarz \(2(\gamma-L/\gamma)\langle v,F\rangle\le2\gamma\|v\|\|F\|\). Write \(\phi=\frac{17}{16}L\|x\|+\frac\gamma8\|v\|\ge\|F\|\). Then

\[\|F\|^2+2\gamma\|v\|\|F\|\le\phi^2+2\gamma\|v\|\phi=\frac{289}{256}L^2\|x\|^2+\frac{153}{64}\gamma L\|x\|\|v\|+\frac{17}{64}\gamma^2\|v\|^2 .\]

We bound the three terms. Young's inequality in the form \(\gamma\|x\|\|v\|\le\frac{\gamma^2}4\|x\|^2+\|v\|^2\) (equivalent to \((\gamma\|x\|-2\|v\|)^2\ge0\)) gives \(\frac{153}{64}\gamma L\|x\|\|v\|\le\frac{153}{256}\gamma^2L\|x\|^2+\frac{153}{64}L\|v\|^2\). From \(L\le\gamma^2/4\): \(\frac{289}{256}L^2\le\frac{289}{1024}\gamma^2L\), and \(-L+\frac{153}{64}L=\frac{89}{64}L\le\frac{89}{256}\gamma^2\). Collecting,

\[L\,\mathcal E(A)\le\frac{901}{1024}\gamma^2L\|x\|^2+\frac{413}{256}\gamma^2\|v\|^2\le\frac{13}{8}\gamma^2\bigl(L\|x\|^2+\|v\|^2\bigr),\]

because \(901/1024\le13/8\) and \(413/256\le13/8\). By \((\ast)\) the right-hand side is at most \(\frac{13}8\gamma^2\cdot2L\,\mathcal E(v,x)\). Dividing by \(L>0\) gives (1).

(2) By \((\ast)\), \(L\,\mathcal E(r)\le\frac32(L\|r_2\|^2+\|r_1\|^2)\). Squaring the hypotheses (both sides are nonnegative) and using \((p+q)^2\le2p^2+2q^2\), which is \((p-q)^2\ge0\),

\[\|r_2\|^2\le h^4\Bigl(\frac{\gamma^2}2\|v\|^2+\frac{L^2}2\|x\|^2\Bigr),\qquad\|r_1\|^2\le h^4\Bigl(\frac{81}{128}\gamma^2L^2\|x\|^2+\frac{25}{32}\gamma^4\|v\|^2\Bigr).\]

Hence

\[L\,\mathcal E(r)\le\frac32h^4\Bigl[L\|x\|^2\Bigl(\frac{L^2}2+\frac{81}{128}\gamma^2L\Bigr)+\|v\|^2\Bigl(\frac{L\gamma^2}2+\frac{25}{32}\gamma^4\Bigr)\Bigr].\]

Using \(L\le\gamma^2/4\): \(\frac{L^2}2+\frac{81}{128}\gamma^2L\le\frac{\gamma^4}{32}+\frac{81}{512}\gamma^4\le\gamma^4\) and \(\frac{L\gamma^2}2+\frac{25}{32}\gamma^4\le\frac{\gamma^4}8+\frac{25}{32}\gamma^4\le\gamma^4\). Therefore \(L\,\mathcal E(r)\le\frac32h^4\gamma^4(L\|x\|^2+\|v\|^2)\le3h^4\gamma^4L\,\mathcal E(v,x)\) by \((\ast)\), and dividing by \(L\) gives (2). \(\square\)

The hypotheses of (1) and (2) are explicit norm bounds on the force and on the components of the remainder; they are verified for the OBABO step in the last step of this module.

steps.title: The error in the centred sector inequality
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma>0\), \(L>0\), \(h\ge0\), with \(4L\le\gamma^2\) and \(\gamma h\le1\). Let \(e\ge0\) and \(v,x\in H\) satisfy

\[e\le hL\Bigl(\frac{\|v\|}2+\frac{\gamma\|x\|}{16}\Bigr).\]

Then

\[h\Bigl(\frac{2e\|x\|}{\gamma}+\frac{e^2}{\gamma L}\Bigr)\le\frac12\gamma^2h^2\,\mathcal E(v,x).\]

Proof. Multiply the left-hand side by \(\gamma^2L>0\); it becomes \(\gamma\bigl(2Lhe\|x\|+he^2\bigr)\), and we bound the two terms.

The term \(he^2\). Squaring the hypothesis (both sides nonnegative) and using \((p+q)^2\le2p^2+2q^2\),

\[e^2\le h^2L^2\Bigl(\frac{\|v\|}2+\frac{\gamma\|x\|}{16}\Bigr)^2\le h^2\Bigl(\frac{L^2}2\|v\|^2+\frac{\gamma^2L^2}{128}\|x\|^2\Bigr).\]

Multiplying by \(\gamma h\ge0\) and using \(\gamma h\le1\), \(\gamma he^2\le h^2\bigl(\frac{L^2}2\|v\|^2+\frac{\gamma^2L^2}{128}\|x\|^2\bigr)\).

The term \(2Lhe\|x\|\). Multiplying the hypothesis by \(2Lh\|x\|\ge0\) gives \(2Lhe\|x\|\le h^2L^2(\|x\|\|v\|+\frac\gamma8\|x\|^2)\). Multiplying by \(\gamma\) and using Young's inequality \(\gamma\|x\|\|v\|\le\frac{\gamma^2}4\|x\|^2+\|v\|^2\),

\[\gamma\cdot2Lhe\|x\|\le h^2L^2\Bigl(\frac{\gamma^2}4\|x\|^2+\|v\|^2+\frac{\gamma^2}8\|x\|^2\Bigr)=h^2\Bigl(\frac38\gamma^2L^2\|x\|^2+L^2\|v\|^2\Bigr).\]

Sum. Adding, \(\gamma(2Lhe\|x\|+he^2)\le h^2\bigl(\frac{49}{128}\gamma^2L^2\|x\|^2+\frac32L^2\|v\|^2\bigr)\). Since \(\frac{49}{128}\le\frac12\), and \(\frac32L^2\le2L^2\le\frac12\gamma^2L\) by \(4L\le\gamma^2\),

\[\gamma(2Lhe\|x\|+he^2)\le\frac12\gamma^2Lh^2\bigl(L\|x\|^2+\|v\|^2\bigr)\le\gamma^2L^2h^2\,\mathcal E(v,x)\le\frac12\gamma^4Lh^2\,\mathcal E(v,x),\]

where the second inequality is \((\ast)\) and the third uses \(L\le\gamma^2/4\le\gamma^2/2\) and \(\mathcal E(v,x)\ge0\). Dividing by \(\gamma^2L\) gives \(\frac{2he\|x\|}{\gamma}+\frac{he^2}{\gamma L}\le\frac12\gamma^2h^2\mathcal E(v,x)\), which is the claim. \(\square\)

In the OBABO step the averaged force difference satisfies a centred sector inequality only up to an error \(e\), proportional to the position displacement during the step; the dissipativity estimate then contains the extra terms \(2e\|x\|/\gamma+e^2/(\gamma L)\), and the claim shows that after multiplication by \(h\) they are of second order in \(h\).

steps.title: The step-size condition from the sum of the remainder bounds
steps.body:
Claim A. Let \(\gamma>0\), \(L>0\), \(h\ge0\), \(m\in\mathbb R\), with

\[4L\le\gamma^2,\qquad\gamma h\le1,\qquad12\gamma^2h^2\le1,\qquad33\gamma^3h\le m .\]

Let \(e\ge0\), \(v,x,F\in H\) and \(r=(r_1,r_2)\in H\times H\) satisfy the hypothesis of the previous step on \(e\), the force bound \(\|F\|\le\frac{17}{16}L\|x\|+\frac\gamma8\|v\|\), the two remainder bounds of the third step, and the perturbed dissipativity inequality

\[\mathcal D(v,x,F)\le-\frac{2m}{3\gamma}\,\mathcal E(v,x)+\frac{2e\|x\|}{\gamma}+\frac{e^2}{\gamma L}.\qquad(1)\]

Then, with \(s=(v,x)\) and \(A=(-\gamma v-F,v)\),

\[\mathcal E(s+hA+r)\le\Bigl(1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma}\Bigr)\mathcal E(s).\]

Proof. Since \(4L\le\gamma^2\) we have \((1/\gamma)^2\le1/(4L)\le1/L\), so the results of the first two steps apply with \(a=1/L\), \(b=1/\gamma\). Write \(\mathcal E=\mathcal E(s)\ge0\). By part 3 of the second step,

\[\mathcal E(s+hA+r)\le\mathcal E+2h\mathcal B(s,A)+2N(s)N(r)+2h^2\mathcal E(A)+2\mathcal E(r).\qquad(2)\]

We bound the four terms after \(\mathcal E\).

  • By part 4 of the second step, \(2h\mathcal B(s,A)=h\mathcal D(v,x,F)\). Multiplying (1) by \(h\ge0\) and applying the previous step, \(2h\mathcal B(s,A)\le-\frac{2mh}{3\gamma}\mathcal E+\frac12\gamma^2h^2\mathcal E\).
  • By the third step, \(N(r)^2=\mathcal E(r)\le3h^4\gamma^4\mathcal E\le\frac{49}{16}h^4\gamma^4N(s)^2\). Both \(N(r)\) and \(\frac74h^2\gamma^2N(s)\) are nonnegative, so \(N(r)\le\frac74h^2\gamma^2N(s)\), and \(2N(s)N(r)\le\frac72\gamma^2h^2\mathcal E\).
  • By the third step, \(2h^2\mathcal E(A)\le\frac{13}2\gamma^2h^2\mathcal E\).
  • By the third step and \(12\gamma^2h^2\le1\), \(2\mathcal E(r)\le6h^4\gamma^4\mathcal E=(12\gamma^2h^2)\cdot\frac12\gamma^2h^2\mathcal E\le\frac12\gamma^2h^2\mathcal E\).

Inserting these four bounds into (2), and using \(\frac12+\frac72+\frac{13}2+\frac12=11\),

\[\mathcal E(s+hA+r)\le\Bigl(1-\frac{2mh}{3\gamma}+11\gamma^2h^2\Bigr)\mathcal E .\]

Finally, multiplying \(33\gamma^3h\le m\) by \(h\ge0\) and dividing by \(3\gamma>0\) gives \(11\gamma^2h^2\le\frac{mh}{3\gamma}\); hence \(1-\frac{2mh}{3\gamma}+11\gamma^2h^2\le1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma}\), and multiplying by \(\mathcal E\ge0\) proves the claim. \(\square\)

Claim B. Let \(\gamma,L,h,m\) satisfy the hypotheses of Claim A, let \(e\ge0\), and let \(\delta\in[0,1]\) satisfy

\[1-\delta\le\frac{\gamma h}2,\qquad0\le\delta^2-1+\gamma h\le\frac{\gamma^2h^2}2 .\qquad(3)\]

Let \(v,x,F_0,F\in H\) with \(\|F_0\|\le L\|x\|\), \(\|F\|\le L\|x\|+e\), \(e\le\frac L2\bigl(h\|v\|+\frac{h^2L}2\|x\|\bigr)\), and the dissipativity inequality (1). Then

\[\mathcal E\Bigl(\delta^2v-h\delta F,\ x+h\delta v-\frac{h^2}2F_0\Bigr)\le\Bigl(1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma}\Bigr)\mathcal E(v,x).\]

Proof. We verify the hypotheses of Claim A for a suitable remainder. First, \(4Lh\le\gamma^2h=\gamma(\gamma h)\le\gamma\), so \(Lh\le\gamma/4\).

Bound on \(e\). \(e\le\frac{hL}2\|v\|+\frac{h^2L^2}4\|x\|\), and \(\frac{h^2L^2}4\|x\|=\frac{hL\|x\|}4\,(Lh)\le\frac{hL\gamma}{16}\|x\|\); hence \(e\le hL(\frac{\|v\|}2+\frac{\gamma\|x\|}{16})\).

Bound on \(F\). \(\|F\|\le L\|x\|+e\le L\|x\|+\frac{hL}2\|v\|+\frac{\gamma hL}{16}\|x\|\le\frac{17}{16}L\|x\|+\frac\gamma8\|v\|\), using \(\gamma h\le1\) and \(Lh\le\gamma/4\).

The remainder. Define \(r=(r_1,r_2)\) by

\[r_1=(\delta^2-1+\gamma h)v+h(1-\delta)F,\qquad r_2=h(\delta-1)v-\frac{h^2}2F_0 .\]

By the triangle inequality, \(0\le1-\delta\le\gamma h/2\) and \(\|F_0\|\le L\|x\|\),

\[\|r_2\|\le h(1-\delta)\|v\|+\frac{h^2}2\|F_0\|\le h^2\Bigl(\frac\gamma2\|v\|+\frac L2\|x\|\Bigr).\]

By the triangle inequality, (3) and the bound on \(F\),

\[\|r_1\|\le\frac{\gamma^2h^2}2\|v\|+\frac{\gamma h^2}2\Bigl(\frac{17}{16}L\|x\|+\frac\gamma8\|v\|\Bigr)=h^2\Bigl(\frac{17}{32}\gamma L\|x\|+\frac9{16}\gamma^2\|v\|\Bigr)\le h^2\Bigl(\frac9{16}\gamma L\|x\|+\frac58\gamma^2\|v\|\Bigr).\]

Thus all hypotheses of Claim A hold. Finally, componentwise,

\[(v,x)+h(-\gamma v-F,v)+r=\Bigl(\delta^2v-h\delta F,\ x+h\delta v-\frac{h^2}2F_0\Bigr),\]

because \(v-\gamma hv-hF+(\delta^2-1+\gamma h)v+h(1-\delta)F=\delta^2v-h\delta F\) and \(x+hv+h(\delta-1)v-\frac{h^2}2F_0=x+h\delta v-\frac{h^2}2F_0\). Claim A gives the result. \(\square\)

In the application \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) is the velocity damping of one Ornstein–Uhlenbeck half step, \(F_0\) is the difference of the two gradients at the initial positions and \(F\) the average of the two gradient differences of the two kicks; the left-hand side of Claim B is then the energy of the difference of two OBABO steps driven by the same Gaussian noise. The inequalities (3) hold for \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) because \(1-u\le e^{-u}\) and \(0\le e^{-u}-1+u\le u^2/2\) for \(u\ge0\).

KineticLangevin/ProductLaw.lean.title: KLMC output laws on independent extensions of initial couplings
KineticLangevin/ProductLaw.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a separable real Hilbert space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, \(\mu\) a probability measure on \(H\) (the law of the initial position) and \(\pi\) a measure on \(H\) with \(\int\|y\|^2\,\pi(dy)<\infty\) (the reference law). A coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) is a measure \(c\) on \(H imes H\) whose image under \((x,y)\mapsto x\) is \(\mu\) and whose image under \((x,y)\mapsto y\) is \(\pi\); its cost is \( igl(\int\|x-y\|^2\,c(dx\,dy) igr)^{1/2}\in[0,\infty]\), and the Wasserstein distance \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\) is the infimum of these costs over all couplings. The randomness of the algorithm is carried by a probability space \((S,Q)\) (the source), on which are given an initial velocity \(V:S o H\) and innovations \(W_k=(W_k^{(1)},W_k^{(2)}):S o H imes H\), \(k\in\mathbb N\), with \(V,W_k^{(1)},W_k^{(2)}\) square integrable.

The KLMC step with force \( abla f\), friction \(\gamma\) and step \(h\) is

\[\Psi igl((v,x),\xi igr)=\Bigl(\psi_0(h)v-\psi_1(h) abla f(x)+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi_1,\ x+\psi_1(h)v-\psi_2(h) abla f(x)+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi_2\Bigr),\]

with \(\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\), \(\psi_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^t\psi_k\). Let \(\Phi_n(x,s)\) be the position after \(n\) steps of the recursion \(z_{k+1}=\Psi(z_k,W_k(s))\) started at \(z_0=(V(s),x)\), and let \( u_n\) be the image of \(\mu\otimes Q\) under \(\Phi_n\): this is the law of the \(n\)-th KLMC position when the initial position is drawn from \(\mu\) independently of the source.

The error analysis is carried out, for each coupling \(c\), on the extension \(P_c=c\otimes Q\) on \((H imes H) imes S\), with square-integrable random variables. The module proves that the position of the KLMC chain computed on this extension has law \( u_n\), whatever the coupling \(c\). This is what allows the transport estimate obtained for one coupling to be minimised over all couplings, which turns it into a bound on \(W_2( u_n,\pi)\). No Gaussian assumption on the innovations is needed for these identities.

steps.title: Velocity and innovations on each product extension
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(c\) be a coupling of the probability measure \(\mu\) and of \(\pi\). Then \(P_c=c\otimes Q\) is a probability measure on \((H\times H)\times S\). Write its points as \(\omega=((x,y),s)\). The maps

\[\omega\mapsto V(s),\qquad\omega\mapsto W_k^{(1)}(s),\qquad\omega\mapsto W_k^{(2)}(s)\]

belong to \(L^2(P_c;H)\) for every \(k\), and so define elements of this Hilbert space: the extended initial velocity \(\bar V\) and the extended innovations \(\bar W_k=(\bar W_k^{(1)},\bar W_k^{(2)})\).

Proof. The image of \(c\) under the first projection is \(\mu\), so \(c(H\times H)=\mu(H)=1\). A product of two probability measures is a probability measure, since \((c\otimes Q)\bigl((H\times H)\times S\bigr)=c(H\times H)\,Q(S)=1\). The projection \(\omega\mapsto s\) maps \(P_c\) to \(Q\) (the first factor has mass one), so by the change-of-variables formula \(\int\|V(s)\|^2\,P_c(d\omega)=\int\|V\|^2\,dQ<\infty\); the composed map is measurable up to a null set because \(V\) is. The same argument applies to each component of each \(W_k\). \(\square\)

The two components of \(\bar W_k\) are built from the same source point \(s\), so the joint law of \((W_k^{(1)},W_k^{(2)})\), in particular the correlation between velocity and position innovations prescribed by the KLMC covariance matrix, is preserved. The initial velocity is the same random variable for every coupling and is independent of the initial positions under \(P_c\).

steps.title: The chosen square-integrable representatives
steps.body:
Claim. In the setting of the previous step, \(\bar V(\omega)=V(s)\) and \(\bigl(\bar W_k^{(1)}(\omega),\bar W_k^{(2)}(\omega)\bigr)=W_k(s)\) for \(P_c\)-almost every \(\omega=((x,y),s)\), for every \(k\).

Proof. An element of \(L^2(P_c;H)\) is an equivalence class of functions that agree almost everywhere; evaluating it at \(\omega\) means evaluating a fixed representative. The class of a square-integrable function \(g\) has a representative that agrees with \(g\) almost everywhere, which is the statement for \(\bar V\). For \(\bar W_k\), each component agrees with the corresponding component of \(W_k(s)\) outside a null set; outside the union of the two null sets, which is null, both components agree, and two pairs with equal components are equal. \(\square\)

This is an almost-everywhere identity of random variables, not merely an equality of moments or covariances.

steps.title: The numerical output law
steps.body:
Definition. For \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(x\in H\) and \(s\in S\), let \(z_0=(V(s),x)\) and \(z_{k+1}=\Psi(z_k,W_k(s))\) for \(k<n\), and let \(\Phi_n(x,s)\in H\) be the position component of \(z_n\). For a measure \( u\) on \(H\), the output law is the image measure

\[ u\otimes Q\circ\Phi_n^{-1},\qquad ext{i.e.}\qquad A\mapsto( u\otimes Q) igl(\{(x,s):\Phi_n(x,s)\in A\} igr).\]

With \( u=\mu\) this is \( u_n\), the law of the \(n\)-th KLMC position when the initial position has law \(\mu\) and is independent of the source. The definition involves neither the reference law \(\pi\) nor a coupling.

steps.title: The square-integrable chain agrees with the pointwise chain
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(c\) be a coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) with finite cost, assume \(\int\|y\|^2\,\pi(dy)<\infty\), and let \(\nabla f\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz. On the extension \(P_c\) define the square-integrable KLMC chain by \(Z_0=(\bar V,X_0)\), where \(X_0(\omega)=x\) is the first coordinate, and \(Z_{k+1}=\Psi(Z_k,\bar W_k)\), the force being applied to square-integrable random variables. Then for every \(n\) the position component of \(Z_n\) satisfies

\[Z_n^{(2)}(\omega)=\Phi_n(x,s)\qquad\text{for }P_c\text{-almost every }\omega=((x,y),s).\]

Proof. Square integrability of \(X_0\). By the triangle inequality \(\|x\|\le\|x-y\|+\|y\|\). The function \(\omega\mapsto x-y\) is square integrable because the cost of \(c\) is finite, and \(\omega\mapsto y\) is square integrable because its law under \(P_c\) is \(\pi\), which has a finite second moment. By Minkowski's inequality \(X_0\in L^2(P_c;H)\). Since \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz, \(\|\nabla f(X)\|\le\|\nabla f(0)\|+M\|X\|\), so \(\nabla f(X)\in L^2(P_c;H)\) whenever \(X\) is; hence every \(Z_k\) is a pair of square-integrable random variables.

Comparison. By the result of the module on square-integrable dynamics, proved by induction on \(n\), the representative of \(Z_n\) agrees almost everywhere with the pointwise chain applied to the representatives of the initial state and of the innovations:

\[Z_n(\omega)=z_n\bigl(Z_0(\omega),(\bar W_k(\omega))_{k}\bigr)\quad P_c\text{-a.e.},\]

where \(z_n(z,(\xi_k)_k)\) denotes the \(n\)-th point of the recursion started at \(z\) with innovations \(\xi_k\). By the previous steps, \(Z_0(\omega)=(V(s),x)\) almost everywhere, and \(\bar W_k(\omega)=W_k(s)\) almost everywhere for each \(k\). A countable union of null sets is null, so there is a single null set outside of which all these identities hold simultaneously for every \(k\). For \(\omega\) outside this set the two recursions have the same initial state and the same innovations, hence \(Z_n(\omega)=z_n((V(s),x),(W_k(s))_k)\), whose position component is \(\Phi_n(x,s)\). \(\square\)

Both chains are started from the same velocity variable, so no separate cost for the initial velocities appears.

steps.title: Independence of the output law from the coupling
steps.body:
Recall that a map \(F\) is measurable \(P\)-almost everywhere if it agrees \(P\)-almost everywhere with a measurable map; image measures under such maps are defined through that measurable version.

Claim. Let \(c\) be a coupling of the probability measure \(\mu\) and of \(\pi\).

  1. If \(F:H\times S\to H\) is measurable \((\mu\otimes Q)\)-almost everywhere, then the image of \(P_c\) under \(((x,y),s)\mapsto F(x,s)\) equals the image of \(\mu\otimes Q\) under \(F\).
  2. If \(\nabla f\) is \(M\)-Lipschitz and \(V,W_k^{(1)},W_k^{(2)}\) are square integrable, then \(\Phi_n\) is measurable \((\mu\otimes Q)\)-almost everywhere.
  3. Under the hypotheses of the previous step, the law of \(Z_n^{(2)}\) under \(P_c\) is \(\nu_n\).

Proof. (1) Let \(\rho((x,y),s)=(x,s)\). The image of a product measure under a product of measurable maps is the product of the images; since \(c\) has first marginal \(\mu\), \(\rho\) maps \(P_c=c\otimes Q\) to \(\mu\otimes Q\). For measurable \(\rho\) and \(F\) measurable almost everywhere with respect to the image measure, the image of \(P_c\) under \(F\circ\rho\) is the image of \(\rho\)'s image under \(F\) (substitute the measurable version of \(F\); the exceptional set has \(P_c\)-null preimage). Hence \(P_c\circ(F\circ\rho)^{-1}=(\mu\otimes Q)\circ F^{-1}\).

(2) The map \((z,\xi)\mapsto\Psi(z,\xi)\) is continuous, being built from addition, multiplication by the constants \(\psi_j(h)\) and \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\), and the continuous (Lipschitz) map \(\nabla f\); hence it is measurable. The projection \((x,s)\mapsto s\) maps \(\mu\otimes Q\) to \(Q\) because \(\mu(H)=1\), so the maps \((x,s)\mapsto V(s)\) and \((x,s)\mapsto W_k(s)\) are measurable almost everywhere. We prove by induction on \(k\) that \(g_k(x,s)=z_k\) is measurable almost everywhere. For \(k=0\), \(g_0(x,s)=(V(s),x)\) is a pair of almost everywhere measurable maps. If \(g_k\) is, then \(g_{k+1}=\Psi\circ(g_k,W_k)\) is a measurable map applied to an almost everywhere measurable pair. Finally \(\Phi_n\) is the position component of \(g_n\).

(3) Image measures of almost everywhere equal maps coincide. By the previous step, \(Z_n^{(2)}=\Phi_n\circ\rho\) \(P_c\)-almost everywhere, so the law of \(Z_n^{(2)}\) is the image of \(P_c\) under \(\Phi_n\circ\rho\), which by (1) and (2) is \((\mu\otimes Q)\circ\Phi_n^{-1}=\nu_n\). \(\square\)

The coupling \(c\) influences the joint law of the algorithm and the reference, and hence the transport cost, but not the marginal law \(\nu_n\) of the algorithm.

steps.title: The output law is a probability measure
steps.body:
Claim. If \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz and \(V,W_k^{(1)},W_k^{(2)}\) are square integrable, then \(\nu_n\) is a probability measure for every \(n\).

Proof. \(\mu\otimes Q\) is a probability measure, and by part 2 of the previous step \(\Phi_n\) is measurable almost everywhere. The image of a probability measure under an almost everywhere measurable map has total mass \((\mu\otimes Q)(\Phi_n^{-1}(H))=(\mu\otimes Q)(H\times S)=1\). \(\square\)

KineticLangevin/OBABOContraction.lean.title: Contraction of the nonlinear OBABO map and its iterates
KineticLangevin/OBABOContraction.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) a differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex function whose gradient is \(M\)-Lipschitz, with \(0\le m\le M\) and \(M>0\). For friction \(\gamma>0\), step \(h\ge0\), damping \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) and a noise coefficient \(\sigma\in\mathbb R\), the OBABO step maps a phase point \(z=(v,x)\) (velocity first) and two noise vectors \(\xi,\xi'\in H\) to \(\Phi(z;\xi,\xi')\), computed by the five substeps

\[\begin{aligned}&v_1=\delta v+\sigma\xi,\quad v_2=v_1-\tfrac h2\nabla f(x),\quad x_1=x+hv_2,\\&v_3=v_2-\tfrac h2\nabla f(x_1),\quad v_4=\delta v_3+\sigma\xi',\qquad\Phi(z;\xi,\xi')=(v_4,x_1):\end{aligned}\]

an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck half step (O), a half kick (B), a drift (A), a half kick (B) and an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck half step (O). With \(\mathcal E=\mathcal E_{1/M,1/\gamma}\), \(\mathcal E(v,x)=\|x\|^2+\frac2\gamma\langle x,v\rangle+\frac1M\|v\|^2\), the module proves that if \(4M\le\gamma^2\) and \(33\gamma^3h\le m\), then for all \(z,w\) and all noise vectors

\[\mathcal E\bigl(\Phi(z;\xi,\xi')-\Phi(w;\xi,\xi')\bigr)\le\Bigl(1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma}\Bigr)\mathcal E(z-w).\]

The two chains are driven by the same noise vectors (synchronous coupling), so the noise cancels in the difference and no distributional assumption on it is needed; the statement holds for every \(\sigma\). Iterating gives geometric decay of \(\mathcal E\) along two coupled OBABO chains, and, when the initial velocities coincide, the position bound \(\|X_n-Y_n\|\le\sqrt{2q^n}\,\|X_0-Y_0\|\) with \(q=1-mh/(3\gamma)\). These bounds are the contraction ingredient of the OBABO convergence analysis.

steps.title: The small-step and exponential damping bounds
steps.body:
Claim. (a) Let \(\gamma>0\), \(h\ge0\), \(m\le L\), \(4L\le\gamma^2\) and \(33\gamma^3h\le m\). Then \(\gamma h\le1\) and \(12\gamma^2h^2\le1\).

(b) Let \(\gamma\ge0\), \(h\ge0\) and \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\). Then

\[0\le\delta\le1,\qquad1-\delta\le\frac{\gamma h}2,\qquad0\le\delta^2-1+\gamma h\le\frac{\gamma^2h^2}2 .\]

Proof. (a) Chaining the hypotheses, \(33\gamma^3h\le m\le L\le\gamma^2/4\). Dividing by \(33\gamma^2>0\) gives \(\gamma h\le1/132\). Hence \(\gamma h\le1\), and since \(0\le\gamma h\le1/132\), squaring gives \(\gamma^2h^2\le1/132^2\), so \(12\gamma^2h^2\le12/17424\le1\).

(b) The exponential is positive, so \(\delta>0\); and \(-\gamma h/2\le0\) gives \(\delta\le e^0=1\). The tangent-line inequality \(e^u\ge1+u\), valid for all real \(u\), applied with \(u=-\gamma h/2\) gives \(\delta\ge1-\gamma h/2\), i.e. \(1-\delta\le\gamma h/2\); applied with \(u=-\gamma h\) and using \(\delta^2=e^{-\gamma h}\), it gives \(\delta^2\ge1-\gamma h\). Finally, for \(u\ge0\) we have \(e^{-u}\le1-u+u^2/2\) (proved earlier: the function \(1-u+u^2/2-e^{-u}\) vanishes at \(0\) and has derivative \(-1+u+e^{-u}\ge0\)); with \(u=\gamma h\ge0\) this gives \(\delta^2-1+\gamma h\le\gamma^2h^2/2\). \(\square\)

Part (b) shows that the exact damping \(\delta\) satisfies the conditions on \(\delta\) in the algebraic contraction theorem of the previous module, and part (a) supplies its small-step conditions.

steps.title: One synchronous OBABO step contracts the energy
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(f\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(0\le m\le M\), \(M>0\), \(\gamma>0\), \(h\ge0\), \(4M\le\gamma^2\) and \(33\gamma^3h\le m\). Let \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) and \(\sigma\in\mathbb R\). Then for all \(z,w\in H\times H\) and \(\xi,\xi'\in H\),

\[\mathcal E\bigl(\Phi(z;\xi,\xi')-\Phi(w;\xi,\xi')\bigr)\le\Bigl(1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma}\Bigr)\mathcal E(z-w).\]

Proof. Write \(z=(v_0,x_0)\), \(w=(w_0,y_0)\), and let \(x_1,y_1\) be the positions after the drift substep for \(z\) and \(w\):

\[x_1=x_0+h\bigl(\delta v_0+\sigma\xi-\tfrac h2\nabla f(x_0)\bigr),\qquad y_1=y_0+h\bigl(\delta w_0+\sigma\xi-\tfrac h2\nabla f(y_0)\bigr).\]

Put \(x=x_0-y_0\), \(v=v_0-w_0\), \(F_0=\nabla f(x_0)-\nabla f(y_0)\),

\[S=\tfrac12\bigl(F_0+\nabla f(x_1)-\nabla f(y_1)\bigr),\qquad e=\frac M2\,\|(x_1-y_1)-x\| .\]

Difference of the two steps. The noise terms \(\sigma\xi\) and \(\sigma\xi'\) are common and cancel. Subtracting the substeps,

\[\Phi(z;\xi,\xi')-\Phi(w;\xi,\xi')=\Bigl(\delta^2v-h\delta S,\ x+h\delta v-\frac{h^2}2F_0\Bigr),\qquad(1)\]

because the velocity difference after the first O and B substeps is \(\delta v-\frac h2F_0\), the position difference after A is \(x+h(\delta v-\frac h2F_0)\), and the velocity difference after the second B and O substeps is \(\delta(\delta v-\frac h2F_0-\frac h2(\nabla f(x_1)-\nabla f(y_1)))=\delta^2v-h\delta S\).

Bounds on \(F_0\) and \(e\). The Lipschitz property gives \(\|F_0\|\le M\|x\|\). By (1), \((x_1-y_1)-x=h\delta v-\frac{h^2}2F_0\), so by the triangle inequality and \(0\le\delta\le1\),

\[\|(x_1-y_1)-x\|\le h\|v\|+\frac{h^2M}2\|x\|,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad e\le\frac M2\Bigl(h\|v\|+\frac{h^2M}2\|x\|\Bigr).\]

Bound on \(S\). For a differentiable \(m\)-strongly convex \(f\) with \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(m\le M\), the interpolation inequality \(mM\|a-b\|^2+\|\nabla f(a)-\nabla f(b)\|^2\le(m+M)\langle\nabla f(a)-\nabla f(b),a-b\rangle\) holds for all \(a,b\), and it is equivalent to the centred bound

\[\Bigl\|\nabla f(a)-\nabla f(b)-\frac{m+M}2(a-b)\Bigr\|\le\frac{M-m}2\|a-b\|\]

(both facts are proved in the overdamped analysis). Applying it at \((x_0,y_0)\) and at \((x_1,y_1)\) and averaging, the module on the OBABO energy shows \(\|S-\frac{m+M}2x\|\le\frac{M-m}2\|x\|+e\). The triangle inequality gives \(\|S\|\le\frac{M-m}2\|x\|+e+\frac{m+M}2\|x\|=M\|x\|+e\).

Dissipativity. The same module proves, for this \(S\) and \(e\) and every \(v\), the perturbed dissipativity inequality \(\mathcal D(v,x,S)\le-\frac{2m}{3\gamma}\mathcal E(v,x)+\frac{2e\|x\|}\gamma+\frac{e^2}{\gamma M}\), where \(\mathcal D\) is the energy derivative along the kinetic drift.

Conclusion. By the previous step, \(\delta\) satisfies \(0\le\delta\le1\), \(1-\delta\le\gamma h/2\) and \(0\le\delta^2-1+\gamma h\le\gamma^2h^2/2\), and \(\gamma h\le1\), \(12\gamma^2h^2\le1\). All hypotheses of the algebraic contraction theorem (Claim B of the last step of the previous module, with \(L=M\), \(F=S\)) are therefore satisfied, and it gives

\[\mathcal E\Bigl(\delta^2v-h\delta S,\ x+h\delta v-\frac{h^2}2F_0\Bigr)\le\Bigl(1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma}\Bigr)\mathcal E(v,x).\]

By (1) the left-hand side is \(\mathcal E(\Phi(z)-\Phi(w))\), and \((v,x)=z-w\). \(\square\)

The proof does not use a mean-value point for the Hessian: the averaged force \(S\) is controlled by the interpolation inequality at the two pairs of positions where the gradient is actually evaluated.

steps.title: Iteration and the position bound
steps.body:
Claim. (a) If \(\gamma>0\), \(h\ge0\), \(m\le L\), \(4L\le\gamma^2\) and \(\gamma h\le1\), then \(q=1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma}\ge0\).

(b) Under the hypotheses of the previous step, let \((Z_n)\) and \((W_n)\) be sequences in \(H\times H\) with \(Z_{n+1}=\Phi(Z_n;\xi_n,\xi'_n)\) and \(W_{n+1}=\Phi(W_n;\xi_n,\xi'_n)\) for all \(n\), for one common sequence of noise vectors \((\xi_n,\xi'_n)\). Then \(\mathcal E(Z_n-W_n)\le q^n\,\mathcal E(Z_0-W_0)\) for all \(n\).

(c) If moreover \(Z_0\) and \(W_0\) have the same velocity, then, writing \(X_n\) and \(Y_n\) for the positions of \(Z_n\) and \(W_n\),

\[\|X_n-Y_n\|\le\sqrt{2q^n}\,\|X_0-Y_0\|\qquad\text{for all }n .\]

Proof. (a) Multiplying \(4L\le\gamma^2\) by \(h\ge0\) and using \(\gamma^2h=\gamma(\gamma h)\le\gamma\), we get \(mh\le Lh\le\gamma/4<3\gamma\) (if \(m<0\) then \(mh\le0\) anyway). Hence \(mh/(3\gamma)\le1\).

(b) Induction on \(n\). For \(n=0\) both sides equal \(\mathcal E(Z_0-W_0)\). If the bound holds for \(n\), the previous step applied to \(Z_n,W_n\) and the common noises gives \(\mathcal E(Z_{n+1}-W_{n+1})\le q\,\mathcal E(Z_n-W_n)\). The hypotheses of the previous step imply \(\gamma h\le1\) (first step), so \(q\ge0\) by (a), and multiplying the induction hypothesis by \(q\) preserves it: \(q\,\mathcal E(Z_n-W_n)\le q\cdot q^n\mathcal E(Z_0-W_0)=q^{n+1}\mathcal E(Z_0-W_0)\).

(c) If the initial velocity difference is zero, \(\mathcal E(Z_0-W_0)=\|X_0-Y_0\|^2\), since the mixed and velocity terms vanish. The lower bound of the metric equivalence (valid because \(4M\le\gamma^2\)) gives \(\frac12\bigl(\|X_n-Y_n\|^2+\frac1M\|V_n-V'_n\|^2\bigr)\le\mathcal E(Z_n-W_n)\), where \(V_n,V'_n\) are the velocities, and the velocity term is nonnegative. With (b),

\[\|X_n-Y_n\|^2\le2\,\mathcal E(Z_n-W_n)\le2q^n\|X_0-Y_0\|^2 .\]

Both \(\|X_n-Y_n\|\) and \(\sqrt{2q^n}\|X_0-Y_0\|\) are nonnegative (here \(q^n\ge0\) by (a)), so the inequality between their squares implies the inequality between them. \(\square\)

KineticLangevin/KineticSplitting.lean.title: The Verlet–Ornstein–Uhlenbeck splitting and its local error
KineticLangevin/KineticSplitting.lean.summary:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a real normed space and give \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) the maximum norm \(\|(v,x)\|=\max(\|v\|,\|x\|)\); phase points are written velocity first. Let \(g:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz (in the application \(g=\nabla f\)), \(\gamma\ge0\) the friction and \(h\ge0\) the step. The kinetic drift is \(d_\gamma(v,x)=(\gamma v+g(x),-v)\), so that the kinetic integral equation reads \(Z_t-Z_0=-\int_0^td_\gamma(Z_s)\,ds+(B_t,0)\) for a velocity forcing \(B\), and one explicit Euler step is \(z-hd_\gamma(z)\).

This module defines the Lie splitting step

\[S_h(z,N)=\bigl(e^{-\gamma h}v'+N,\ x'\bigr),\qquad(v',x')=V_h(z),\]

a velocity Verlet step \(V_h\) for the Hamiltonian part followed by exact exponential damping of the velocity and an additive velocity increment \(N\in\mathcal X\). It proves that \(S_h\) is Lipschitz in \(z\) with constant \(1+(M+1)^2h\), that it differs from the kinetic Euler step \(z-hd_\gamma(z)+(N,0)\) by at most \(h^2C(\|z\|+\|g(0)\|)\) with an explicit constant \(C\), and that the filtered increment

\[N_{a,h}=B(a+h)-B(a)-\gamma\int_0^he^{-\gamma(h-s)}\bigl(B(a+s)-B(a)\bigr)\,ds\]

of a forcing path \(B\) differs from the plain increment \(B(a+h)-B(a)\) by at most \(\gamma h\) times the oscillation of \(B\) on \([a,a+h]\). By the identities proved for Brownian segments, \(N_{a,h}\) is exactly the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck velocity response \(\int_a^{a+h}e^{-\gamma(a+h-r)}\,dB_r\) when \(B\) is the Brownian motion. These deterministic estimates are the consistency and stability ingredients of the convergence of the splitting to the kinetic diffusion, proved in the next modules.

steps.title: Damping the velocity is nonexpansive
steps.body:
Definition. For \(\delta\in\mathbb R\), \(D_\delta(v,x)=(\delta v,x)\).

Claim. If \(0\le\delta\le1\), then \(\|D_\delta z-D_\delta w\|\le\|z-w\|\) for all \(z,w\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\).

Proof. Write \(z=(v,x)\), \(w=(v',x')\). Then \(D_\delta z-D_\delta w=(\delta(v-v'),x-x')\), and by the definition of the maximum norm \(\|D_\delta z-D_\delta w\|=\max\bigl(\delta\|v-v'\|,\|x-x'\|\bigr)\), using \(\|\delta u\|=|\delta|\|u\|=\delta\|u\|\). Since \(0\le\delta\le1\), \(\delta\|v-v'\|\le\|v-v'\|\le\|z-w\|\), and \(\|x-x'\|\le\|z-w\|\). A maximum of two numbers bounded by \(\|z-w\|\) is bounded by \(\|z-w\|\). \(\square\)
