steps.title: The splitting step and its stability
steps.body:
Definition. With \(V_h=K_{h/2}\circ D'_h\circ K_{h/2}\) the velocity Verlet step (kick \(K_s(v,x)=(v-sg(x),x)\), drift \(D'_h(v,x)=(v,x+hv)\)), let \(S_h(z,N)=\bigl(e^{-\gamma h}v'+N,x'\bigr)\) where \((v',x')=V_h(z)\).

Claim. Let \(g\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz, \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(0\le h\le1\). Then for all \(z,w\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) and \(N\in\mathcal X\),

\[\|S_h(z,N)-S_h(w,N)\|\le\bigl(1+(M+1)^2h\bigr)\|z-w\| .\]

Proof. The increment \(N\) is the same in both steps and cancels: \(S_h(z,N)-S_h(w,N)=D_\delta(V_hz)-D_\delta(V_hw)\) with \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h}\). Since \(\gamma h\ge0\), \(0<\delta\le1\), so by the previous step \(\|D_\delta(V_hz)-D_\delta(V_hw)\|\le\|V_hz-V_hw\|\). The stability of velocity Verlet, proved in the module on Hamiltonian convergence (by composing the Lipschitz bounds \(1+sM\) of the kicks and \(1+h\) of the drift), gives \(\|V_hz-V_hw\|\le(1+(M+1)^2h)\|z-w\|\) for \(0\le h\le1\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Exponential damping errors without division by the friction
steps.body:
Claim. For \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(h\ge0\),

\[\bigl|e^{-\gamma h}-1+\gamma h\bigr|\le\frac{\gamma^2h^2}2\qquad\text{and}\qquad0\le1-e^{-\gamma h}\le\gamma h .\]

Proof. Recall \(\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\), \(\psi_1(t)=\int_0^t\psi_0\), \(\psi_2(t)=\int_0^t\psi_1\), and the identities \(\gamma\psi_1(t)=1-e^{-\gamma t}\) and \(\gamma\psi_2(t)=t-\psi_1(t)\), valid for every real \(\gamma\) and \(t\) (the second is the integral of the first). Multiplying the second by \(\gamma\) and substituting the first,

\[\gamma^2\psi_2(h)=\gamma h-\gamma\psi_1(h)=\gamma h-1+e^{-\gamma h}.\]

For \(h\ge0\), \(\psi_2(h)\ge0\) (integral of a nonnegative function), so the absolute value equals \(\gamma^2\psi_2(h)\). For \(\gamma\ge0\), \(\psi_0\le1\) on \([0,\infty)\), hence \(\psi_1(s)\le s\) and \(\psi_2(h)\le\int_0^hs\,ds=h^2/2\); multiplying by \(\gamma^2\ge0\) gives the first inequality. For the second, \(-\gamma h\le0\) gives \(e^{-\gamma h}\le1\), and the tangent-line inequality \(e^u\ge1+u\) with \(u=-\gamma h\) gives \(1-e^{-\gamma h}\le\gamma h\). \(\square\)

No division by \(\gamma\) occurs, so the estimates include \(\gamma=0\).

steps.title: The damped Hamiltonian Euler stage versus kinetic Euler
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(g\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz, \(\gamma\ge0\), \(h\ge0\), \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h}\). Then for every \(z\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\)

\[\bigl\|D_\delta\bigl(z-hd_0(z)\bigr)-\bigl(z-hd_\gamma(z)\bigr)\bigr\|\le h^2\Bigl(\frac{\gamma^2}2+\gamma(M+1)\Bigr)\bigl(\|z\|+\|g(0)\|\bigr).\]

Proof. Write \(z=(v,x)\). Then \(z-hd_0(z)=(v-hg(x),x+hv)\), whose damped version is \((\delta v-\delta hg(x),x+hv)\), and \(z-hd_\gamma(z)=(v-\gamma hv-hg(x),x+hv)\). The position components agree, so

\[D_\delta\bigl(z-hd_0(z)\bigr)-\bigl(z-hd_\gamma(z)\bigr)=\bigl((\delta-1+\gamma h)v+(1-\delta)h\,g(x),\ 0\bigr),\]

and its norm is the norm of the velocity component. By the Lipschitz property and the triangle inequality, \(\|g(x)\|\le\|g(x)-g(0)\|+\|g(0)\|\le M\|x\|+\|g(0)\|\le M\|z\|+\|g(0)\|\). Using the triangle inequality, the previous step (\(|\delta-1+\gamma h|\le\gamma^2h^2/2\), \(0\le1-\delta\le\gamma h\)) and \(\|v\|\le\|z\|\),

\[\begin{aligned} &\bigl\|(\delta-1+\gamma h)v+(1-\delta)hg(x)\bigr\|\\ &\quad\le\frac{\gamma^2h^2}2\|z\| +\gamma h\cdot h\bigl(M\|z\|+\|g(0)\|\bigr)\\ &\quad=h^2\Bigl(\bigl(\tfrac{\gamma^2}2+\gamma M\bigr)\|z\| +\gamma\|g(0)\|\Bigr)\\ &\quad\le h^2\Bigl(\frac{\gamma^2}2+\gamma(M+1)\Bigr) \bigl(\|z\|+\|g(0)\|\bigr). \end{aligned}\]

where the last inequality holds because the difference of the two sides is \(h^2\bigl[(\frac{\gamma^2}2+\gamma M)\|g(0)\|+\gamma\|z\|\bigr]\ge0\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The local defect of the splitting step
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(g\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz, \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(0\le h\le1\). Then for all \(z\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) and \(N\in\mathcal X\)

\[\bigl\|S_h(z,N)-\bigl(z-hd_\gamma(z)+(N,0)\bigr)\bigr\|\le h^2C\bigl(\|z\|+\|g(0)\|\bigr),\qquad C=(M+1)(M+2)+\frac{\gamma^2}2+\gamma(M+1).\]

\[\bigl\|D_\delta(V_hz)-(z-hd_\gamma z)\bigr\|\le\bigl\|D_\delta(V_hz)-D_\delta(z-hd_0z)\bigr\|+\bigl\|D_\delta(z-hd_0z)-(z-hd_\gamma z)\bigr\|.\]

By the first step and the Verlet defect estimate of the module on Hamiltonian convergence (valid for \(0\le h\le1\)), the first term is at most \(\|V_hz-(z-hd_0z)\|\le h^2(M+1)(M+2)(\|z\|+\|g(0)\|)\). The second term is bounded by the previous step. Adding the two bounds gives the claim. \(\square\)

steps.title: The filtered increment of a forcing path
steps.body:
Definition. For a path \(B:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X\), a starting time \(a\) and a step \(h\),

\[N_{a,h}=B(a+h)-B(a)-\gamma\int_0^he^{-\gamma(h-s)}\bigl(B(a+s)-B(a)\bigr)\,ds .\]

(As always for the Bochner integral, the integral of a function that is not integrable is taken to be \(0\); in the applications \(B\) is continuous.) When \(B\) is the Brownian motion, the integration-by-parts identity of the module on Brownian segment equations shows that \(N_{a,h}\) equals the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck response \(\int_a^{a+h}e^{-\gamma(a+h-r)}\,dB_r\).

Claim. Let \(\gamma\ge0\), \(h\ge0\), \(\varepsilon\ge0\), and suppose \(\|B(a+s)-B(a)\|\le\varepsilon\) for all \(s\in[0,h]\). Then

\[\bigl\|N_{a,h}-\bigl(B(a+h)-B(a)\bigr)\bigr\|\le\gamma h\varepsilon .\]

Proof. By definition \(N_{a,h}-(B(a+h)-B(a))=-\gamma\int_0^he^{-\gamma(h-s)}(B(a+s)-B(a))\,ds\), whose norm is \(\gamma\) times the norm of the integral, since \(\gamma\ge0\). For \(s\in(0,h]\) we have \(-\gamma(h-s)\le0\), hence \(0<e^{-\gamma(h-s)}\le1\), and the integrand has norm at most \(\|B(a+s)-B(a)\|\le\varepsilon\). The norm of an integral over an interval of length \(h\) of a function bounded in norm by \(\varepsilon\) is at most \(\varepsilon h\) (this holds also when the integral is \(0\) by convention). Therefore the left-hand side is at most \(\gamma\varepsilon h\). \(\square\)

In the convergence proof \(\varepsilon\) is the modulus of continuity of \(B\) at scale \(h\), so the difference between the filtered and the plain increments is \(o(h)\) uniformly in \(a\) on a bounded horizon.

KineticLangevin/CanonicalVectorSegments..title: Vector Brownian responses and independent Gaussian initial velocity
KineticLangevin/CanonicalVectorSegments..summary:
The KLMC algorithm of Dalalyan and Riou-Durand draws, at every iteration \(n\) and in every spatial coordinate \(i\in\{1,\dots,p\}\), a pair \((\xi_{n,i},\xi'_{n,i})\) of centred jointly Gaussian variables with covariance matrix \(\mathbf C=\int_0^h(\psi_0(t),\psi_1(t))^\top(\psi_0(t),\psi_1(t))\,dt\), independently over \(n\) and \(i\), and independently of the initial condition. This module realises all these variables from Brownian motions and proves that the resulting family has exactly this joint law.

Let \((\Omega_1,\mathbb P_1)\) be the probability space carrying the scalar Brownian motion \(B\) of the module on Brownian segments, and for a continuous kernel \(k\) let \(J^a_t(k)=\int_a^{a+t}k(a+t-r)\,dB_r\). For a finite family of continuous kernels \((k_j)_{j\in\kappa}\) and a step \(h\ge0\), the block on the \(n\)-th grid interval \((nh,(n+1)h]\) is the random vector \(\beta_n=(J^{nh}_h(k_j))_{j\in\kappa}\in\mathbb R^\kappa\). It was shown there that \((\beta_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) are independent and that each \(\beta_n\) is centred Gaussian with the Gram covariance \(G^h_{jl}=\int_0^hk_j(t)k_l(t)\,dt\); write \(\mathcal N(0,G^h)\) for this law. For an index set \(\iota\) of spatial coordinates, the vector source is the product \((\Omega,\mathbb P)=(\Omega_1^\iota,\mathbb P_1^{\otimes\iota})\), whose coordinates \(\omega_i\) carry independent copies \(B^{(i)}\) of the Brownian motion, and the vector blocks are \(\beta_n^{(i)}(\omega)=\beta_n(\omega_i)\).

The module proves that the array \((\beta^{(i)}_n)_{n,i}\) is independent with every entry distributed as \(\mathcal N(0,G^h)\); specialises to \(\iota=\{1,\dots,p\}\) and the kernels \((\psi_0,\psi_1)\) to obtain the KLMC innovations with exactly the law prescribed by the paper; and adjoins an independent standard Gaussian initial velocity, independent of all innovations. These are the source variables \(V\) and \(W_n\) to which the coupling arguments of the module on product laws are applied.

steps.title: Independence is preserved under a map with a prescribed law
steps.body:
Recall that random variables \((X_a)_{a\in A}\) on a probability space, with values in measurable spaces \(S_a\), are mutually independent if \(\mathbb P(\bigcap_{a\in F}\{X_a\in E_a\})=\prod_{a\in F}\mathbb P(X_a\in E_a)\) for every finite \(F\subseteq A\) and measurable \(E_a\subseteq S_a\); equivalently, the joint law of \((X_a)_{a\in A}\) on \(\prod_aS_a\) is the product of the individual laws.

Claim. Let \((\Xi,Q)\) be a probability space, \((X_a)_{a\in A}\) measurable maps on \(\Xi\) that are mutually independent under \(Q\), and \(Y:\Omega\to\Xi\) a measurable map with law \(Q\) under a measure \(P\) (that is, \(P\circ Y^{-1}=Q\)). Then \((X_a\circ Y)_{a\in A}\) are mutually independent under \(P\).

Proof. Since \(P(\Omega)=Q(\Xi)=1\), \(P\) is a probability measure. Let \(X=(X_a)_a:\Xi\to\prod_aS_a\). By the composition rule for image measures and \(P\circ Y^{-1}=Q\),

\[P\circ(X\circ Y)^{-1}=(P\circ Y^{-1})\circ X^{-1}=Q\circ X^{-1}=\bigotimes_a Q\circ X_a^{-1}=\bigotimes_a P\circ(X_a\circ Y)^{-1},\]

where the third equality is the independence of the \(X_a\) under \(Q\) and the last uses the composition rule once more for each \(a\). By the characterisation recalled above, the \(X_a\circ Y\) are mutually independent. \(\square\)

  1. the family \(\bigl(\beta_n(\omega_i)\bigr)_{(n,i)\in\mathbb N\times\iota}\) is mutually independent;
  2. its joint law is \(\bigotimes_{(n,i)}\mathcal N(0,G^h)\);
  3. the sequence of vector blocks \(n\mapsto\beta^\iota_n\) has law \(\bigotimes_{n\in\mathbb N}\bigl(\bigotimes_{i\in\iota}\mathcal N(0,G^h)\bigr)\);
  4. the vector blocks \((\beta^\iota_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) are mutually independent.

Proof. (1) We use the following regrouping principle: a doubly indexed family \((X_{i,n})\) is mutually independent if the "rows" \(R_i=(X_{i,n})_{n}\) are mutually independent over \(i\) and, for each fixed \(i\), the variables \((X_{i,n})_n\) are mutually independent. With \(X_{i,n}(\omega)=\beta_n(\omega_i)\), the row \(R_i\) is a measurable function of the single coordinate \(\omega_i\); coordinates of a product probability measure are independent, so the rows are independent. For fixed \(i\), the evaluation \(\omega\mapsto\omega_i\) has law \(\mathbb P_1\) (marginal of the product measure), and \((\beta_n)_n\) are independent under \(\mathbb P_1\) (disjoint grid intervals give orthogonal kernels, and orthogonal jointly Gaussian blocks are independent; this is the earlier result); by the previous step \((\beta_n(\omega_i))_n\) are independent under \(\mathbb P\). Hence the family indexed by pairs \((i,n)\) is independent, and so is its reindexing by \((n,i)\), since reindexing by a bijection does not affect mutual independence.

(2) For an independent family, the joint law is the product of the marginal laws. Each marginal \(\beta_n(\omega_i)\) is the image of \(\mathbb P\) under \(\beta_n\circ(\omega\mapsto\omega_i)\), i.e. the image of \(\mathbb P_1\) under \(\beta_n\), which is \(\mathcal N(0,G^h)\) by the earlier result. Measurability of the joint map holds coordinatewise.

(3) Currying \((a_{(n,i)})_{(n,i)}\mapsto\bigl((a_{(n,i)})_{i}\bigr)_{n}\) is a measurable bijection with measurable inverse between \((\mathbb R^\kappa)^{\mathbb N\times\iota}\) and \(((\mathbb R^\kappa)^\iota)^{\mathbb N}\), and it maps the product measure \(\bigotimes_{(n,i)}\mu\) to \(\bigotimes_n\bigotimes_i\mu\) (both measures agree on measurable rectangles, which determine product measures). Composing with (2) gives (3).

(4) Under the product measure \(\bigotimes_n\nu_n\), the coordinate maps \(a\mapsto a_n\) are mutually independent. By (3) the map \(\omega\mapsto(\beta^\iota_n(\omega))_n\) has this product law, so by the previous step the compositions \(\omega\mapsto\beta^\iota_n(\omega)\) are mutually independent. \(\square\)

steps.title: Equality with the KLMC Gaussian innovation sequence
steps.body:
Let \(p\in\mathbb N\) be the dimension. The reference law of the KLMC noise array is \(\mathcal G=\bigotimes_{(n,i)\in\mathbb N\times\{1,\dots,p\}}\mathcal N(0,\mathbf C)\) on \((\mathbb R^2)^{\mathbb N\times\{1,\dots,p\}}\), with \(\mathbf C=G^h\) for the two kernels \((\psi_0,\psi_1)\); the paper's innovation at step \(n\) is the image of \(\mathcal G\) under \(\eta_n:a\mapsto\bigl((a_{(n,i),0})_{i\le p},(a_{(n,i),1})_{i\le p}\bigr)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^p\), which collects the first entries into the velocity innovation and the second entries into the position innovation.

Definition. The Brownian KLMC innovation is

\[\Xi_n(\omega)=\Bigl(\bigl(J^{nh}_h(\psi_0)(\omega_i)\bigr)_{i\le p},\ \bigl(J^{nh}_h(\psi_1)(\omega_i)\bigr)_{i\le p}\Bigr)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^p,\qquad\omega\in\Omega_1^{p}.\]

Claim. With \(\iota=\{1,\dots,p\}\):

  1. for arbitrary continuous kernels, the array \((\beta_n(\omega_i))_{(n,i)\in\mathbb N\times\{1,\dots,p\}}\) has law \(\bigotimes_{(n,i)}\mathcal N(0,G^h)\);
  2. \(\Xi_n\) is measurable and its law is the image of \(\mathcal G\) under \(\eta_n\), i.e. the law of the paper's innovation;
  3. \((\Xi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) are mutually independent;
  4. both components of \(\Xi_n\) are square integrable.

Proof. (1) This is part (2) of the previous step for the index set \(\{1,\dots,p\}\), with the array indexed by ordinary pairs \((n,i)\) instead of dependent pairs; the reindexing preserves independence and the marginal laws.

(2) By construction \(\Xi_n=\eta_n\circ\mathcal A\), where \(\mathcal A(\omega)=(\beta_n(\omega_i))_{(n,i)}\) is the array for the kernels \((\psi_0,\psi_1)\). The map \(\eta_n\) is measurable (it only selects coordinates), so \(\Xi_n\) is measurable, and by (1) its law is \((\mathbb P\circ\mathcal A^{-1})\circ\eta_n^{-1}=\mathcal G\circ\eta_n^{-1}\).

(3) \(\Xi_n\) is a fixed measurable function (the regrouping into velocity and position vectors) of the vector block \(\beta^\iota_n\); measurable functions of mutually independent variables, applied index by index, are mutually independent, and the blocks are independent by part (4) of the previous step.

(4) A random vector in \(\mathbb R^p\) is square integrable if each coordinate is. The \(i\)-th coordinate of the velocity component is \(\omega\mapsto J^{nh}_h(\psi_0)(\omega_i)\), the composition of an element of \(L^2(\mathbb P_1)\) with the evaluation \(\omega\mapsto\omega_i\), which maps \(\mathbb P\) to \(\mathbb P_1\); hence it lies in \(L^2(\mathbb P)\). The position component is treated in the same way. \(\square\)

Thus the innovations are not merely Gaussian with the correct covariance: the whole sequence has the law of the paper's independent innovation sequence, while each innovation is a functional of the Brownian increments on its own grid interval.

steps.title: Adjoining an independent Gaussian initial velocity
steps.body:
Definition. The source of the KLMC sampler in dimension \(p\) is the probability space \(S=\mathbb R^p\times\Omega_1^{p}\) with \(Q=\mathcal N(0,I_p)\otimes\mathbb P\), where \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\) is the standard Gaussian measure on \(\mathbb R^p\). A point of \(S\) is written \((u,\omega)\); the initial velocity is \(V(u,\omega)=u\) and the innovations are \(W_n(u,\omega)=\Xi_n(\omega)\).

Claim.

  1. \(Q\) is a probability measure, \(V\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\) under \(Q\), and \(V\) is square integrable.
  2. Each \(W_n\) has the law of the paper's innovation (as in the previous step), the \(W_n\) are mutually independent, and both components of each \(W_n\) are square integrable under \(Q\).
  3. \(V\) is independent of the whole sequence \((W_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\).

Proof. (1) A product of probability measures is a probability measure. The first projection maps \(Q\) to \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\) because the second factor has mass one; so \(V\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\), and \(\int\|V\|^2\,dQ=\int\|u\|^2\,\mathcal N(0,I_p)(du)=p<\infty\) (Gaussian measures have finite moments of all orders).

(2) The second projection \((u,\omega)\mapsto\omega\) maps \(Q\) to \(\mathbb P\) and is measurable. Since \(W_n=\Xi_n\circ\mathrm{pr}_2\), the law of \(W_n\) under \(Q\) equals the law of \(\Xi_n\) under \(\mathbb P\); the mutual independence transfers by the first step; and square integrability transfers because composition with a measure-preserving map preserves \(L^2\) norms.

(3) Under a product measure \(\mu\otimes\nu\), a measurable function of the first coordinate and a measurable function of the second coordinate are independent, because \((\mu\otimes\nu)\bigl((A\times\Omega_1^p)\cap(\mathbb R^p\times C)\bigr)=(\mu\otimes\nu)(A\times C)=\mu(A)\,\nu(C)\) for measurable \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) and \(C\subseteq\Omega_1^p\). Here \(V\) depends only on \(u\), and the sequence \((W_n)_n\), viewed as one random element of a countable product space, depends only on \(\omega\) and is measurable because each of its coordinates is. \(\square\)

Independence of \(V\) from the entire innovation sequence, rather than from each \(W_n\) separately, is what is needed for the KLMC chain to be a Markov chain started from the product law \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\otimes\nu_0\) of the paper.

KineticLangevin/VectorSegmentEquations.l.title: Vector Brownian response equations in \(L^{2}\)
KineticLangevin/VectorSegmentEquations.l.summary:
Let \(\iota\) be a finite set of spatial coordinates, \((\Omega,\mathbb P)=(\Omega_1^\iota,\mathbb P_1^{\otimes\iota})\) the vector Brownian source, whose coordinates \(\omega_i\) carry independent copies \(B^{(i)}_t(\omega)=B_t(\omega_i)\) of the scalar Brownian motion, and \(\mathbb R^\iota\) the Euclidean space. This module transfers the scalar identities of the module on Brownian segment equations to random vectors. It introduces the spatial lift

\[\Lambda:L^2(\mathbb P_1;\mathbb R)\to L^2(\mathbb P;\mathbb R^\iota),\qquad\Lambda(Z)(\omega)=\bigl(Z(\omega_i)\bigr)_{i\in\iota},\]

which applies one scalar random variable to each independent coordinate, and proves that it is a bounded linear map. With \(J^a_t(k)\), \(V^a_t=J^a_t(\psi_0)\), \(P^a_t=J^a_t(\psi_1)\) and \(W^a_t=B_{a+t}-B_a\) as before, define the vector responses and the vector Brownian increment

\[\mathbf V^a_t=\Lambda(V^a_t),\qquad\mathbf P^a_t=\Lambda(P^a_t),\qquad\mathbf W^a_t=\Lambda(W^a_t)=\bigl(B^{(i)}_{a+t}-B^{(i)}_a\bigr)_{i\in\iota}.\]

Because \(\Lambda\) is bounded and linear, it commutes with Bochner integrals in time, and the scalar identities give, for \(\gamma\ge0\),

\[\mathbf P^a_t=\int_0^t\mathbf V^a_s\,ds,\qquad\mathbf V^a_t=\mathbf W^a_t-\gamma\int_0^t\mathbf V^a_s\,ds=\mathbf W^a_t-\gamma\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\mathbf W^a_s\,ds .\]

Finally, on the grid interval \((nh,(n+1)h]\) the pair \((\mathbf V^{nh}_h,\mathbf P^{nh}_h)\) is almost surely the KLMC innovation \(\Xi_n\) of the previous module. Hence the same random vectors serve as the forcing of the continuous kinetic diffusion on that interval (through the mild equation) and as the Gaussian innovation of the numerical step, which is the synchronous coupling used in the error analysis.

steps.title: The spatial lift is a bounded linear map
steps.body:
Definition. For \(i\in\iota\) let \(\mathrm{ev}_i(\omega)=\omega_i\); it maps \(\mathbb P\) to \(\mathbb P_1\) (a marginal of a product of probability measures). Let \(e_i\) be the \(i\)-th standard basis vector of \(\mathbb R^\iota\). Define

\[\Lambda(Z)=\sum_{i\in\iota}(Z\circ\mathrm{ev}_i)\,e_i .\]

Claim. (a) \(\Lambda\) is a bounded linear map from \(L^2(\mathbb P_1;\mathbb R)\) to \(L^2(\mathbb P;\mathbb R^\iota)\). (b) For finitely many \(Z_1,\dots,Z_r\in L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) (any normed space \(E\)), \((Z_1+\dots+Z_r)(\omega)=Z_1(\omega)+\dots+Z_r(\omega)\) for \(\mathbb P\)-almost every \(\omega\). (c) For every \(Z\in L^2(\mathbb P_1)\), \(\Lambda(Z)(\omega)=(Z(\omega_i))_{i\in\iota}\) for \(\mathbb P\)-almost every \(\omega\).

Proof. (a) Since \(\mathrm{ev}_i\) maps \(\mathbb P\) to \(\mathbb P_1\), the change-of-variables formula gives \(\int|Z\circ\mathrm{ev}_i|^2\,d\mathbb P=\int|Z|^2\,d\mathbb P_1\), so \(Z\mapsto Z\circ\mathrm{ev}_i\) is a well-defined linear isometry \(L^2(\mathbb P_1)\to L^2(\mathbb P)\) (almost everywhere equal functions have almost everywhere equal compositions, because \(\mathrm{ev}_i\) preserves null sets). The map \(r\mapsto re_i\) from \(\mathbb R\) to \(\mathbb R^\iota\) is linear and bounded, so composing a random variable with it is a bounded linear map \(L^2(\mathbb P;\mathbb R)\to L^2(\mathbb P;\mathbb R^\iota)\). A finite sum of bounded linear maps is bounded and linear.

(b) Induction on \(r\). For \(r=0\) the zero element of \(L^2\) is represented by the zero function almost everywhere. For the inductive step, the representative of \(Z_1+(Z_2+\dots+Z_r)\) agrees almost everywhere with the sum of the representatives of \(Z_1\) and of \(Z_2+\dots+Z_r\), and the latter agrees almost everywhere with \(Z_2(\omega)+\dots+Z_r(\omega)\) by the induction hypothesis; the union of the two exceptional null sets is null.

(c) For each \(i\), the representative of \((Z\circ\mathrm{ev}_i)e_i\) equals \(Z(\omega_i)e_i\) almost everywhere: composition of a class with a measure-preserving map is represented by the composition of the representatives, and composition with \(r\mapsto re_i\) acts on representatives pointwise. Since \(\iota\) is finite, outside a single null set these identities hold for all \(i\), and by (b) \(\Lambda(Z)(\omega)=\sum_iZ(\omega_i)e_i\). The \(j\)-th coordinate of \(\sum_iZ(\omega_i)e_i\) is \(Z(\omega_j)\), which proves (c). \(\square\)

steps.title: Vector responses and their continuity
steps.body:
Definitions. For a continuous kernel \(k\) and \(a,t\ge0\), the vector response is \(\mathbf J^a_t(k)=\Lambda\bigl(J^a_t(k)\bigr)\), and the vector Brownian increment is \(\mathbf W^a_t=\Lambda(W^a_t)\).

Claim. (a) \(\mathbf J^a_t(k)(\omega)=\bigl(J^a_t(k)(\omega_i)\bigr)_{i\in\iota}\) almost surely. (b) For fixed \(a\), \(t\mapsto\mathbf J^a_t(k)\) is continuous from \([0,\infty)\) into \(L^2(\mathbb P;\mathbb R^\iota)\).

Proof. (a) is part (c) of the previous step with \(Z=J^a_t(k)\). (b) The scalar map \(t\mapsto J^a_t(k)\) is continuous into \(L^2(\mathbb P_1)\) (module on Brownian segment equations), and \(\Lambda\) is continuous, being bounded and linear. \(\square\)

By (a), the coordinates of \(\mathbf J^a_t(k)\) are the Wiener integrals \(\int_a^{a+t}k(a+t-r)\,dB^{(i)}_r\) against the independent Brownian motions \(B^{(i)}\).

steps.title: The primitive and damped integral equations for vectors
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(a,t\ge0\). Then, in \(L^2(\mathbb P;\mathbb R^\iota)\),

\[\mathbf P^a_t=\int_0^t\mathbf V^a_s\,ds\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbf V^a_t=\mathbf W^a_t-\gamma\int_0^t\mathbf V^a_s\,ds .\]

Proof. The scalar identities \(P^a_t=\int_0^tV^a_s\,ds\) and \(V^a_t=W^a_t-\gamma\int_0^tV^a_s\,ds\) hold for \(\gamma\ge0\). Apply \(\Lambda\) to both. Linearity gives \(\Lambda(W^a_t-\gamma I)=\mathbf W^a_t-\gamma\Lambda(I)\), and since \(\Lambda\) is bounded and linear and \(s\mapsto V^a_s\) is continuous (hence integrable on \([0,t]\)),

\[\Lambda\Bigl(\int_0^tV^a_s\,ds\Bigr)=\int_0^t\Lambda(V^a_s)\,ds=\int_0^t\mathbf V^a_s\,ds .\qquad\square\]

The second identity is the forcing equation required by the mild form of the velocity equation (module on the exponential integral formula), now for random vectors driven by the vector Brownian increments.

steps.title: The vector Brownian increment
steps.body:
Claim. (a) For \(a,t\ge0\), \(\mathbf W^a_t(\omega)=\bigl(B^{(i)}_{a+t}(\omega)-B^{(i)}_a(\omega)\bigr)_{i\in\iota}\) for \(\mathbb P\)-almost every \(\omega\). (b) For fixed \(a\), \(t\mapsto\mathbf W^a_t\) is continuous into \(L^2(\mathbb P;\mathbb R^\iota)\).

For each \(i\), the scalar class \(W^a_t=B_{a+t}-B_a\) is represented almost everywhere (for \(\mathbb P_1\)) by the difference of the representatives of \(B_{a+t}\) and \(B_a\); since \(\mathrm{ev}_i\) maps \(\mathbb P\) to \(\mathbb P_1\), the preimage of the exceptional null set is \(\mathbb P\)-null, so \(W^a_t(\omega_i)=B_{a+t}(\omega_i)-B_a(\omega_i)=B^{(i)}_{a+t}(\omega)-B^{(i)}_a(\omega)\) almost surely. Intersecting over the finitely many \(i\) gives (a).

(b) By the first step of the module on Brownian segment equations, \(W^a_t=J^a_t(1)\) for the constant kernel \(1\); hence \(\mathbf W^a_t=\mathbf J^a_t(1)\), which is continuous in \(t\) by the second step. \(\square\)

steps.title: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck increment and the numerical innovations
steps.body:
Claim. (a) For \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(a,t\ge0\),

\[\mathbf V^a_t=\mathbf W^a_t-\gamma\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\,\mathbf W^a_s\,ds\qquad\text{in }L^2(\mathbb P;\mathbb R^\iota).\]

(b) Let \(\iota=\{1,\dots,p\}\), \(h\ge0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\). Then \(\bigl(\mathbf V^{nh}_h(\omega),\mathbf P^{nh}_h(\omega)\bigr)=\Xi_n(\omega)\) for \(\mathbb P\)-almost every \(\omega\), where \(\Xi_n\) is the KLMC innovation of the previous module.

Proof. (a) The scalar identity \(V^a_t=W^a_t-\gamma\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}W^a_s\,ds\) holds for \(\gamma\ge0\). The integrand \(s\mapsto e^{-\gamma(t-s)}W^a_s\) is continuous, because \(s\mapsto W^a_s=J^a_s(1)\) is. Apply \(\Lambda\): by linearity and commutation with the integral, \(\Lambda\bigl(\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}W^a_s\,ds\bigr)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\Lambda(W^a_s)\,ds=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\mathbf W^a_s\,ds\).

(b) By part (a) of the second step, almost surely \(\mathbf V^{nh}_h(\omega)=(J^{nh}_h(\psi_0)(\omega_i))_i\) and \(\mathbf P^{nh}_h(\omega)=(J^{nh}_h(\psi_1)(\omega_i))_i\). These are by definition the two components of \(\Xi_n(\omega)\), and two pairs with equal components are equal. \(\square\)

By (a), \(\mathbf V^{nh}_h\) is the filtered increment \(N_{nh,h}\) of the module on the kinetic splitting, computed from the vector Brownian path; by (b), the same random vectors are the innovations of the KLMC step, whose joint law was identified in the previous module.

KineticLangevin/KineticSplittingConverge.title: Convergence of the Verlet–Ornstein–Uhlenbeck splitting
KineticLangevin/KineticSplittingConverge.summary:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a real Banach space, \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) with the maximum norm, \(g:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\) an \(M\)-Lipschitz map, \(\gamma\ge0\), and \(d(v,x)=(\gamma v+g(x),-v)\) the kinetic drift with unit inverse mass. For a forcing path \(B:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X\) with \(B(0)=0\), a solution of the kinetic integral equation on \([0,T]\) is a continuous \(Y:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) with

\[Y_t-z_0=-\int_0^td(Y_s)\,ds+(B_t,0)\qquad(0\le t\le T).\]

The splitting chain with step \(h\) is \(X_0=z_0\), \(X_{k+1}=S_h(X_k,N_{kh,h})\), where \(S_h\) is the Verlet–Ornstein–Uhlenbeck step and \(N_{a,h}\) the filtered increment of \(B\) on \([a,a+h]\) (module on the kinetic splitting). This module proves an explicit finite-horizon error bound for \(\|X_n-Y_T\|\) when \(nh=T\), in terms of oscillation moduli of \(t\mapsto d(Y_t)\) and of \(B\), and deduces that \(X_{n+1}\) computed with step \(T/(n+1)\) converges to \(Y_T\) as \(n\to\infty\) whenever \(B\) is continuous.

steps.title: A finite-horizon error bound in terms of oscillation moduli
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(g\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz, \(\gamma\ge0\), \(B(0)=0\), and let \(Y\) be continuous and solve the kinetic integral equation on \([0,T]\). Let \(T\ge0\), \(0\le h\le1\), \(\eta\ge0\), \(R\ge0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(nh=T\). Assume \(\|Y_t\|\le R\) for \(t\in[0,T]\) and, for all \(s,t\in[0,T]\) with \(|s-t|\le h\),

\[\|d(Y_s)-d(Y_t)\|\le\eta,\qquad\|B(s)-B(t)\|\le\eta .\]

Then, with \(C=(M+1)(M+2)+\frac{\gamma^2}2+\gamma(M+1)\),

\[\|X_n-Y_T\|\le T\Bigl(hC\bigl(R+\|g(0)\|\bigr)+(1+\gamma)\eta\Bigr)e^{(M+1)^2T}.\]

Proof. Put \(e_k=\|X_k-Y_{kh}\|\), \(q=1+(M+1)^2h\) and \(\varepsilon=hC(R+\|g(0)\|)+(1+\gamma)\eta\ge0\).

Initial error. At \(t=0\) the integral equation gives \(Y_0-z_0=(B(0),0)=0\), so \(e_0=\|z_0-Y_0\|=0\).

One step. Fix \(k<n\) and put \(a=kh\). Then \(a\) and \(a+h=(k+1)h\) lie in \([0,T]\) because \((k+1)h\le nh=T\), and so does \(a+s\) for \(s\in[0,h]\). Let \(N=N_{a,h}\).

  1. Exact increment. Subtracting the integral equations at \(a\) and \(a+h\), and using additivity of the integral over adjacent intervals (the integrand \(s\mapsto d(Y_s)\) is continuous because \(d\) is Lipschitz and \(Y\) is continuous), then the substitution \(s\mapsto a+s\), \[Y_{a+h}-Y_a=-\int_0^hd(Y_{a+s})\,ds+\bigl(B(a+h)-B(a),0\bigr).\] With the local defect \(D=\int_0^h\bigl(d(Y_{a+s})-d(Y_a)\bigr)\,ds\) this is the Euler identity \(Y_{a+h}=Y_a-hd(Y_a)+(B(a+h)-B(a),0)-D\).
  2. Local defect. For \(s\in(0,h]\), \(|a+s-a|=s\le h\), so the integrand of \(D\) has norm at most \(\eta\) and \(\|D\|\le h\eta\).
  3. Filtered increment. For \(s\in[0,h]\), \(\|B(a+s)-B(a)\|\le\eta\); by the last step of the module on the kinetic splitting, \(\|N-(B(a+h)-B(a))\|\le\gamma h\eta\).
  4. Consistency. By item 1, \(Y_a-hd(Y_a)+(N,0)-Y_{a+h}=\bigl(N-(B(a+h)-B(a)),0\bigr)+D\), whose norm is at most \(\gamma h\eta+h\eta\) by items 2 and 3 (in the maximum norm \(\|(u,0)\|=\|u\|\)). The local defect estimate of the splitting step, with \(\|Y_a\|\le R\), gives \(\|S_h(Y_a,N)-(Y_a-hd(Y_a)+(N,0))\|\le h^2C(R+\|g(0)\|)\). By the triangle inequality, \[\|S_h(Y_a,N)-Y_{a+h}\|\le h^2C(R+\|g(0)\|)+(1+\gamma)h\eta=h\varepsilon .\]
  5. Stability. By the stability of the splitting step, \(\|S_h(X_k,N)-S_h(Y_a,N)\|\le q\,\|X_k-Y_a\|=q\,e_k\).

Since \(X_{k+1}=S_h(X_k,N)\), the triangle inequality and items 4 and 5 give

\[e_{k+1}\le q\,e_k+h\varepsilon\qquad(0\le k<n).\qquad(1)\]

Summation. If \(e_0=0\), \(q\ge1\), \(b\ge0\) and \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\) for \(k<n\), then \(e_n\le nbq^n\): by induction, \(e_{k+1}\le q\cdot kbq^k+b\le(k+1)bq^{k+1}\) because \(q^{k+1}\ge1\). Applied to (1), \(e_n\le n\,h\varepsilon\,q^n\). By \(1+u\le e^u\), \(q^n\le\bigl(e^{(M+1)^2h}\bigr)^n=e^{(M+1)^2nh}=e^{(M+1)^2T}\). Since \(nh=T\) and \(Y_{nh}=Y_T\),

\[\|X_n-Y_T\|=e_n\le T\varepsilon\,e^{(M+1)^2T},\]

which is the claim. \(\square\)

The bound separates the deterministic consistency of the scheme (the term \(hC(R+\|g(0)\|)\)) from the regularity of the exact solution and of the forcing (the term \((1+\gamma)\eta\)); the hypothesis \(h\le1\) is needed for the stability and consistency estimates of the Verlet step.

steps.title: Convergence for a continuous forcing path
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(g\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz, \(\gamma\ge0\), \(B\) continuous with \(B(0)=0\), \(T\ge0\), and let \(Y\) be continuous and solve the kinetic integral equation on \([0,T]\). Then, with \(h_n=T/(n+1)\),

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}X^{(h_n)}_{n+1}=Y_T,\]

where \(X^{(h)}\) denotes the splitting chain with step \(h\).

Proof. The continuous function \(t\mapsto\|Y_t\|\) is bounded on the compact interval \([0,T]\), say by \(R\ge0\). Put \(C\) as in the previous step and \(D=T\bigl(C(R+\|g(0)\|)+1+\gamma\bigr)e^{(M+1)^2T}\ge0\). Let \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\eta=\varepsilon/(D+1)>0\); then \(\eta D<\eta(D+1)=\varepsilon\).

The maps \(t\mapsto d(Y_t)\) (continuous, because \(d\) is Lipschitz) and \(B\) are continuous on the compact interval \([0,T]\), hence uniformly continuous there (Heine–Cantor theorem): there are \(\delta_D,\delta_B>0\) such that \(\|d(Y_s)-d(Y_t)\|\le\eta\) whenever \(s,t\in[0,T]\), \(|s-t|\le\delta_D\), and \(\|B(s)-B(t)\|\le\eta\) whenever \(|s-t|\le\delta_B\). Since \(h_n\to0\), there is \(n_0\) such that for \(n\ge n_0\)

\[h_n\le1,\qquad h_n\le\eta,\qquad h_n\le\delta_D,\qquad h_n\le\delta_B .\]

Fix \(n\ge n_0\). The oscillation hypotheses of the previous step hold with step \(h_n\) and tolerance \(\eta\), and \((n+1)h_n=T\). The previous step gives

\[\begin{aligned} &\|X^{(h_n)}_{n+1}-Y_T\|\\ &\quad\le T\bigl(h_nC(R+\|g(0)\|)+(1+\gamma)\eta\bigr)e^{(M+1)^2T}\\ &\quad\le T\,\eta\bigl(C(R+\|g(0)\|)+1+\gamma\bigr)e^{(M+1)^2T}\\ &\quad=\eta D<\varepsilon. \end{aligned}\]

using \(h_n\le\eta\) and \(C(R+\|g(0)\|)\ge0\). As \(\varepsilon>0\) was arbitrary, the sequence converges to \(Y_T\). \(\square\)

The theorem does not assume uniqueness of \(Y\): every continuous solution is the limit of the same splitting chain, so it is in particular unique.

The normalized kinetic target is the independent product of a standard Gaussian velocity and the intended Gibbs position measure. This section identifies that product with an explicit scalar normalization of the Hamiltonian weighted measure, transfers the proved Hamiltonian invariance, and proves exact Gaussian thermostat invariance on the correct independent-noise product. Its position and velocity marginals are exact pushforward identities. These two invariant substeps are ingredients for kinetic Gibbs stationarity; passage to the continuous kinetic limit is a separate theorem.

The phase target is identified by normalized measure equalities. Its exact product structure supplies both invariant building blocks, the desired position marginal, and the Gaussian moments used in numerical error analysis.

The Gaussian proposal density at step \(h=1/2\) and center zero is exactly the standard Gaussian. Its scalar precision is \(1/(4h)=1/2\), and its affine map is the identity. Consequently its density is \(c_Ge^{-\|v\|^2/2}\), where \(c_G\) is the inverse of the finite Gaussian integral. First, the argument normalizes the precision and the identity pushforward, then factors the positive normalizer out of the density using scaling of a density-weighted measure and multiplicativity of the nonnegative embedding. The remaining real exponential identity follows by scalar algebra. This is an equality with the standard Gaussian probability measure, not an informal naming of a radial weight.

The standard Gaussian velocity law has a density proportional to \(e^{-\|v\|^2/2}\) with respect to Euclidean volume. This identifies the explicit Gaussian measure with the kinetic factor in the Hamiltonian Gibbs weight. The normalization is therefore known, not left implicit.

KineticLangevin/OBABOPosition.lean.title: The OBABO error bound for position distributions
KineticLangevin/OBABOPosition.lean.summary:
This section transfers the Wasserstein bound for the OBABO splitting scheme, proved earlier in a weighted phase-space metric, to the laws of the positions alone. Phase points are written velocity first, \((v,x)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^p\). Fix \(\gamma>0\) and \(M>0\) with \(4M\le\gamma^2\), and put \(a=1/M\), \(b=1/\gamma\) and \(c=\sqrt{a-b^2}\), which is positive. The weighted coordinates are given by the linear map

\[T(v,x)=(x+bv,\;cv),\qquad \|T(v,x)\|^2=\|x\|^2+2b\langle x,v\rangle+a\|v\|^2,\]

where the image space \(\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^p\) carries the Euclidean norm \(\|(y_1,y_2)\|^2=\|y_1\|^2+\|y_2\|^2\). The OBABO chain contracts in this metric.

We prove three facts. First, the position is recovered from the weighted coordinates by a linear map that is \(\sqrt2\)-Lipschitz. Second, adjoining the same standard Gaussian velocity to two position laws does not increase their Wasserstein distance in the weighted coordinates. Third, combining these with the weighted OBABO bound, the position law \(\nu_n\) after \(n\) OBABO steps started from \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\otimes\mu\) satisfies \(W_2(\nu_n,\pi)<\infty\) and

\[W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le\sqrt2\,r^nW_2(\mu,\pi)+\frac{6\sqrt2\,\gamma}{m}\,h\sqrt p\,\Bigl(4\sqrt M+\frac{Mh}{2}\Bigr),\qquad r=\sqrt{1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma}}.\]

The factor \(\sqrt2\) is paid once, at the final time, and not once per iteration. This position bound is the one applied to the OBABO-based particle sampler of the kinetic interacting-particle report.

steps.title: The weighted coordinates and the position read-out
steps.body:
Setting. Let \(\gamma>0\) and \(M>0\) satisfy \(4M\le\gamma^2\), and put \(a=1/M\) and \(b=1/\gamma\). Dividing \(4M\le\gamma^2\) by \(M\gamma^2>0\) gives \(4b^2\le a\), hence \(b^2\le a/4<a\), and \(c=\sqrt{a-b^2}\) is a positive real number. Let \(Y=\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^p\) carry the Euclidean norm \(\|(y_1,y_2)\|=(\|y_1\|^2+\|y_2\|^2)^{1/2}\) and the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of this norm. Define \(T:\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^p\to Y\) and \(S:Y\to\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^p\) by

\[T(v,x)=(x+bv,\;cv),\qquad S(y_1,y_2)=\bigl(c^{-1}y_2,\;y_1-bc^{-1}y_2\bigr),\]

and the position read-out \(\Pi:Y\to\mathbb R^p\), \(\Pi(y)=y_1-bc^{-1}y_2\), the second component of \(S(y)\).

Claim. \(S\circ T\) is the identity of \(\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^p\) and \(T\circ S\) is the identity of \(Y\). Consequently \(\Pi(T(v,x))=x\) for every phase point \((v,x)\).

Proof. Let \((v,x)\) be a phase point. Then \(T(v,x)=(x+bv,cv)\) and, since \(c\neq0\),

\[S(T(v,x))=\bigl(c^{-1}cv,\;x+bv-bc^{-1}cv\bigr)=(v,\;x+bv-bv)=(v,x).\]

Conversely, for \(y=(y_1,y_2)\in Y\),

\[T(S(y))=\bigl(y_1-bc^{-1}y_2+bc^{-1}y_2,\;c\,c^{-1}y_2\bigr)=(y_1,y_2).\]

The second component of the identity \(S(T(v,x))=(v,x)\) is \(\Pi(T(v,x))=x\). \(\square\)

Since \(c^2=a-b^2\), the squared norm of the weighted coordinates is

\[\|T(v,x)\|^2=\|x+bv\|^2+c^2\|v\|^2=\|x\|^2+2b\langle x,v\rangle+b^2\|v\|^2+(a-b^2)\|v\|^2=\|x\|^2+2b\langle x,v\rangle+a\|v\|^2.\]

We write \(\mathcal E(v,x)\) for this quantity; it is the weighted phase energy in which the OBABO chain was shown to contract. Both \(T\) and \(\Pi\) are linear, hence continuous and Borel measurable.

steps.title: The position read-out is \(\sqrt2\)-Lipschitz
steps.body:
Claim. In the setting of the previous step (\(\gamma>0\), \(M>0\), \(4M\le\gamma^2\)), for all \(y,z\in Y\),

\[\|\Pi(y)-\Pi(z)\|\le\sqrt2\,\|y-z\|.\]

Proof. Put \(r=(r_1,r_2)=S(y)-S(z)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^p\). Its second component is \(r_2=\Pi(y)-\Pi(z)\), the vector to be estimated. Since \(T\) is linear and \(T\circ S\) is the identity (previous step),

\[T(r)=T(S(y))-T(S(z))=y-z.\]

Taking squared norms and using the formula for \(\|T(\cdot)\|^2\) from the previous step,

\[\|y-z\|^2=\|T(r)\|^2=\mathcal E(r)=\|r_2\|^2+2b\langle r_2,r_1\rangle+a\|r_1\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

We bound the mixed term from below. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and Young's inequality \(2st\le\tfrac12s^2+2t^2\) (which is \((s/\sqrt2-\sqrt2\,t)^2\ge0\)), applied with \(s=\|r_2\|\) and \(t=b\|r_1\|\), where \(b>0\),

\[\bigl|2b\langle r_2,r_1\rangle\bigr|\le2\|r_2\|\,b\|r_1\|\le\tfrac12\|r_2\|^2+2b^2\|r_1\|^2\le\tfrac12\|r_2\|^2+\tfrac12a\|r_1\|^2.\]

The last inequality is \(4b^2\le a\), which is the hypothesis \(4M\le\gamma^2\) rewritten. Inserting this into (1), and using \(a\|r_1\|^2\ge0\),

\[\|y-z\|^2\ge\tfrac12\bigl(\|r_2\|^2+a\|r_1\|^2\bigr)\ge\tfrac12\|r_2\|^2.\qquad(2)\]

Thus \(\|r_2\|^2\le2\|y-z\|^2=(\sqrt2\,\|y-z\|)^2\). Both \(\|r_2\|\) and \(\sqrt2\,\|y-z\|\) are nonnegative, and for nonnegative reals \(s^2\le t^2\) implies \(s\le t\). Hence \(\|\Pi(y)-\Pi(z)\|=\|r_2\|\le\sqrt2\,\|y-z\|\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(4M\le\gamma^2\) enters twice: it makes \(c\) well defined and positive, so that \(S\) exists, and it gives the lower bound (2) on the weighted energy. Because \(\Pi\) is linear, the Lipschitz bound is the operator-norm bound \(\|\Pi\|\le\sqrt2\).

Claim. Let \(\gamma>0\), \(M>0\) with \(4M\le\gamma^2\), and let \(T\) be the weighted coordinate map of the first step. For all probability measures \(\mu, u\) on \(\mathbb R^p\),

\[W_2 igl(T_\#(\mathcal N\otimes\mu),\;T_\#(\mathcal N\otimes u) igr)\le W_2(\mu, u)\qquad ext{in }[0,\infty].\]

Proof. Define \(F:\mathbb R^p imes\mathbb R^p o Y\) by \(F(x,s)=T(s,x)\): the first argument is the position and the second the velocity.

Step 1: \(F\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz in its first argument, uniformly in the second. By linearity of \(T\), \(T(s,x)-T(s,y)=T(0,x-y)=(x-y,\,0)\), whose Euclidean norm is \(\|x-y\|\). Equivalently, \(\|T(0,w)\|^2=\mathcal E(0,w)=\|w\|^2\). Hence \(\|F(x,s)-F(y,s)\|=\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y,s\).

Step 2: a coupling for each coupling of \(\mu\) and \( u\). Let \(\varrho\) be a coupling of \(\mu\) and \( u\). On the probability space \( igl((\mathbb R^p imes\mathbb R^p) imes\mathbb R^p,\ \varrho\otimes\mathcal N igr)\) let \((X,Y)\) be the first coordinate and \(G\) the second. Under the product measure \(G\) is independent of \((X,Y)\), so \((X,G)\) has law \(\mu\otimes\mathcal N\) and \((Y,G)\) has law \( u\otimes\mathcal N\). Therefore the joint law of \((F(X,G),F(Y,G))\) is a coupling of \(F_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N)\) and \(F_\#( u\otimes\mathcal N)\), and by Step 1

\[\mathbb E\,\|F(X,G)-F(Y,G)\|^2=\mathbb E\,\|X-Y\|^2=\int\|x-y\|^2\,\varrho(dx,dy).\]

By the definition of \(W_2\) as an infimum, \(W_2(F_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N),F_\#( u\otimes\mathcal N))\le(\int\|x-y\|^2d\varrho)^{1/2}\). Since \(\varrho\) was arbitrary, taking the infimum over \(\varrho\) gives \(W_2(F_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N),F_\#( u\otimes\mathcal N))\le W_2(\mu, u)\). If no coupling has finite cost, the right-hand side is \(+\infty\) and the inequality holds trivially.

Step 3: identification of the image laws. Let \( au(x,s)=(s,x)\) be the coordinate swap. Then \(F=T\circ au\), and \( au_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N)=\mathcal N\otimes\mu\), because both are probability measures that agree on measurable rectangles: \((\mu\otimes\mathcal N)( au^{-1}(A imes B))=\mu(B)\mathcal N(A)\). Hence \(F_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N)=T_\#( au_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N))=T_\#(\mathcal N\otimes\mu)\), and likewise for \( u\). Substituting into Step 2 proves the claim. \(\square\)

No optimal coupling of \(\mu\) and \( u\) is needed: every coupling produces a phase-space coupling of the same cost, and the infimum is taken at the end.

steps.title: The position estimate and finiteness of the transport distance
steps.body:
Setting. Let \(f:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), that is, \(f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)-\tfrac m2t(1-t)\|x-y\|^2\) for all \(x,y\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), and let \(\nabla f\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz with \(m\le M\). Let \(\pi(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-f(x)}dx\) with \(Z=\int e^{-f}\) be the Gibbs (target) measure; strong convexity makes \(0<Z<\infty\), so \(\pi\) is a probability measure. Let \(\gamma>0\) and \(h>0\), put \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\), and let \(\sigma\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(\delta^2+\sigma^2=1\). For a phase point \((v,x)\) and \(\xi,\xi'\in\mathbb R^p\) the OBABO step is

\[\begin{aligned} v_1&=\delta v+\sigma\xi, & v_2&=v_1-\tfrac h2\nabla f(x), & x^+&=x+hv_2,\\ v_3&=v_2-\tfrac h2\nabla f(x^+), & v^+&=\delta v_3+\sigma\xi', & &(v,x)\mapsto(v^+,x^+). \end{aligned}\]

Let \(\rho_0=\mathcal N\otimes\mu\), where \(\mu\) is a probability measure on \(\mathbb R^p\), and let \(\rho_{k+1}\) be the law of the OBABO step applied to \(Z_k\sim\rho_k\) and an independent pair \((\xi_k,\xi'_k)\sim\mathcal N\otimes\mathcal N\). Let \(\nu_n\) be the second (position) marginal of \(\rho_n\).

Claim. Assume in addition \(4M\le\gamma^2\), \(33\gamma^3h\le m\) and \(W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\). Then for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(W_2(\nu_n,\pi)<\infty\) and

\[W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le\sqrt2\,r^n\,W_2(\mu,\pi)+\frac{6\sqrt2\,\gamma}{m}\,h\sqrt p\,\Bigl(4\sqrt M+\frac{Mh}{2}\Bigr),\qquad r=\sqrt{1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma}}.\]

Proof. Let \(\bar\pi=\mathcal N\otimes\pi\) be the kinetic Gibbs measure, velocity first, and let \(T\), \(\Pi\) be as in the first step; they are defined because \(M\ge m>0\).

Initial distance. By the previous step with \(\nu=\pi\),

\[W_2(T_\#\rho_0,\,T_\#\bar\pi)\le W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty.\qquad(1)\]

Weighted bound. The earlier weighted OBABO theorem applies under exactly the present hypotheses and the finiteness (1). It gives \(W_2(T_\#\rho_n,T_\#\bar\pi)<\infty\) and

\[W_2(T_\#\rho_n,\,T_\#\bar\pi)\le r^n\,W_2(T_\#\rho_0,\,T_\#\bar\pi)+B,\qquad B=\frac{6\gamma}{m}\,h\sqrt p\,\Bigl(4\sqrt M+\frac{Mh}{2}\Bigr).\qquad(2)\]

Projection. Each \(\rho_n\) is a probability measure, because the OBABO step is continuous (\(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz), hence measurable. By the first step, \(\Pi\circ T\) is the position map \((v,x)\mapsto x\), so \(\Pi_\#(T_\#\rho_n)=\nu_n\), and \(\Pi_\#(T_\#\bar\pi)\) is the position marginal of \(\mathcal N\otimes\pi\), which is \(\pi\) because \(\mathcal N\) has total mass one. A map \(\Pi\) that is \(L\)-Lipschitz contracts Wasserstein distances by \(L\): if \((A,B)\) has a coupling law of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), then \((\Pi(A),\Pi(B))\) couples \(\Pi_\#\alpha\) and \(\Pi_\#\beta\) with \(\|\Pi(A)-\Pi(B)\|\le L\|A-B\|\), and one takes the infimum. With \(L=\sqrt2\) from the second step,

\[W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le\sqrt2\,W_2(T_\#\rho_n,\,T_\#\bar\pi).\qquad(3)\]

The right-hand side is finite by (2), which proves \(W_2(\nu_n,\pi)<\infty\).

Conclusion. All distances are now finite real numbers. Using (3), then (2) multiplied by \(\sqrt2\ge0\), then (1) multiplied by \(\sqrt2\,r^n\ge0\),

\[W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le\sqrt2\bigl(r^nW_2(T_\#\rho_0,T_\#\bar\pi)+B\bigr)\le\sqrt2\,r^nW_2(\mu,\pi)+\sqrt2\,B,\]

and \(\sqrt2\,B\) is the second term of the claim. \(\square\)

The weighted metric is used throughout the iteration, and the conversion to positions costs the single factor \(\sqrt2\) at the end. The finiteness statement is proved before the real-valued inequality, so that the inequality is not an identity between truncated infinite values.

KineticLangevin/GaussianTail.lean.title: A positive-part tail bound for the squared Gaussian norm
KineticLangevin/GaussianTail.lean.summary:
Let \(G\) be a standard Gaussian vector in \(\mathbb R^p\), that is, a random vector whose \(p\) coordinates are independent with the standard normal law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) of density \(\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}\). Write \(u_+=\max(u,0)\) for the positive part. This section proves the tail estimate

\[\mathbb E\bigl(\|G\|^2-a\bigr)_+\le4\,e^{-(a-p)/4}\qquad\text{for every }a\ge5p,\]

which is the \(\chi^2\) bound used in the paper's comparison of two second-order updates. The proof is a Chernoff-type argument: the exponential moment \(\mathbb E\,e^{\|G\|^2/3}=(\sqrt3)^p\) is computed exactly from the Gaussian density, the positive part is dominated pointwise by an exponential, and the threshold \(a\ge5p\) absorbs the dimension factor.

The bound concerns the expected excess of \(\|G\|^2\) above the level \(a\), not merely the probability of exceeding \(a\). In the final step it is transferred to any random vector whose law is \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\), on any probability space. No independence between this vector and other random variables is required, which is what the comparison of two coupled second-order chains needs: there the Gaussian velocity and the position discrepancy are built from the same past noise.

steps.title: The scalar exponential square moment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(g\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\). The function \(x\mapsto e^{x^2/3}\) is integrable with respect to \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), and

\[\mathbb E\,e^{g^2/3}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{x^2/3}\,\phi(x)\,dx=\sqrt3.\]

Proof. For every real \(x\),

\[\phi(x)\,e^{x^2/3}=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^2}{3}\Bigr)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/6}.\qquad(1)\]

The function \(e^{-bx^2}\) is Lebesgue integrable on \(\mathbb R\) for every \(b>0\), with \(\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-bx^2}dx=\sqrt{\pi/b}\) (the Gaussian integral). Taking \(b=1/6\), the right-hand side of (1) is Lebesgue integrable. Since \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) has density \(\phi\) with respect to Lebesgue measure, a function \(u\) is \(\mathcal N(0,1)\)-integrable exactly when \(\phi u\) is Lebesgue integrable, and then \(\int u\,d\mathcal N(0,1)=\int\phi u\,dx\). This proves integrability, and

\[\int_{\mathbb R}e^{x^2/3}\phi(x)\,dx=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{1/6}}=\sqrt{\frac{6\pi}{2\pi}}=\sqrt3.\]

Equivalently, both sides are nonnegative and their squares are \(6\pi/(2\pi)=3\). \(\square\)

Integrability is established before the integral is evaluated. This matters below, where \(e^{\|G\|^2/3}\) serves as an integrable majorant.

steps.title: The exponential moment of the squared Gaussian norm
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(G\sim\mathcal N(0,I_p)\) on \(\mathbb R^p\), \(p\ge0\). The function \(z\mapsto e^{\|z\|^2/3}\) is \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\)-integrable and

\[\mathbb E\,e^{\|G\|^2/3}=(\sqrt3)^p.\]

Proof. The law \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\) is the image of the product measure \(\mathcal N(0,1)^{\otimes p}\) on \(\mathbb R^p\) under the identification of coordinate vectors with Euclidean vectors. Hence it suffices to integrate \(w\mapsto e^{\|w\|^2/3}\) against the product measure. For \(w=(w_1,\dots,w_p)\), \(\|w\|^2=\sum_iw_i^2\), so

\[e^{\|w\|^2/3}=\exp\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^p\frac{w_i^2}{3}\Bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^pe^{w_i^2/3}.\qquad(1)\]

Each factor is integrable with respect to its coordinate measure \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) by the previous step. A product \(\prod_iu_i(w_i)\) of functions each integrable in its own variable is integrable with respect to the product measure, and by Fubini's theorem its integral is the product of the integrals. Therefore the function (1) is integrable and

\[\int e^{\|w\|^2/3}\,\mathcal N(0,1)^{\otimes p}(dw)=\prod_{i=1}^p\int_{\mathbb R}e^{x^2/3}\,\mathcal N(0,1)(dx)=(\sqrt3)^p.\]

Integrability and the value of the integral transfer to the image measure \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\) by the change-of-variables formula for image measures. For \(p=0\) the space is a single point, the integrand is \(e^0=1\) and both sides equal \(1\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Two elementary exponential inequalities
steps.body:
Claim. (a) \(\sqrt3\le e^{2/3}\). (b) For all real \(y\) and \(a\), \((y-a)_+\le3\,e^{(y-a)/3}\).

Proof. Both parts use the inequality \(e^u\ge1+u\), valid for every real \(u\) (the exponential is convex and \(1+u\) is its tangent line at \(0\)).

(a) With \(u=1/3\), \(e^{1/3}\ge4/3\). Since both sides are nonnegative, raising to the fourth power preserves the inequality:

\[\bigl(e^{2/3}\bigr)^2=e^{4/3}=\bigl(e^{1/3}\bigr)^4\ge\Bigl(\frac43\Bigr)^4=\frac{256}{81}\ge3=\bigl(\sqrt3\bigr)^2.\]

Since \(e^{2/3}>0\) and \(\sqrt3\ge0\), the inequality between squares gives \(\sqrt3\le e^{2/3}\).

(b) The positive part is the larger of \(y-a\) and \(0\), so it suffices to bound both. With \(u=(y-a)/3\), \(3e^u\ge3+3u\ge3u=y-a\). Also \(3e^u>0\). \(\square\)

Part (b) holds for every \(y\), on both sides of the cutoff \(a\); it is the pointwise Chernoff bound with parameter \(1/3\). Part (a) converts the factor \((\sqrt3)^p\) into the exponential \(e^{2p/3}\).

steps.title: The tail bound for the standard Gaussian law
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(p\ge0\) and \(a\in\mathbb R\) with \(a\ge5p\). Then the function \(z\mapsto(\|z\|^2-a)_+\) is \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\)-integrable and

\[\int_{\mathbb R^p}\bigl(\|z\|^2-a\bigr)_+\,\mathcal N(0,I_p)(dz)\le4\,e^{-(a-p)/4}.\]

Proof. By the previous step (b) with \(y=\|z\|^2\), and \(e^{(y-a)/3}=e^{-a/3}e^{y/3}\),

\[\bigl(\|z\|^2-a\bigr)_+\le3e^{-a/3}\,e^{\|z\|^2/3}\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb R^p.\qquad(1)\]

The right-hand side of (1) is integrable by the second step. The left-hand side is continuous, hence measurable, and nonnegative, so (1) dominates its absolute value; therefore it is integrable. Integrating (1) (monotonicity of the integral) and using the second step,

\[\int\bigl(\|z\|^2-a\bigr)_+\,d\mathcal N(0,I_p)\le3e^{-a/3}(\sqrt3)^p.\]

By part (a) of the previous step and monotonicity of \(t\mapsto t^p\) on \([0,\infty)\), \((\sqrt3)^p\le(e^{2/3})^p=e^{2p/3}\). Hence the integral is at most \(3\exp(-a/3+2p/3)\). The exponent satisfies

\[-\frac a3+\frac{2p}{3}\le-\frac{a-p}{4}\iff-4a+8p\le-3a+3p\iff5p\le a,\]

which is the hypothesis. Since the exponential is increasing, the integral is at most \(3e^{-(a-p)/4}\le4e^{-(a-p)/4}\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(a\ge5p\) is used only in the comparison of exponents; it absorbs the dimension factor \(e^{2p/3}\) of the exponential moment. The constant \(4\) is the one of the paper; the proof gives \(3\).

steps.title: Transfer to any standard Gaussian random vector
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a measure space and \(V:\Omega\to\mathbb R^p\) an almost everywhere measurable map whose law (image measure) \(\mathbb P\circ V^{-1}\) is \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\). Then for every \(a\ge5p\),

\[\mathbb E\bigl(\|V\|^2-a\bigr)_+=\int_\Omega\bigl(\|V(\omega)\|^2-a\bigr)_+\,\mathbb P(d\omega)\le4\,e^{-(a-p)/4}.\]

Proof. The function \(u(x)=(\|x\|^2-a)_+\) is continuous on \(\mathbb R^p\). By the change-of-variables formula for image measures, \(\int_\Omega u(V)\,d\mathbb P=\int_{\mathbb R^p}u\,d(\mathbb P\circ V^{-1})=\int u\,d\mathcal N(0,I_p)\). The previous step bounds the last integral by \(4e^{-(a-p)/4}\). \(\square\)

Only the law of \(V\) enters. The probability space may carry other random variables, such as a position discrepancy produced by the same noise, with an arbitrary joint law with \(V\).

KineticLangevin/ProductContinuousFlow.le.title: Continuous kinetic laws and the Wasserstein coupling infimum
KineticLangevin/ProductContinuousFlow.le.summary:
This section proves the Wasserstein contraction of the continuous kinetic dynamics, Theorem 1 of the paper in the form (exp2), for an abstract forcing. Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra and a countable base of its topology, and let \((S,Q)\) be a probability space, called the source. The source carries a common initial velocity \(V\in L^2(Q;H)\) and a forcing path \(t\mapsto B_t\in L^2(Q;H)\) that is continuous with \(B_0=0\); for the kinetic diffusion \(B_t=\sqrt{2\gamma}\,W_t\). Given an \(M\)-Lipschitz vector field \(g\) (later \(g= abla f\)), friction \(\gamma\ge0\) and a horizon \(T\ge0\), the kinetic equation with inverse mass one is the integral equation

\[V_t-V_0=-\int_0^t igl(\gamma V_s+g(L_s) igr)\,ds+B_t,\qquad L_t-L_0=\int_0^tV_s\,ds,\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

For a position law \(\mu\) with finite second moment, the equation is solved on the product space \(H imes S\) with law \(\mu\otimes Q\), initial position the first coordinate and initial velocity \(V\) of the source coordinate, and \(P^\mu_T\) denotes the law of the position at time \(T\). Because the source is the same for every \(\mu\), \(P^\mu_T\) depends only on \(\mu\) and not on any coupling.

The main result: if \(f\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, \( abla f\) is \(M\)-Lipschitz, \(m\le M\), and \(a\) is a real number with \(\gamma-2a>0\), then for all \(\mu, u\) with finite second moments

\[W_2(P^\mu_T,P^ u_T)\le rac{\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}}{\gamma-2a}\exp\Bigl( rac{\max\{a^2-m,\;M-(\gamma-a)^2\}}{\gamma-2a}\,T\Bigr)W_2(\mu, u).\]

The proof places an arbitrary coupling of \(\mu\) and \( u\) on a common extension of the source, applies the synchronous \(L^2\) contraction of the kinetic flow there, and takes the infimum over couplings. The next section specializes the source to Brownian motion.

steps.title: The kinetic solution on an independent source and its position law
steps.body:
Construction. Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(H\) with finite second moment, \(\int\|x\|^2\mu(dx)<\infty\). Put \(\Omega_\mu=H\times S\) with the product probability \(\mathbb P_\mu=\mu\otimes Q\). On \(\Omega_\mu\) consider the square-integrable random vectors

\[\bar V(x,s)=V(s),\qquad \bar L(x,s)=x,\qquad \bar B_t(x,s)=B_t(s).\]

Here \(\bar L\in L^2(\mathbb P_\mu;H)\) because \(\mu\) has finite second moment, and \(\bar V,\bar B_t\) are the compositions of \(V,B_t\) with the projection \((x,s)\mapsto s\), which maps \(\mathbb P_\mu\) to \(Q\); composition with a measure-preserving map is a linear isometry of \(L^2\) spaces, so \(t\mapsto\bar B_t\) is again continuous with \(\bar B_0=0\). For \(g:H\to H\) that is \(M\)-Lipschitz, the map \(X\mapsto g\circ X\) sends \(L^2(\mathbb P_\mu;H)\) into itself and is \(M\)-Lipschitz there. Define the negative drift on \(L^2\times L^2\) by \(N(v,x)=(\gamma v+g\circ x,\;-v)\). The flow \(t\mapsto Y_t=(V_t,L_t)\in L^2(\mathbb P_\mu;H)^2\) is the continuous solution, constructed earlier by Picard iteration for Lipschitz integral equations with continuous additive input, of

\[Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^tN(Y_s)\,ds+(\bar B_t,0),\qquad Y_0=(\bar V,\bar L),\qquad t\in[0,T],\qquad(1)\]

where the integral is the Bochner integral of a continuous \(L^2\)-valued function. The position law at time \(T\) is the image measure \(P^\mu_T=\mathbb P_\mu\circ L_T^{-1}\) of any representative of \(L_T\).

Claim. Assume \(B\) is continuous with \(B_0=0\) and \(T\ge0\). Then \(t\mapsto Y_t\) is continuous, \(Y_0=(\bar V,\bar L)\), and (1) holds for every \(t\in[0,T]\). Moreover \(P^\mu_T\) is a probability measure with finite second moment.

Proof. The first three properties are the defining properties of the Picard solution of an integral equation with Lipschitz drift and continuous input that vanishes at time \(0\), applied with input \(\bar B\); the hypothesis \(B_0=0\) gives \(\bar B_0=0\) because composition with the projection is linear. The random vector \(L_T\) is an element of \(L^2(\mathbb P_\mu;H)\); it is therefore almost everywhere measurable, so its image measure has total mass \(\mathbb P_\mu(\Omega_\mu)=1\). By the change-of-variables formula, \(\int\|x\|^2P^\mu_T(dx)=\mathbb E\|L_T\|^2<\infty\). \(\square\)

The source \((S,Q)\), the velocity \(V\) and the forcing \(B\) are fixed once and for all. The law \(P^\mu_T\) is therefore a function of \(\mu\) alone, which is what allows two such laws to be compared through an arbitrary coupling of their initial positions.

steps.title: Placing an initial coupling on a common source
steps.body:
Recall that a coupling of probability measures \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) on \(H\) is a probability measure \(\varrho\) on \(H\times H\) with marginals \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). A map \(\phi:(\Omega,\mathbb P)\to(\Omega',\mathbb P')\) is measure preserving if it is measurable and \(\mathbb P\circ\phi^{-1}=\mathbb P'\).

Setting. Let \(\varrho\) be a coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). The extension is \(\Omega_\varrho=(H\times H)\times S\) with the probability \(\mathbb P_\varrho=\varrho\otimes Q\). Define \(\ell(x,y,s)=(x,s)\), \(r(x,y,s)=(y,s)\) and \(\sigma(x,y,s)=s\).

Claim. (a) \(\varrho\) and \(\mathbb P_\varrho\) are probability measures. (b) \(\ell\) is measure preserving from \(\mathbb P_\varrho\) to \(\mu\otimes Q\), and \(r\) from \(\mathbb P_\varrho\) to \(\nu\otimes Q\). (c) For every \(Z\in L^2(Q;H)\), pulling \(Z\) back first to \(H\times S\) and then along \(\ell\), or first to \(H\times S\) and then along \(r\), gives in both cases the random vector \(Z\circ\sigma\) on \(\Omega_\varrho\). (d) The initial phase \((\bar V,\bar L)\) of the previous step equals \((x,s)\mapsto(V(s),x)\) almost everywhere.

Proof. (a) A coupling has total mass one because its first marginal is the probability \(\mu\); a product of two probability measures is a probability measure.

(b) \(\ell\) is the product of the measurable maps \((x,y,s)\mapsto x\) and \((x,y,s)\mapsto s\). On measurable rectangles,

\[\mathbb P_\varrho\bigl(\ell^{-1}(A\times C)\bigr)=\varrho(A\times H)\,Q(C)=\mu(A)\,Q(C),\]

since the first marginal of \(\varrho\) is \(\mu\). Two finite measures on \(H\times S\) that agree on the \(\pi\)-system of measurable rectangles generating the product \(\sigma\)-algebra are equal, so \(\mathbb P_\varrho\circ\ell^{-1}=\mu\otimes Q\). The same computation with the second marginal of \(\varrho\) gives the statement for \(r\).

(c) Pullback along a measure-preserving map acts on representatives by composition, and composition is associative: \((Z\circ\mathrm{pr}_S)\circ\ell=Z\circ(\mathrm{pr}_S\circ\ell)=Z\circ\sigma\), where \(\mathrm{pr}_S(x,s)=s\); likewise \(\mathrm{pr}_S\circ r=\sigma\).

(d) The velocity coordinate \(\bar V\) has representative \((x,s)\mapsto V(s)\) and the position coordinate \(\bar L\) has representative \((x,s)\mapsto x\), each almost everywhere; the intersection of two sets of full measure has full measure. \(\square\)

The coupling \(\varrho\) may correlate the two initial positions arbitrarily. Adjoining one common independent source variable \(s\) leaves both position marginals unchanged and provides both solutions with the same initial velocity \(V(s)\) and the same forcing \(B(s)\).

steps.title: The bound for one initial coupling
steps.body:
Write \(C(a)=\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}/(\gamma-2a)\) and \(k(a)=\max\{a^2-m,\;M-(\gamma-a)^2\}/(\gamma-2a)\).

Claim. Let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, with \(\nabla f\) \(M\)-Lipschitz and \(m\le M\); let \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(a\in\mathbb R\) with \(\gamma-2a>0\); let \(T\ge0\), \(V\in L^2(Q;H)\), and \(B\) continuous with \(B_0=0\). Let \(\mu,\nu\) have finite second moments, let \(P^\mu_T,P^\nu_T\) be the position laws of the first step with \(g=\nabla f\), and let \(\varrho\) be a coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). Then

\[W_2(P^\mu_T,P^\nu_T)\le C(a)\,e^{k(a)T}\Bigl(\int\|x-y\|^2\,\varrho(dx,dy)\Bigr)^{1/2}.\]

The integral on the right is finite, since \(\|x-y\|^2\le2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2\) and both marginals have finite second moments.

Proof. Let \(Y\) be the solution of the first step on \(\Omega_\mu\) and \(Z\) the solution on \(\Omega_\nu\). On the extension \(\Omega_\varrho\) of the previous step define \(A_t=Y_t\circ\ell\) and \(C_t=Z_t\circ r\), coordinatewise in velocity and position.

Both are solutions on the same space with the same forcing. Composition with a measure-preserving map is a continuous linear isometry of \(L^2\) spaces; it commutes with the Bochner integral and with the lift \(X\mapsto\nabla f\circ X\). Applying it to the integral equation (1) of the first step gives, for \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[A_t-A_0=-\int_0^tN(A_s)\,ds+(B_t\circ\sigma,0),\qquad C_t-C_0=-\int_0^tN(C_s)\,ds+(B_t\circ\sigma,0),\]

where the forcing terms coincide by part (c) of the previous step. Both paths are continuous.

Equal initial velocities. By part (c), the initial velocities are \(V\circ\sigma\) for both, so the velocity components of \(A_0\) and \(C_0\) are equal.

Initial position difference. By part (d) and part (b), the position components of \(A_0\) and \(C_0\) have representatives \((x,y,s)\mapsto x\) and \((x,y,s)\mapsto y\). Hence, since \(Q\) is a probability measure and the integrand does not depend on \(s\),

\[\|A_0^{\mathrm{pos}}-C_0^{\mathrm{pos}}\|_{L^2}^2=\int\|x-y\|^2\,(\varrho\otimes Q)(dx,dy,ds)=\int\|x-y\|^2\,\varrho(dx,dy).\]

Synchronous contraction. The \(L^2\) form of the paper's Proposition 1 applies to two continuous solutions of the same kinetic integral equation with the same forcing and equal initial velocities, under exactly the present hypotheses on \(f\), \(m\), \(M\), \(\gamma\) and \(a\). It gives

\[\|A_T^{\mathrm{pos}}-C_T^{\mathrm{pos}}\|_{L^2}\le C(a)\,e^{k(a)T}\Bigl(\int\|x-y\|^2\,d\varrho\Bigr)^{1/2}.\qquad(2)\]

Laws. Since \(\ell\) is measure preserving, the law of \(A_T^{\mathrm{pos}}=L^\mu_T\circ\ell\) under \(\mathbb P_\varrho\) equals the law of \(L^\mu_T\) under \(\mathbb P_\mu\), which is \(P^\mu_T\); likewise the law of \(C_T^{\mathrm{pos}}\) is \(P^\nu_T\). The joint law of two square-integrable random vectors on one probability space is a coupling of their laws, so \(W_2(P^\mu_T,P^\nu_T)\le\|A_T^{\mathrm{pos}}-C_T^{\mathrm{pos}}\|_{L^2}\). Combining with (2) proves the claim. \(\square\)

steps.title: Passing to the Wasserstein distance
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step (without a fixed coupling),

\[W_2(P^\mu_T,P^ u_T)\le rac{\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}}{\gamma-2a}\exp\Bigl( rac{\max\{a^2-m,\;M-(\gamma-a)^2\}}{\gamma-2a}\,T\Bigr)W_2(\mu, u),\]

Here \(W_2\) is understood as a real number; the proof shows that both distances are finite.

Proof. Finiteness. If two probability measures \(\alpha, eta\) have finite second moments, the product measure \(\alpha\otimes eta\) is a coupling with cost \(\int\|x-y\|^2d(\alpha\otimes eta)\le2\int\|x\|^2d\alpha+2\int\|y\|^2d eta<\infty\), so \(W_2(\alpha, eta)<\infty\). This applies to \(\mu, u\) by hypothesis and to \(P^\mu_T,P^ u_T\) by the first step.

Infimum. Put \(q=C(a)e^{k(a)T}\), which is nonnegative because \(\gamma-2a>0\). By the previous step, \(W_2(P^\mu_T,P^ u_T)\le q\,c(\varrho)\) for every coupling \(\varrho\), where \(c(\varrho)=(\int\|x-y\|^2d\varrho)^{1/2}\). Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(W_2(\mu, u)\) is a finite infimum, there is a coupling \(\varrho_\varepsilon\) with \(c(\varrho_\varepsilon)\le W_2(\mu, u)+\varepsilon\). Then

\[W_2(P^\mu_T,P^ u_T)\le q\,c(\varrho_\varepsilon)\le q\,W_2(\mu, u)+q\,\varepsilon.\]

Letting \(\varepsilon o0\) proves the claim. \(\square\)

No optimal coupling is used. The bound holds for every square-integrable common initial velocity \(V\) and every continuous square-integrable forcing \(B\) with \(B_0=0\); Brownian forcing is the special case treated in the next section. For \(a=0\) and \(\gamma^2\ge m+M\) the exponent is \(-m/\gamma\) and the prefactor is \(\sqrt2\), the corrected constant of the paper's (exp1).

KineticLangevin/CanonicalContinuousMixin.title: Position contraction for Brownian kinetic diffusions
KineticLangevin/CanonicalContinuousMixin.summary:
This section specializes the abstract contraction theorem of the previous section to Brownian forcing, which gives Theorem 1 of the paper, in the form (exp2), for the kinetic Langevin diffusion with unit inverse mass:

\[V_t-V_0=-\int_0^t igl(\gamma V_s+ abla f(L_s) igr)\,ds+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,W_t,\qquad L_t-L_0=\int_0^tV_s\,ds.\]

Here \(W\) is a \(p\)-dimensional Brownian motion: \(W_0=0\), its coordinates are independent, and \(W_t-W_s\) is centred Gaussian with covariance \((t-s)I_p\) for \(s\le t\). The initial velocity \(V_0\sim ho\), the initial position \(L_0\sim\mu\) and \(W\) are independent; \( ho\) is an arbitrary probability measure with finite second moment, not necessarily Gaussian. For two initial position laws \(\mu, u\) with finite second moments, the time-\(T\) position laws satisfy

\[W_2(P^{ ho,\mu}_T,P^{ ho, u}_T)\le rac{\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}}{\gamma-2a}\exp\Bigl( rac{\max\{a^2-m,\;M-(\gamma-a)^2\}}{\gamma-2a}\,T\Bigr)W_2(\mu, u)\]

for every real \(a<\gamma/2\). With \(a=0\) and \(\gamma^2\ge m+M\) this reads \(W_2(P^{ ho,\mu}_T,P^{ ho, u}_T)\le\sqrt2\,e^{-mT/\gamma}W_2(\mu, u)\): the prefactor is \(\sqrt2\), not the value \(\sqrt2/\gamma\) printed in the paper's (exp1).

steps.title: Initial velocity and Brownian forcing on one source
steps.body:
Setting. Let \(p\) be the dimension and \(\mathbb R^p\) carry its Euclidean norm. Let \((\Omega_W,\mathbb P_W)\) be the probability space of the \(p\)-dimensional Brownian motion constructed earlier: it is the product of \(p\) copies of the scalar construction, in which a Brownian motion is the isonormal Gaussian process \(t\mapsto W_t=I(\mathbf 1_{[0,t]})\) on \(L^2([0,\infty))\), built from an orthonormal basis and independent standard normal variables. Regarded as a map \(t\mapsto W_t\in L^2(\mathbb P_W;\mathbb R^p)\), it satisfies \(W_0=0\) and \(\mathbb E\|W_t-W_s\|^2=p\,|t-s|\). For \(t<0\) we put \(W_t=W_0=0\).

Let \(\rho\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb R^p\) with \(\int\|v\|^2\rho(dv)<\infty\). The source is \(S=\mathbb R^p\times\Omega_W\) with \(Q_\rho=\rho\otimes\mathbb P_W\). On it define the initial velocity and the forcing

\[V(v,w)=v,\qquad B_t(v,w)=\sqrt{2\gamma}\,W_t(w)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).\]

Claim. \(Q_\rho\) is a probability measure; \(V\in L^2(Q_\rho;\mathbb R^p)\); the map \(t\mapsto B_t\in L^2(Q_\rho;\mathbb R^p)\) is continuous; and \(B_0=0\).

Proof. A product of probability measures is a probability measure. The projection \((v,w)\mapsto v\) maps \(Q_\rho\) to \(\rho\), so \(\mathbb E\|V\|^2=\int\|v\|^2\rho(dv)<\infty\). The projection \((v,w)\mapsto w\) maps \(Q_\rho\) to \(\mathbb P_W\); composition with it is a linear isometry from \(L^2(\mathbb P_W)\) to \(L^2(Q_\rho)\). Hence \(\|B_t-B_s\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\|W_{t^+}-W_{s^+}\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{2\gamma\,p\,|t^+-s^+|}\), where \(t^+=\max(t,0)\), and this tends to \(0\) as \(s\to t\) because \(t\mapsto t^+\) is continuous. Finally \(B_0=\sqrt{2\gamma}\,W_0=0\), since the isometry is linear. \(\square\)

The velocity law \(\rho\) need not be Gaussian. Only its finite second moment is used, which places the initial phase in \(L^2\).

steps.title: Position laws and the mixing bound for every admissible shift
steps.body:
Definition. For probability measures \( ho\) and \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^p\) with finite second moments, for \(f\) with \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(T\ge0\), let \(P^{ ho,\mu}_T\) be the law at time \(T\) of the position \(L_T\) of the kinetic solution of the previous section, constructed on \(\mathbb R^p imes S\) with the probability \(\mu\otimes Q_ ho\), drift \( abla f\), initial velocity \(V\) and forcing \(B=\sqrt{2\gamma}\,W\). Under \(\mu\otimes ho\otimes\mathbb P_W\) the initial position, the initial velocity and the Brownian motion are independent, with laws \(\mu\), \( ho\) and \(\mathbb P_W\), and \((V_t,L_t)\) solves the kinetic integral equation of the summary on \([0,T]\).

Claim. Let \(f:\mathbb R^p o\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, with \( abla f\) \(M\)-Lipschitz and \(m\le M\). Let \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(a\in\mathbb R\) with \(\gamma-2a>0\), and \(T\ge0\). Let \( ho,\mu, u\) be probability measures on \(\mathbb R^p\) with finite second moments. Then

\[W_2(P^{ ho,\mu}_T,P^{ ho, u}_T)\le rac{\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}}{\gamma-2a}\exp\Bigl( rac{\max\{a^2-m,\;M-(\gamma-a)^2\}}{\gamma-2a}\,T\Bigr)W_2(\mu, u).\]

Proof. By the previous step, the source \((S,Q_ ho)\) with velocity \(V\) and forcing \(B\) satisfies the hypotheses of the abstract contraction theorem of the previous section: \(V\in L^2(Q_ ho)\), \(B\) is continuous into \(L^2(Q_ ho)\) and \(B_0=0\). Since \(P^{ ho,\mu}_T\) and \(P^{ ho, u}_T\) are by definition the position laws of that section for this source, the abstract theorem gives the claim, with the same hypotheses on \(f\), \(m\), \(M\), \(\gamma\), \(a\) and \(T\). \(\square\)

Special cases. For \(a=0\) and \(\gamma>0\) the prefactor is \(\sqrt{2\gamma^2}/\gamma=\sqrt2\) and the exponent is \(\max\{-m,\,M-\gamma^2\}/\gamma\); if \(\gamma^2\ge m+M\) then \(M-\gamma^2\le-m\), so

\[W_2(P^{ ho,\mu}_T,P^{ ho, u}_T)\le\sqrt2\,e^{-mT/\gamma}\,W_2(\mu, u).\]

This corrects the prefactor \(\alpha\le\sqrt2/\gamma\) of the paper's (exp1), which is inconsistent with (exp2) at \(v=0\). The paper states the bound with \(W_2( ho\otimes\mu, ho\otimes u)\) on phase space on the right; this equals \(W_2(\mu, u)\), because coupling \((V,X)\) with \((V,Y)\) for a common \(V\sim ho\) independent of a coupling \((X,Y)\) gives \(\le\), and the position projection is \(1\)-Lipschitz for the Euclidean norm on \(\mathbb R^{2p}\), which gives \(\ge\).

KineticLangevin/GaussianTruncation.lean.title: Gaussian truncation for dependent displacement and velocity
KineticLangevin/GaussianTruncation.lean.summary:
In the comparison of two second-order updates, a random matrix \(\nabla^2f(x)-\nabla^2f(y)\) multiplies a standard Gaussian velocity \(V\). The matrix is controlled in two ways: its operator norm is at most \(M-m\) everywhere, and at most \(M_2\|x-y\|\) by the Lipschitz continuity of the Hessian. This section combines the two controls with the Gaussian tail bound of the previous section. Its main result: if \(D\), \(X\), \(V\) are square-integrable random vectors on one probability space, \(V\sim\mathcal N(0,I_p)\), and \(\|D\|\le\min\{B,L\|X\|\}\,\|V\|\) almost surely, then for every \(a\ge5p\)

\[\|D\|_{L^2}\le L\sqrt a\,\|X\|_{L^2}+2B\,e^{-(a-p)/8}.\]

No independence between \(V\) and \((D,X)\) is assumed; only the law of \(V\) enters. The proof splits each sample according to whether \(\|V\|^2\le a\): on the moderate part the Lipschitz control is used, and on the excess \((\|V\|^2-a)_+\) the uniform control.

steps.title: The pointwise cutoff inequality
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(d,x,v,B,L,a\) be nonnegative real numbers with \(d\le\min\{B,Lx\}\,v\). Then

\[d^2\le L^2a\,x^2+B^2\,(v^2-a)_+,\qquad\text{where }u_+=\max(u,0).\]

Proof. Put \(k=\min\{B,Lx\}\), which is nonnegative because \(B\ge0\) and \(Lx\ge0\). Since \(0\le d\le kv\) and squaring is increasing on \([0,\infty)\),

\[d^2\le k^2v^2.\qquad(1)\]

For the same reason \(k\le B\) and \(k\le Lx\) give \(k^2\le B^2\) and \(k^2\le(Lx)^2\). We distinguish two cases.

Case \(v^2\le a\). Then \((v^2-a)_+=0\), and by (1), \(k^2\ge0\) and \(a\ge0\),

\[d^2\le k^2v^2\le k^2a\le(Lx)^2a=L^2a\,x^2.\]

Case \(v^2>a\). Then \((v^2-a)_+=v^2-a\ge0\). Splitting \(v^2=a+(v^2-a)\) in (1) and using \(k^2\le(Lx)^2\) on the first term and \(k^2\le B^2\) on the second, both multiplied by nonnegative numbers,

\[d^2\le k^2a+k^2(v^2-a)\le L^2x^2a+B^2(v^2-a).\]

In both cases the claimed bound holds. \(\square\)

The local control \(Lx\) is used on the moderate part \(\min(v^2,a)\) of \(v^2\), and the uniform control \(B\) only on the excess \((v^2-a)_+\). The subtraction of \(a\) in the excess is kept, so that the expected excess, rather than \(\mathbb E\,v^2\), is what has to be estimated.

steps.title: Squared \(L^2\) norms are second moments
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((\Omega,\mathbb P)\) be a measure space, \(E\) a real inner product space and \(X\in L^2(\mathbb P;E)\). Then

\[\|X\|_{L^2}^2=\int_\Omega\|X(\omega)\|^2\,\mathbb P(d\omega).\]

Proof. The norm of \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) is induced by the inner product \(\langle X,Y\rangle_{L^2}=\int\langle X(\omega),Y(\omega)\rangle\,\mathbb P(d\omega)\). Hence \(\|X\|_{L^2}^2=\langle X,X\rangle_{L^2}=\int\langle X(\omega),X(\omega)\rangle\,d\mathbb P=\int\|X(\omega)\|^2\,d\mathbb P\). \(\square\)

For \(X\in L^2\) the integral on the right is finite, so the identity relates two finite real numbers.

steps.title: Integration of the cutoff and the Gaussian tail
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((\Omega,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space and let \(D,X,V\in L^2(\mathbb P;\mathbb R^p)\), where \(V\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\). Let \(B\ge0\), \(L\ge0\) and \(a\ge5p\), and assume

\[\|D(\omega)\|\le\min\{B,\;L\|X(\omega)\|\}\,\|V(\omega)\|\qquad\text{for }\mathbb P\text{-almost every }\omega.\]

Then

\[\|D\|_{L^2}\le L\sqrt a\,\|X\|_{L^2}+2B\,e^{-(a-p)/8}.\]

Proof. Since \(p\ge0\), \(a\ge5p\ge0\).

Integrability. The functions \(\|D\|^2\), \(\|X\|^2\), \(\|V\|^2\) are integrable because \(D,X,V\in L^2\). The excess \((\|V\|^2-a)_+\) is measurable and satisfies \(0\le(\|V\|^2-a)_+\le\|V\|^2+|a|\); the right side is integrable because constants are integrable for a probability measure. Hence the excess is integrable, and so is \(L^2a\|X\|^2+B^2(\|V\|^2-a)_+\).

Pointwise bound. For almost every \(\omega\), the previous step applied to \(d=\|D(\omega)\|\), \(x=\|X(\omega)\|\), \(v=\|V(\omega)\|\) gives

\[\|D(\omega)\|^2\le L^2a\,\|X(\omega)\|^2+B^2\bigl(\|V(\omega)\|^2-a\bigr)_+.\]

Integration. By monotonicity of the integral for integrable functions that are ordered almost everywhere, linearity, and the previous step (\(\|Y\|_{L^2}^2=\mathbb E\|Y\|^2\)),

\[\|D\|_{L^2}^2\le L^2a\,\|X\|_{L^2}^2+B^2\,\mathbb E\bigl(\|V\|^2-a\bigr)_+.\]

The Gaussian tail bound of the previous section, which uses only the law of \(V\), gives \(\mathbb E(\|V\|^2-a)_+\le4e^{-(a-p)/4}\) because \(a\ge5p\). Multiplying by \(B^2\ge0\),

\[\|D\|_{L^2}^2\le L^2a\,\|X\|_{L^2}^2+4B^2e^{-(a-p)/4}.\qquad(1)\]

Square root. Let \(R=L\sqrt a\,\|X\|_{L^2}+2Be^{-(a-p)/8}\ge0\). Since \((e^{-(a-p)/8})^2=e^{-(a-p)/4}\) and \((\sqrt a)^2=a\),

\[R^2=L^2a\,\|X\|_{L^2}^2+2\cdot L\sqrt a\,\|X\|_{L^2}\cdot2Be^{-(a-p)/8}+4B^2e^{-(a-p)/4}.\]

The middle term is nonnegative, so \(R^2\) is at least the right side of (1), and \(\|D\|_{L^2}^2\le R^2\). Both \(\|D\|_{L^2}\) and \(R\) are nonnegative, hence \(\|D\|_{L^2}\le R\). \(\square\)

No property of the joint law of \((D,X,V)\) is used beyond the almost sure bound: the tail estimate needs only the marginal law of \(V\). In the application \(D=(\nabla^2f(L_0)-\nabla^2f(\tilde L_0))V\), \(X=L_0-\tilde L_0\), \(B=M-m\) and \(L=M_2\), and \(V\) depends on the same past noise as \(X\).

KineticLangevin/HessianRemainder.lean.title: The quadratic force remainder from a Lipschitz Hessian
KineticLangevin/HessianRemainder.lean.summary:
Let \(E\) be a real Hilbert space and \(H:E\to\mathcal L(E)\) a map into the bounded linear operators on \(E\), Lipschitz with constant \(M_2\) for the operator norm. In the application \(H=\nabla^2f\) is the Hessian of the potential and \(g=\nabla f\) the force. For \(x,y\in E\), the averaged Hessian on the segment from \(y\) to \(x\) is the operator

\[\bar H(x,y)=\int_0^1H\bigl(y+t(x-y)\bigr)\,dt,\]

a Bochner integral in the Banach space \(\mathcal L(E)\). This section proves \(\|\bar H(x,y)-H(y)\|\le\frac{M_2}{2}\|x-y\|\) and, when \(H(x)\) is the derivative of \(g\) at every \(x\), the Taylor remainder bound

\[\bigl\|g(x)-g(y)-H(y)(x-y)\bigr\|\le\frac{M_2}{2}\,\|x-y\|^2.\]

This is the deterministic estimate behind the term \(M_2\|L_s-L_0\|^2/2\) in the local error of the second-order algorithm; the factor \(\frac12\) is \(\int_0^1t\,dt\). No probability enters this section.

steps.title: Variation of the Hessian along the segment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H:E\to\mathcal L(E)\) be \(M_2\)-Lipschitz, \(\|H(u)-H(w)\|\le M_2\|u-w\|\) for all \(u,w\), with \(M_2\ge0\). Then for all \(x,y\in E\),

\[\bigl\|\bar H(x,y)-H(y)\bigr\|\le\frac{M_2}{2}\,\|x-y\|.\]

Proof. The map \(t\mapsto H(y+t(x-y))\) is continuous, as the composition of the Lipschitz map \(H\) with a continuous path; hence it is Bochner integrable on \([0,1]\). The integral of the constant \(H(y)\) over \([0,1]\) is \(H(y)\), and the integral is linear, so

\[\bar H(x,y)-H(y)=\int_0^1\Bigl(H\bigl(y+t(x-y)\bigr)-H(y)\Bigr)\,dt.\]

For \(t\in(0,1]\) the Lipschitz condition gives

\[\bigl\|H(y+t(x-y))-H(y)\bigr\|\le M_2\,\|t(x-y)\|=M_2\,t\,\|x-y\|,\]

using \(t\ge0\). The norm of a Bochner integral is at most the integral of any integrable bound on the norm of the integrand, so

\[\bigl\|\bar H(x,y)-H(y)\bigr\|\le\int_0^1M_2\,t\,\|x-y\|\,dt=M_2\|x-y\|\int_0^1t\,dt=\frac{M_2}{2}\|x-y\|.\qquad\square\]

steps.title: The first-order Taylor remainder of the force
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(g:E\to E\) be Fréchet differentiable at every point with derivative \(Dg(u)=H(u)\), and let \(H\) be \(M_2\)-Lipschitz. Then for all \(x,y\in E\),

\[\bigl\|g(x)-g(y)-H(y)(x-y)\bigr\|\le\frac{M_2}{2}\,\|x-y\|^2.\]

Proof. Integral form of the increment. The path \(c(t)=y+t(x-y)\) has derivative \(x-y\), so by the chain rule \(\frac{d}{dt}g(c(t))=H(c(t))(x-y)\), which is continuous in \(t\) because \(H\) is continuous. By the fundamental theorem of calculus,

\[g(x)-g(y)=\int_0^1H\bigl(c(t)\bigr)(x-y)\,dt=\bar H(x,y)(x-y).\]

The second equality holds because evaluation at the fixed vector \(x-y\) is a bounded linear map on \(\mathcal L(E)\), and bounded linear maps commute with Bochner integrals. This identity was proved in the earlier section on the averaged Hessian.

Estimate. Consequently \(g(x)-g(y)-H(y)(x-y)=\bigl(\bar H(x,y)-H(y)\bigr)(x-y)\). By the definition of the operator norm and the previous step,

\[\bigl\|(\bar H(x,y)-H(y))(x-y)\bigr\|\le\bigl\|\bar H(x,y)-H(y)\bigr\|\,\|x-y\|\le\frac{M_2}{2}\|x-y\|\cdot\|x-y\|.\qquad\square\]

The operator \(\bar H(x,y)\) is an average of Hessians along the whole segment; it is not the Hessian at a single intermediate point, which would not exist in general for vector-valued maps.
