KineticLangevin/RandomOperatorLp.lean.title: The action of bounded random operators on \(L^2\)
KineticLangevin/RandomOperatorLp.lean.summary:
A Hessian evaluated at a random position is a random linear operator. To use such an operator inside time integrals of square-integrable random vectors, this section constructs its action on \(L^2\). Let \((\Omega,\mathbb P)\) be a measure space, \(E\) a real normed space, and \(A:\Omega\to\mathcal L(E)\) a strongly measurable (up to null sets) random operator with \(\|A(\omega)\|\le M\) for almost every \(\omega\). Then

\[\mathcal A:L^2(\mathbb P;E)\to L^2(\mathbb P;E),\qquad(\mathcal AX)(\omega)=A(\omega)X(\omega),\]

is a bounded linear operator with \(\|\mathcal AX\|_{L^2}\le M\|X\|_{L^2}\) and, if \(M\ge0\), \(\|\mathcal A\|\le M\). The operator \(A\) may depend on \(X\) in an arbitrary way: no independence is involved, because the construction acts sample by sample. In the second-order analysis \(A=\nabla^2f(L_0)\) or a difference of two such Hessians.

steps.title: Construction by Hölder multiplication
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(A:\Omega\to\mathcal L(E)\) be almost everywhere strongly measurable with \(\|A(\omega)\|\le M\) for almost every \(\omega\). There is a bounded linear operator \(\mathcal A\) on \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) such that \(\mathcal AX\) is the class of \(\omega\mapsto A(\omega)X(\omega)\) (the representative identity is the next step).

Proof. Recall that \(L^\infty(\mathbb P;F)\) consists of the classes of almost everywhere strongly measurable functions that are essentially bounded. By hypothesis \(A\) is such a function with values in \(F=\mathcal L(E)\), with essential bound \(M\), so \(A\in L^\infty(\mathbb P;\mathcal L(E))\). The evaluation map \(\mathcal L(E)\times E\to E\), \((T,v)\mapsto Tv\), is bilinear with \(\|Tv\|\le\|T\|\,\|v\|\). Hölder's inequality for such a bilinear map, with exponents \(\frac12=\frac1\infty+\frac12\), states that for \(A\in L^\infty\) and \(X\in L^2\) the function \(\omega\mapsto A(\omega)X(\omega)\) is in \(L^2\), with

\[\|AX\|_{L^2}\le\|A\|_{L^\infty}\,\|X\|_{L^2},\]

and that this product is bilinear and jointly continuous on \(L^\infty\times L^2\). Fixing the first argument \(A\) gives a bounded linear map \(\mathcal A\) on \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Identification of representatives
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(X\in L^2(\mathbb P;E)\), \((\mathcal AX)(\omega)=A(\omega)X(\omega)\) for \(\mathbb P\)-almost every \(\omega\).

Proof. The Hölder product of two classes is represented almost everywhere by the pointwise product of representatives, and the \(L^\infty\) class of \(A\) is represented by \(A\) itself almost everywhere. On the intersection of these two sets of full measure, \((\mathcal AX)(\omega)=A(\omega)X(\omega)\). \(\square\)

The identity keeps the original probability space: \(A(\omega)\) and \(X(\omega)\) are evaluated at the same sample point, so pointwise inequalities such as the Taylor remainder bound or the Gaussian truncation can be applied to \(\mathcal AX\).

steps.title: The deterministic operator bound
steps.body:
Claim. (a) For every \(X\in L^2(\mathbb P;E)\), \(\|\mathcal AX\|_{L^2}\le M\|X\|_{L^2}\). (b) If moreover \(M\ge0\), the operator norm satisfies \(\|\mathcal A\|\le M\).

\[\|(\mathcal AX)(\omega)\|=\|A(\omega)X(\omega)\|\le\|A(\omega)\|\,\|X(\omega)\|\le M\,\|X(\omega)\|.\]

If \(M\ge0\), squaring and integrating gives \(\|\mathcal AX\|_{L^2}^2\le M^2\|X\|_{L^2}^2\), and taking square roots gives (a). If \(M<0\), the hypothesis \(\|A(\omega)\|\le M\) can only hold almost everywhere when \(\mathbb P\) is the zero measure; then \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)=\{0\}\) and (a) reads \(0\le0\).

(b) The operator norm of a bounded linear map is the smallest \(C\ge0\) with \(\|\mathcal AX\|\le C\|X\|\) for every \(X\); by (a), \(C=M\) is such a constant. \(\square\)

The bound passes from the pointwise operator norm to the \(L^2\) operator norm without any assumption on the joint law of \(A\) and \(X\).

KineticLangevin/LpMomentIntegral.lean.title: Fourth moments of Bochner time integrals in \(L^2\)
KineticLangevin/LpMomentIntegral.lean.summary:
In the analysis of the second-order algorithm, the displacement \(L_s-L_0=\int_0^sV_r\,dr\) of the kinetic diffusion is a Bochner integral in the Hilbert space \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)\), while the Taylor remainder requires its fourth moment. This section bounds fourth moments of such integrals. For a measure space \((\Omega,\mathbb P)\), a Banach space \(E\) and \(X\in L^2(\mathbb P;E)\), write

\[\|X\|_{L^4}=\Bigl(\int_\Omega\|X(\omega)\|^4\,\mathbb P(d\omega)\Bigr)^{1/4}\in[0,\infty],\]

which may be infinite. For \(R\in[0,\infty]\) let \(\mathcal B_4(R)=\{X\in L^2(\mathbb P;E):\|X\|_{L^4}\le R\}\). We prove that \(\mathcal B_4(R)\) is a closed convex subset of \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) and deduce: if \(t\mapsto v(t)\in L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) is continuous and \(\|v(t)\|_{L^4}\le R\) for \(t\in[0,T]\), then

\[\Bigl\|\int_0^Tv(t)\,dt\Bigr\|_{L^4}\le T\,R.\]

The integral is the one already defined in \(L^2\); no continuity of \(v\) as a map into \(L^4\) is needed. For a stationary kinetic diffusion \(\|V_r\|_{L^4}=(p^2+2p)^{1/4}\), and the bound gives \(\|L_s-L_0\|_{L^4}\le s(p^2+2p)^{1/4}\).

steps.title: The fourth-moment ball is closed in \(L^2\)
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(R\in[0,\infty]\), the set \(\mathcal B_4(R)\) is closed in \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)\).

Proof. \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) is a metric space, so it suffices to show that \(\mathcal B_4(R)\) is sequentially closed. Let \(X_n\in\mathcal B_4(R)\) converge to \(X\) in \(L^2\).

Convergence in measure. For \(\varepsilon>0\), Chebyshev's inequality gives \(\mathbb P(\|X_n-X\|>\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon^{-2}\|X_n-X\|_{L^2}^2\to0\), so \(X_n\to X\) in measure.

Lower semicontinuity. A sequence converging in measure has a subsequence \(X_{n_k}\) converging to \(X\) almost everywhere. Then \(\|X_{n_k}(\omega)\|^4\to\|X(\omega)\|^4\) almost everywhere, and Fatou's lemma gives

\[\int\|X\|^4\,d\mathbb P\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}\int\|X_{n_k}\|^4\,d\mathbb P\le R^4.\]

Hence \(\|X\|_{L^4}\le R\) and \(X\in\mathcal B_4(R)\). \(\square\)

The set is defined inside \(L^2\): its elements are square-integrable classes whose fourth moment is moreover at most \(R^4\). The fourth-moment condition is never used to obtain square integrability.

steps.title: Convexity of the fourth-moment ball
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(R\in[0,\infty]\), \(\mathcal B_4(R)\) is convex.

Proof. Let \(X,Y\in\mathcal B_4(R)\) and \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\). The class \(aX+bY\in L^2\) is represented almost everywhere by \(\omega\mapsto aX(\omega)+bY(\omega)\), and \(\|\cdot\|_{L^4}\) depends only on the class. By Minkowski's inequality in \(L^4\) (valid for extended values) and absolute homogeneity,

\[\|aX+bY\|_{L^4}\le\|aX\|_{L^4}+\|bY\|_{L^4}=a\|X\|_{L^4}+b\|Y\|_{L^4}\le aR+bR=(a+b)R=R.\qquad\square\]

The computation is carried out in \([0,\infty]\), so it needs no prior finiteness of the fourth moments; if \(R<\infty\), finiteness follows from the bound.

In convex_lpFourthBall, hcoe is the almost-everywhere representative of \(aX+bY\), obtained with filter_upwards from Lp.coeFn_add and Lp.coeFn_smul; eLpNorm_congr_ae transfers the norm to that representative. The calc is the displayed chain: eLpNorm_add_le (Minkowski, with exponent \(4\ge1\)), eLpNorm_const_smul with Real.enorm_eq_ofReal for homogeneity, gcongr with the two membership hypotheses, and ENNReal.ofReal_add with hab for \(a+b=1\).

steps.title: The fourth moment of a time integral
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(v:\mathbb R\to L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) be continuous, \(T\ge0\) and \(R\in[0,\infty]\), and suppose \(\|v(t)\|_{L^4}\le R\) for every \(t\in[0,T]\). Then

\[\Bigl\|\int_0^Tv(t)\,dt\Bigr\|_{L^4}\le T\,R,\]

where the integral is the Bochner integral in \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) and the product is taken in \([0,\infty]\).

Proof. If \(T=0\) the integral is the zero class, whose \(L^4\) norm is \(0\).

Let \(T>0\). The interval \((0,T]\) has Lebesgue measure \(T\), which is positive and finite, and \(v\) is integrable on it because it is continuous. Every \(v(t)\), \(t\in(0,T]\), lies in \(\mathcal B_4(R)\), which is closed and convex by the two previous steps. The average of an integrable function with values in a closed convex subset \(C\) of a Banach space lies in \(C\). (If the average \(\bar v\) were outside \(C\), the Hahn–Banach separation theorem would give a continuous linear functional \(\ell\) and \(c\in\mathbb R\) with \(\ell(\bar v)>c\ge\ell(y)\) for all \(y\in C\); since \(\ell\) commutes with the Bochner integral, \(\ell(\bar v)\) is the average of \(\ell(v(t))\le c\), a contradiction.) Hence

\[\bar v=\frac1T\int_0^Tv(t)\,dt\in\mathcal B_4(R),\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad\frac1T\Bigl\|\int_0^Tv(t)\,dt\Bigr\|_{L^4}\le R,\]

using homogeneity \(\|cX\|_{L^4}=|c|\,\|X\|_{L^4}\). Multiplying by \(T\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

The argument uses only the \(L^2\)-valued integral and the closed convex structure of \(\mathcal B_4(R)\) inside \(L^2\). It applies, for instance, to \(v(r)=V_r\), whose fourth moments are known from its Gaussian law, without any assumption on the joint law of the velocities at different times.

KineticLangevin/FreeOU.lean.title: The Gaussian marginal and primitive of the free Ornstein–Uhlenbeck velocity
KineticLangevin/FreeOU.lean.summary:
The free Ornstein–Uhlenbeck velocity is the solution of the kinetic velocity equation without force: started at \(V\) and driven by \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\,dW\), it equals

\[U_t=\psi_0(t)V+N_t,\qquad\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t},\qquad N_t=\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\,dW_s.\]

It appears in the second-order algorithm, where the Hessian at the initial position multiplies \(\int_0^t\int_0^sU_r\,dr\,ds\), the part of the displacement that is linear in the initial velocity and in the fresh noise. This section treats \(U\) as a path in \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) for a given initial velocity \(V\) and a given continuous innovation path \(N\). We prove: its primitive is \(\int_0^tU_s\,ds=\psi_1(t)V+\int_0^tN_s\,ds\) with \(\psi_1(t)=\int_0^t\psi_0\); and if \(V\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) and \(N_t\) is independent of \(V\) with law \(\mathcal N(0,(1-\psi_0(t)^2)I)\), then \(U_t\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\). The independence hypothesis is verified later for the Brownian reference process, from the independence of past and future Brownian increments.

steps.title: An independent thermal innovation preserves the standard Gaussian law
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra and standard Gaussian law \(\mathcal N=\mathcal N(0,I)\). Let \(a\in\mathbb R\) with \(a^2\le1\), and let \(\mathcal N_c\) be the image of \(\mathcal N\) under \(z\mapsto cz\), \(c=\sqrt{1-a^2}\). Then the image of \(\mathcal N\otimes\mathcal N_c\) under \((x,y)\mapsto ax+y\) is \(\mathcal N\). In terms of random vectors: if \(Z\sim\mathcal N\) and \(Y\sim\mathcal N_c\) are independent, then \(aZ+Y\sim\mathcal N\).

Proof. The product of two image measures is the image of the product measure under the product map: \(\mathcal N\otimes\mathcal N_c\) is the image of \(\mathcal N\otimes\mathcal N\) under \((z,z')\mapsto(z,cz')\). Composing the two maps, the measure in question is the image of \(\mathcal N\otimes\mathcal N\) under \((z,z')\mapsto az+cz'\). Since \(a^2+c^2=a^2+(1-a^2)=1\), the earlier linear-combination lemma for independent standard Gaussians applies: for independent \(Z,Z'\sim\mathcal N\) and \(a^2+c^2=1\), \(aZ+cZ'\sim\mathcal N\). (Its proof compares characteristic functions: \(\mathbb E\,e^{i\langle\xi,aZ+cZ'\rangle}=e^{-a^2\|\xi\|^2/2}e^{-c^2\|\xi\|^2/2}=e^{-\|\xi\|^2/2}\), and a law on \(E\) is determined by its characteristic function.) \(\square\)

The conclusion is an identity of probability measures, not a statement about covariances only.

The goal is then the earlier lemma stdGaussian_linear_combination with coefficients \(a\) and \(\sqrt{1-a^2}\); its hypothesis \(a^2+(\sqrt{1-a^2})^2=1\) is proved by Real.sq_sqrt (using \(1-a^2\ge0\), from sub_nonneg.mpr ha) and ring.

steps.title: The free Ornstein–Uhlenbeck path and its primitive
steps.body:
Definition. Let \((\Omega,\mathbb P)\) be a measure space, \(E\) a real normed space, \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(V\in L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) and \(N:\mathbb R\to L^2(\mathbb P;E)\). The free Ornstein–Uhlenbeck velocity is the path

\[U_t=\psi_0(t)\,V+N_t\in L^2(\mathbb P;E),\qquad\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}.\]

Claim. (a) If \(N\) is continuous, then \(t\mapsto U_t\) is continuous. (b) If moreover \(E\) is complete, then for every \(t\in\mathbb R\),

\[\int_0^tU_s\,ds=\psi_1(t)\,V+\int_0^tN_s\,ds,\qquad\psi_1(t)=\int_0^t\psi_0(s)\,ds,\]

with Bochner integrals in \(L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) (oriented integrals when \(t<0\)).

Proof. (a) \(t\mapsto\psi_0(t)\) is continuous, scalar multiplication \(\mathbb R\times L^2\to L^2\) is continuous, and the sum of continuous paths is continuous.

(b) Both \(s\mapsto\psi_0(s)V\) and \(s\mapsto N_s\) are continuous, hence integrable on the interval between \(0\) and \(t\). By linearity of the integral, \(\int_0^tU_s\,ds=\int_0^t\psi_0(s)V\,ds+\int_0^tN_s\,ds\). For a fixed vector \(V\), \(\int_0^t\psi_0(s)V\,ds=\bigl(\int_0^t\psi_0(s)\,ds\bigr)V=\psi_1(t)V\), which is the definition of \(\psi_1\). \(\square\)

For the Brownian reference process, \(N_t=\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}dW_s\) and the second term is the position innovation \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_0^t\psi_1(t-s)\,dW_s\). The initial-velocity part and the noise part of the displacement are thus integrated on the same Brownian interval.

steps.title: The Gaussian marginal of the free velocity
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, \((\Omega,\mathbb P)\) a measure space, \(\gamma\ge0\), \(t\ge0\), \(V\in L^2(\mathbb P;E)\) and \(N:\mathbb R\to L^2(\mathbb P;E)\). Suppose the pair \((V,N_t)\) has the law

\[\mathcal N(0,I)\otimes\bigl(\text{image of }\mathcal N(0,I)\text{ under }z\mapsto\sqrt{1-\psi_0(t)^2}\,z\bigr),\]

that is, \(V\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), \(N_t\sim\mathcal N(0,(1-\psi_0(t)^2)I)\), and \(V\), \(N_t\) are independent. Then \(U_t=\psi_0(t)V+N_t\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,I)\).

Proof. Since \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), \(0\le\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\le1\), so \(\psi_0(t)^2\le1\). By the first step with \(a=\psi_0(t)\), the image of the pair law under \((x,y)\mapsto\psi_0(t)x+y\) is \(\mathcal N(0,I)\). The law of a measurable function of the pair \((V,N_t)\) is the image of the pair law under that function, so \(\psi_0(t)V+N_t\), computed pointwise, has law \(\mathcal N(0,I)\). Finally, the \(L^2\) class \(U_t\) is represented almost everywhere by \(\omega\mapsto\psi_0(t)V(\omega)+N_t(\omega)\), and almost everywhere equal random vectors have the same law. \(\square\)

The hypothesis involves only the joint law of \((V,N_t)\). In the second-order comparison, \(V\) is the stationary velocity at the start of a step and \(N_t\) is built from the Brownian increments after that time; the required independence follows from the independence of past and future Brownian increments, proved later. No independence between \(U_t\) and the position discrepancy of the coupled algorithm is needed.

KineticLangevin/LpMomentBounds.lean.title: Fourth displacement moments and the quadratic force remainder
KineticLangevin/LpMomentBounds.lean.summary:
The Taylor remainder of the force is bounded by \(\frac{M_2}{2}\|L_s-L_0\|^2\), a quadratic function of the displacement. Its \(L^2\) norm is therefore controlled by the fourth moment of the displacement: if \(\|D\|\le a\|X\|^2\) almost surely, then \(\|D\|_{L^2}\le a\|X\|_{L^4}^2\). This section proves that estimate, computes the \(L^4\) norm of a standard Gaussian vector in \(\mathbb R^p\),

\[\bigl(\mathbb E\|V\|^4\bigr)^{1/4}=(p^2+2p)^{1/4},\]

and combines the two with the averaging bound of the previous section: if \(X_t-X_0=\int_0^tV_r\,dr\) in \(L^2\) and every \(V_r\) is standard Gaussian, then \(\|X_t-X_0\|_{L^4}\le t\,(p^2+2p)^{1/4}\). Squaring gives the factor \(t^2\sqrt{p^2+2p}\) of the second-order local error. The exact value \(p^2+2p\) is kept; no simplification valid only for \(p\ge2\) is made here.

steps.title: A quadratic pointwise bound in second mean
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((\Omega,\mathbb P)\) be a measure space, \(E\) a normed space, \(D,X\in L^2(\mathbb P;E)\), and \(a,C\ge0\). Assume \(\|X\|_{L^4}\le C\) and \(\|D(\omega)\|\le a\|X(\omega)\|^2\) for almost every \(\omega\). Then \(\|D\|_{L^2}\le aC^2\).

Proof. Work with the extended norms \(\|\cdot\|_{L^q}\in[0,\infty]\). The \(L^2\) norm is monotone with respect to almost-everywhere pointwise bounds and absolutely homogeneous, so the hypothesis gives

\[\|D\|_{L^2}\le a\,\bigl\|\,\|X\|^2\bigr\|_{L^2}.\]

Since \(\int(\|X\|^2)^2\,d\mathbb P=\int\|X\|^4\,d\mathbb P\),

\[\bigl\|\,\|X\|^2\bigr\|_{L^2}=\Bigl(\int\|X\|^4\,d\mathbb P\Bigr)^{1/2}=\|X\|_{L^4}^2\le C^2.\]

Hence \(\|D\|_{L^2}\le aC^2\), a finite number; for an element of \(L^2\) the extended norm is the usual norm. \(\square\)

steps.title: The \(L^4\) norm of a standard Gaussian vector
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(V:\Omega\to\mathbb R^p\) have law \(\mathcal N(0,I_p)\) under \(\mathbb P\). Then

\[\|V\|_{L^4}=\bigl(p^2+2p\bigr)^{1/4}.\]

Proof. A Gaussian measure on a finite-dimensional space has finite moments of every order (for instance by Fernique's theorem, or directly from the integrability of \(e^{\|z\|^2/3}\) shown in the section on Gaussian tails); since \(V\) has a Gaussian law, \(\mathbb E\|V\|^4<\infty\). Hence \(\|V\|_{L^4}=(\mathbb E\|V\|^4)^{1/4}\). The fourth moment was computed in the section on Gaussian fourth moments: with independent standard normal coordinates \(V_i\),

\[\mathbb E\|V\|^4=\mathbb E\Bigl(\sum_iV_i^2\Bigr)^2=\sum_i\mathbb EV_i^4+\sum_{i\ne j}\mathbb EV_i^2\,\mathbb EV_j^2=3p+p(p-1)=p^2+2p.\qquad\square\]

Only the law of \(V\) is used, so the value holds on every probability space carrying such a vector. For \(p=1\) it gives \(3^{1/4}\), and \(\sqrt{p^2+2p}\) is \(\sqrt3\), larger than \(\sqrt2\,p=\sqrt2\).

steps.title: The displacement of a Gaussian-velocity path in \(L^4\)
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(X,V:\mathbb R\to L^2(\mathbb P;\mathbb R^p)\) with \(V\) continuous, let \(T\in\mathbb R\), and assume for every \(t\in[0,T]\)

\[X_t-X_0=\int_0^tV_r\,dr\quad\text{in }L^2,\qquad V_t\sim\mathcal N(0,I_p).\]

Then for every \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[\|X_t-X_0\|_{L^4}\le t\,\bigl(p^2+2p\bigr)^{1/4}.\]

Proof. Fix \(t\in[0,T]\) and put \(R=(p^2+2p)^{1/4}\). For \(s\in[0,t]\subseteq[0,T]\), the previous step gives \(\|V_s\|_{L^4}=R\). By the kinematic identity and the fourth-moment bound for time integrals proved in the previous section (applied on \([0,t]\), with \(t\ge0\)),

\[\|X_t-X_0\|_{L^4}=\Bigl\|\int_0^tV_r\,dr\Bigr\|_{L^4}\le t\,R.\qquad\square\]

The velocities at different times are not assumed independent; only their individual Gaussian laws and the continuity of the path in \(L^2\) are used. Combined with the first step and the Taylor remainder bound \(\frac{M_2}{2}\|L_s-L_0\|^2\), this gives \(\|\text{remainder}\|_{L^2}\le\frac{M_2}{2}s^2\sqrt{p^2+2p}\).

After rw [hkin t ht], the calc applies eLpNorm_four_integral_le on \([0,t]\) with radius ENNReal.ofReal R; the pointwise radius condition is an equality supplied by gaussian_eLpNorm_four, using hlaw at \(s\in[0,t]\). KineticLangevin/KernelConvolution.lean.title: Convolution and time-primitive identities for Wiener responses
KineticLangevin/KernelConvolution.lean.summary:
The Gaussian innovations of the kinetic algorithms are Wiener integrals of deterministic kernels. Let \(\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R)\) with Lebesgue measure. For a continuous \(k:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) and \(t\ge0\), the time kernel \(K_k(t)\in\mathcal H\) is

\[K_k(t)(r)=\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}(r)\,k(t-r),\qquad\langle f,K_k(t)\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\int_{(0,t]}f(r)\,k(t-r)\,dr.\]

If \(I:\mathcal H\to L^2(\mathbb P_W)\) is the isonormal (Wiener) map of the Brownian motion, \(I(\mathbf 1_{(0,t]})=W_t\), and \(\tau_a\) is translation by \(a\ge0\), then \(N_k(a,t)=I(\tau_aK_k(t))=\int_a^{a+t}k(a+t-r)\,dW_r\) is the response of the kernel \(k\) to the Brownian increments on \((a,a+t]\). For instance \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\,N_{\psi_0}(a,h)\) and \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\,N_{\psi_1}(a,h)\) are the velocity and position innovations of a KLMC step, and \(N_{\varphi_2},N_{\varphi_3}\) the additional noises of KLMC2.

This section proves, for \(\gamma\ge0\) and every \(k\in\mathbb N\), the identities

\[N_{\varphi_{k+1}}(a,t)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}N_{\psi_k}(a,s)\,ds,\qquad N_{\psi_{k+1}}(a,t)=\int_0^tN_{\psi_k}(a,s)\,ds,\]

the second for every real \(\gamma\), as equalities of random variables, both scalar and vector-valued, on the same Brownian source. They are the stochastic Fubini identities used in the paper's derivation of KLMC2. They are obtained by proving the corresponding deterministic identities in \(\mathcal H\), with the ordinary Fubini theorem, and then applying the continuous linear map \(I\circ\tau_a\), which commutes with Bochner integrals.

steps.title: The causal exponential convolution
steps.body:
Definition. For \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) and \(k:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), the causal exponential convolution is

\[(\mathcal E_\beta k)(t)=\int_0^te^{-\beta(t-s)}k(s)\,ds\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),\]

an oriented integral when \(t<0\). With \(\beta=\gamma\) and \(k=\psi_j\) it is \(\varphi_{j+1}\); with \(\beta=0\) it is the primitive \(\psi_{j+1}\).

Claim. (a) \((\mathcal E_\beta k)(t)=e^{-\beta t}\int_0^te^{\beta s}k(s)\,ds\) for every \(t\). (b) If \(k\) is continuous, then \(\mathcal E_\beta k\) is continuous.

Proof. (a) For every \(s\), \(e^{-\beta(t-s)}=e^{-\beta t}e^{\beta s}\) by the addition law of the exponential, and the constant \(e^{-\beta t}\) can be taken out of the integral.

(b) The function \(s\mapsto e^{\beta s}k(s)\) is continuous, hence integrable on bounded intervals, and its primitive \(t\mapsto\int_0^te^{\beta s}k(s)\,ds\) is continuous. The product with the continuous function \(e^{-\beta t}\) is continuous, and by (a) this product is \(\mathcal E_\beta k\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The two orders of integration over the triangle
steps.body:
The double integrals below range over the triangle \(\{(s,r):0<r\le s\le t\}\). The two identities express its sections in each order of integration.

Claim. Let \(t\in\mathbb R\) and \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\). (a) For any \(k\) and \(s\in(0,t]\),

\[\int_{(0,t]}\mathbf 1_{\{r\le s\}}\,k(s-r)\,f(r)\,dr=\int_{(0,s]}f(r)\,k(s-r)\,dr.\]

(b) For \(\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(j\in\mathbb N\) and \(r\in(0,t]\),

\[\int_{(0,t]}\mathbf 1_{\{r\le s\}}\,e^{-\beta(t-s)}\psi_j(s-r)\,f(r)\,ds=f(r)\,(\mathcal E_\beta\psi_j)(t-r).\]

In both identities the two sides are integrals of the same function over the same set after the rewriting below, so they hold whenever either side is defined.

Proof. (a) The integrand equals the indicator of \((-\infty,s]\) times \(r\mapsto f(r)k(s-r)\). Integrating an indicator over \((0,t]\) is integrating over the intersection \((-\infty,s]\cap(0,t]\), which is \((0,s]\) because \(s\le t\).

(b) In the variable \(s\), the integrand is the indicator of \([r,\infty)\) times \(s\mapsto e^{-\beta(t-s)}\psi_j(s-r)f(r)\). Since \(r>0\), \([r,\infty)\cap(0,t]=[r,t]\), and the endpoint \(r\) has Lebesgue measure zero, so the integral is \(f(r)\int_r^te^{-\beta(t-s)}\psi_j(s-r)\,ds\). The substitution \(u=s-r\) gives

\[\int_r^te^{-\beta(t-s)}\psi_j(s-r)\,ds=\int_0^{t-r}e^{-\beta((t-r)-u)}\psi_j(u)\,du=(\mathcal E_\beta\psi_j)(t-r).\qquad\square\]

steps.title: The deterministic Fubini identity in \(L^2(\mathbb R)\)
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\beta\ge0\), \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(j\in\mathbb N\) and \(t\ge0\). Then, in \(\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R)\),

\[K_{\mathcal E_\beta\psi_j}(t)=\int_0^te^{-\beta(t-s)}\,K_{\psi_j}(s)\,ds,\]

where the right side is the Bochner integral of the continuous \(\mathcal H\)-valued function \(s\mapsto e^{-\beta(t-s)}K_{\psi_j}(s)\).

Proof. Two elements of a Hilbert space are equal if they have the same inner product with every \(f\in\mathcal H\). Fix \(f\in\mathcal H\) and let \(\mu\) be Lebesgue measure on \((0,t]\).

An integrable function on the square. Define on \((0,t]^2\)

\[w(s,r)=\begin{cases}e^{-\beta(t-s)}\psi_j(s-r)&\text{if }0<r\le s\le t,\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]

The function \(\psi_j\) is continuous, so it is bounded on the compact interval \([0,t]\), say \(|\psi_j|\le C\) with \(C\ge0\). On the triangle, \(s\le t\) and \(\beta\ge0\) give \(e^{-\beta(t-s)}\le1\), and \(s-r\in[0,t]\), so \(|w|\le C\) everywhere; \(w\) is measurable as a piecewise definition on a measurable set. Since \(f\in L^2\) and \((0,t]\) has finite measure, \(f\) is integrable on \((0,t]\) by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. Hence \(F(s,r)=w(s,r)f(r)\) is integrable for \(\mu\otimes\mu\): it is a bounded measurable function times an integrable function of \(r\). By Fubini's theorem,

\[\int_{(0,t]}\int_{(0,t]}F(s,r)\,dr\,ds=\int_{(0,t]}\int_{(0,t]}F(s,r)\,ds\,dr.\qquad(1)\]

Integrating first in \(r\). For \(s\in(0,t]\), the previous step (a) gives

\[\int_{(0,t]}F(s,r)\,dr=e^{-\beta(t-s)}\int_{(0,s]}f(r)\psi_j(s-r)\,dr=e^{-\beta(t-s)}\langle f,K_{\psi_j}(s)\rangle.\]

Integrating first in \(s\). For \(r\in(0,t]\), the previous step (b) gives \(\int_{(0,t]}F(s,r)\,ds=f(r)(\mathcal E_\beta\psi_j)(t-r)\), and integrating over \(r\in(0,t]\) gives \(\langle f,K_{\mathcal E_\beta\psi_j}(t)\rangle\).

Conclusion. By (1), \(\langle f,K_{\mathcal E_\beta\psi_j}(t)\rangle=\int_0^te^{-\beta(t-s)}\langle f,K_{\psi_j}(s)\rangle\,ds\). The map \(g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle\) is a continuous linear functional on \(\mathcal H\), so it commutes with the Bochner integral of the continuous function \(s\mapsto e^{-\beta(t-s)}K_{\psi_j}(s)\); the right side is therefore \(\langle f,\int_0^te^{-\beta(t-s)}K_{\psi_j}(s)\,ds\rangle\). Since \(f\) was arbitrary, the claim follows. \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(\beta\ge0\) is used only to bound the damping factor by \(1\) on the triangle, which yields the integrable majorant for Fubini's theorem.

steps.title: Transfer to the Brownian responses, scalar and vector
steps.body:
Setting. Let \(I:\mathcal H\to L^2(\mathbb P_W)\) be the isonormal map defining the scalar Brownian motion: a linear isometry with \(I(\mathbf 1_{(0,t]})=W_t\), so that \(I(g)=\int g(r)\,dW_r\) for deterministic \(g\in\mathcal H\). Let \(\tau_a g(r)=g(r-a)\), a linear isometry of \(\mathcal H\). For a continuous kernel \(k\) and \(a,t\ge0\), the scalar response is \(N_k(a,t)=I(\tau_aK_k(t))\). For \(p\) coordinates, the vector response \(\mathbf N_k(a,t)\in L^2(\mathbb P_W^{\otimes p};\mathbb R^p)\) is obtained by the spatial lift \(S\), which evaluates a scalar \(L^2\) variable on the \(i\)-th independent copy of the Brownian source and places it in the \(i\)-th coordinate: \(S(X)(\omega)=\sum_iX(\omega_i)e_i\). Both \(I\circ\tau_a\) and \(S\) are continuous linear maps.

Claim. For \(j\in\mathbb N\) and \(a,t\ge0\):

\[N_{\varphi_{j+1}}(a,t)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}N_{\psi_j}(a,s)\,ds\quad(\gamma\ge0),\qquad N_{\psi_{j+1}}(a,t)=\int_0^tN_{\psi_j}(a,s)\,ds\quad(\gamma\in\mathbb R),\]

and the same two identities hold for the vector responses \(\mathbf N\). The integrals are Bochner integrals of continuous paths in \(L^2\).

Proof. Let \(L=I\circ\tau_a\). By definition \(N_k(a,t)=L(K_k(t))\). Apply \(L\) to the identities of the previous step. A continuous linear map commutes with the Bochner integral of an integrable function, here the continuous integrand \(s\mapsto e^{-\gamma(t-s)}K_{\psi_j}(s)\) (respectively \(s\mapsto K_{\psi_j}(s)\)) on \([0,t]\); and it commutes with multiplication by the scalar \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\). Hence

\[L\bigl(K_{\varphi_{j+1}}(t)\bigr)=\int_0^tL\bigl(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}K_{\psi_j}(s)\bigr)\,ds=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}N_{\psi_j}(a,s)\,ds,\]

and similarly for the primitive identity. For the vector responses, \(\mathbf N_k(a,t)=S(N_k(a,t))\); the scalar paths \(s\mapsto N_{\psi_j}(a,s)\) are continuous, and applying the continuous linear map \(S\) to the scalar identities gives the vector identities by the same commutation. \(\square\)

All responses are built from the same Brownian increments on \((a,a+t]\), so the identities are equalities of random vectors on one probability space, not only of their laws. The boundary terms vanish because positive-index response primitives are zero at the origin. Integration by parts can therefore transfer one primitive from one convolution factor to the other without a remainder. Repeating this operation yields the full index-addition convolution identity.

KineticLangevin/GaussianFactor.lean.title: A Cholesky factor for the Gaussian response covariance
KineticLangevin/GaussianFactor.lean.summary:
A Gaussian law specified through its covariance must agree with the specified Gaussian construction to multiply independent standard normals by a Cholesky factor. This section proves that exact identity, constructs the positive-diagonal lower-triangular \(2\times2\) factor, and applies it to the strictly positive exponential Gram covariance.

An explicit lower-triangular factor of the response Gram covariance maps independent scalar standard normals to the exact sampler innovation law. The proof includes positive pivots and Gaussian measure equality.

steps.title: Identify every covariance factor by mean and covariance
steps.body:
If \(AA^\mathsf T=S\), then applying \(A\) to a standard Gaussian gives a centered Gaussian with covariance \(S\). View the matrix as a linear operator on Euclidean space. Its transpose is the adjoint, and matrix multiplication is composition. The mean passes through the continuous linear map and remains zero. The covariance pushforward is \(\langle A^\mathsf Tx,A^\mathsf Ty\rangle=\langle x,AA^\mathsf Ty\rangle\), which is the target covariance. Uniqueness of Gaussian measures with equal mean and covariance proves equality of measures, not only equality of moments.

A deterministic linear image of independent standard normals is jointly Gaussian. Its covariance is the factor times its transpose. Equality of centered Gaussian covariances determines equality of measures, which is why any verified covariance factor gives the exact response law.

Expanding its four matrix entries, using the two square-root-square identities and symmetry, gives \(LL^\mathsf T=S\). The general Gaussian-factor theorem therefore proves that this triangular factor generates exactly the target Gaussian measure.

The first pivot is positive by positive definiteness. The determinant condition makes the Schur complement positive, so both diagonal square roots are real and nonzero. Expanding the lower-triangular product verifies each matrix entry without an implicit numerical factorization assumption.
